**Surat Yusuf**, peace be upon him

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. And with Him is the help. Amin.

Its purpose is to describe the Book as making clear everything that necessitates guidance, by what has been established in what came before. In this surah comes the completeness of His knowledge of His creation, both the unseen and the witnessed, and the all-encompassing reach of His power in word and deed. This story, as you can see, is the most fitting of things for this purpose, and therefore the surah was named Surat Yusuf. And Allah knows best.

"In the name of Allah," who encompasses everything in power and knowledge. "The Most Gracious," who left no ambiguity about the generality of His mercy on the path of guidance. "The Most Merciful," who singled out His party by keeping them far from the place of ruin.

When He, glory be to Him, interwove those [previous surahs] with the stories and decisive verses He had woven into them, showing that the Qur'an descended from Him and by His leave, that none believes except whom He wills to believe, that whatever He wills comes to be, and that He demonstrated His great power over the like of what He punished the nations with (p-2), and over bringing together whom He wills and causing discord among whom He wills; and He indicated that He had decreed victory for His worshippers, so what He intends must come to pass, for to Him the whole affair returns. He followed this with this surah to clarify these aims through this great and long story, in which Yusuf, peace be upon him, met what he met from those closest to him and from others, and from estrangement and the scattering of his household. Then the outcome was his in the most complete form, because of the patience with which he armoured himself against severe trial and his entrusting of the matter to Allah, exalted is He. This serves as consolation for this Trustworthy Prophet and as an example from the brother messengers who came before him, regarding what he meets in his life from his disbelieving relatives, and after his death from those among his family who entered the religion. It is like what befell Yusuf, peace be upon him, of persecution inflicted on his descendants and the descendants of his brothers by those who had shown the greatest kindness to them. Indeed, what the disbelieving relatives of the Prophet ﷺ intended to do to him actually happened to Yusuf, peace be upon him, as Allah related in His saying: ﴿That they may confine you, or kill you, or expel you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30]. Yusuf was saved from them, so that none of him remained in their hands, except for what was the confinement in the valley of Abu Talib and the emigration by the command of the All-Wise, All-Knowing. Then Allah gave Yusuf, peace be upon him, victory over his brothers who had done that to him, and made him their ruler. So the telling of his story, following the announcement that the purpose of these stories is to strengthen the Prophet ﷺ (p-3), came in the context of his taking control of them on the Day of the Conquest, subduing their obstinacy, pardoning them, and showing kindness to them. In its allusion there is also good news that the one who is envied will be prevailed for and will rise, if he does what is most fitting and best for him. Among the benefits of mentioning it is the warning that envy is a great disease, deeply rooted in souls, to the point that by the strength of its hold, the abundance of its occurrences and the multiplicity of its forms, it may overcome people of righteousness, except those among them who hasten to repentance, the caller to success. The story was left out of its repetition, among the other stories, in order to protect the great ones from mention of what might lead to the belief in a defect, or to the directing of a slander or a disparagement, or to the easing of the disease of envy in the eyes of the rash and the contentious. He, glory be to Him, interwove it with eloquent wisdoms, and concluded it with what it produced of the establishment of the matter of the Qur'an and the clearing of this Great Prophet from accusation.

This is the connection between the two surahs. As for the connection of the first to the latter: when He, exalted is He, informed at the end of the former [surah] of His complete knowledge and all-encompassing power, the people of precedence in eloquence and the masters of rhetoric pointed to this at the beginning of this one, through what He did in His speech, in that He, exalted is He, is able to bring forth what minds and intellects will take in every direction in its meaning, despite the passing of ages, the succession of eras, the sequence of days and the lengthening of nights, and every flying creature will take flight in it, while the drives are abundant and the powers are gathered. Yet one does not stop at a fixed matter or a known intention from it, nor at a meaning that the first glance understands as its lowest sense in a way one can be confident is intended. Then it continues to bring forth from it subtle meanings whenever one repeats reflection and understanding penetrates deeply, to the point where one knows that one is unable to grasp all of its sublime meanings and subtle structures. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾.

Al-Rumani said: the verse-endings (fawasil) were not counted, because they do not resemble the verse-endings (ru'us al-ayat), since they consist of two letters, so they were treated like incomplete names. Fawasil are only counted when they are complete. As for "Ta Ha," it is counted because it resembles the endings of its verses. End of quote.

This is the view of one who went astray through inadvertence, holding that rhymed prose (saj') is intended in the Qur'an. It is a rejected view, not to be relied upon, as has been discussed in the end of Surat Bara'a. There is no difference between attributing it to poetry and attributing it to rhymed prose, because saj' is the craft of soothsayers, and that would lead to the claim that it is soothsaying, which is undoubtedly disbelief. I have elaborated on this in my book Masa'id al-Nazar, and I have explained the positions of those who count the verses (al-'adin li'l-ayat), and that their basis is revelation (tawqif), like the transmission of the readings (qira'at), and this is the same. And Allah is the Guide.

When the previous surah began by saying that this Book is muhkam (firmly decisive), and concluded with the wisdom intended in relating the reports of the messengers, and the context was to refute them in their denial of it, in His saying: ﴿Or do they say, "He has forged it"?﴾ [Hud: 13], and it indicated that it was sent down with His knowledge, this one began to complete that indication by pointing to what He possesses of exalted station and lofty rank. So, after the enigma He had placed in the disconnected letters, He, glory be to Him, followed it with a clarification which shows that, despite its difficulty, it is clear upon reflection, in His saying, alluding to what preceded of the Qur'an and to this surah: ﴿Those are﴾, meaning these great, high verses, ﴿the verses of the Book﴾, meaning the one that comprises all intended meanings.

Since the beginning of the surahs of Yunus and Hud described it with wisdom, firmness and detailed explanation, it is described here with something more specific than that, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿the Clear﴾, meaning clear in itself, that it is comprehensive and inimitable, not confused for the Arabs in any way, and clarifying all that it contains, that is all the intended meanings, for whoever reflects deeply and considers carefully; and because it is from Allah: ﴿It was not a narration that could be fabricated, but a confirmation of what was before it﴾ [Yusuf: 111], and ﴿an admonition and a reminder for the believers﴾ [Hud: 120]. Bayan (clarity) is making a meaning manifest to the self by what distinguishes it from others, and it is the aim of every wise speaker in his speech. Burhan (proof) adds to it, being the manifestation of the soundness of the meaning by what testifies to it. And abana (to make clear) is intransitive and transitive.

Then he gave the reason for "clear" with his words, using the verb "sending down" because the context concerns their denial of it, unlike the verb "making" used in az-Zukhruf, as will come: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down﴾ with the plural of majesty, that is, the Book explained in this surah, or the whole Qur'an ﴿as an Arabic Qur'an﴾. Part of it was named by this because "Qur'an" is a generic noun that applies to the whole and to a part. He gave the reason for sending it down in this way with his words: ﴿so that you may understand﴾, that is, so that you may be hopeful of being among the people of intellect, or of understanding what is required of you. Abu Hayyan said: "la'alla" (perhaps/so that) expresses hope, and in it there is the sense of causation.

This verse indicates that the Arabic tongue is the most eloquent, the most expansive, the most upright and the most just of languages, because it is established that speech, even if it is addressed specifically to one people, is general for others besides them.

(p-7) When he had made clear that He relates to him [some of] the reports of the messengers, by which his heart would be strengthened, He said, affirming and giving a reason, that it is the Book, for another reason that is observable and more specific than the first: ﴿We relate to you﴾. He magnified this story by means of the appearance of greatness, and confirmed that with His words, exalted is He: ﴿the best of narratives﴾, meaning the act of narrating, or the narrated matter itself, by following some of the account as We teach it to one another, and explaining it in the best of explanation, for it is "from qassa al-athar" (following the trace). This is to strengthen your heart, to confirm your prophethood, and to support you, in the best arrangement, the most sound order, the most complete style, the most thorough composition, and the most original method, together with what We detail through it of the pearls of wisdom and the wondrous meanings, both foundational and derivative. This is the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him. It is a long story; it is in the Torah across more than twenty leaves, and only the most skilled of their rabbis can master it. Whoever reflects on its narration, either in it or in their other histories, tastes the meaning of His words, exalted is He, ﴿the best of narratives﴾. Indeed, a group of the Jews embraced Islam because of how well it was narrated. Al-Bayhaqi related in the closing part of Dala'il al-Nubuwwa, with his chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that "a rabbi of the Jews came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ one day, and he was a reader of the Torah. He found him reciting Surat Yusuf, peace be upon him, as it was revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, in the Torah. The rabbi said [to him]: 'O Muhammad! Who taught you this?' He said: 'Allah taught it to me.' So the rabbi returned to the Jews and said [to them]: 'Do you know, by Allah, that Muhammad recites the Qur'an as it was revealed in the Torah!' He set out with a group of them until they came to him. They recognized him by the description, and they looked at the seal of prophethood between his shoulders. They began listening to his recitation of Surat Yusuf, and they marvelled at it and said: 'O Muhammad! Who taught you this?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Allah taught it to me.' At that, the people embraced Islam."

He, glorified is He, included in it, of subtle points, lessons and wisdoms, a great matter. He mentioned in it the fine conduct of Yusuf, peace be upon him, toward his brothers, his patience with their harm, his forbearance toward them, his restraint when they met, his refraining from rebuking them, and his generosity in pardoning. [It also contains mention of] the prophets, the righteous, the angels, the devils, mankind, the jinn, the cattle, the birds, the histories of kings, slaves, merchants, scholars, the ignorant, men and women, and their guile; tawhid (divine oneness), prophethood, i'jaz (the inimitability of the Qur'an), ta'bir (interpretation of dreams), politics, social conduct, the management of livelihood, and all the benefits that suit religion and worldly life. He mentioned the beloved and the one loved. He did not introduce into it anything from outside it, unlike the other stories. Its outcome was toward good and safety, the reunion of the scattered, pardon from Allah, and forgiveness of all. ﴿by what We have revealed﴾, meaning because of Our revelation ﴿to you﴾.

When the sending down of the Qur'an was the gathering of all goods, He specified the intended referent by demonstrative and proper name, and said: ﴿this Qur'an﴾, of which they said: "It is fabricated." So We follow in it stories after story, and wisdom in the wake of wisdom, so that no doubter doubts and no skeptic wavers that it is from Us and by Our leave, and its being far from confusion is clearer than the sun.

Although they knew him, peace be upon him, and recognized that he kept far from knowledge and scholars, and their conduct in denial was the conduct of one who rejects that, He said: ﴿And indeed you were﴾, meaning, indeed the matter and the account ﴿were﴾. Since his being was not for the whole of past time, He affirmed the preposition, and said: ﴿before it﴾, meaning before this Book, or before Our revelation of it to you ﴿among the unaware﴾, meaning unaware of this story and others, emphasizing this with all kinds of emphasis. It looks to His words at the end of it: ﴿And you were not with them when they resolved their affair while they were scheming﴾ [Yusuf 12:102], after its turning away from close to another, which precedes it: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾ [Hud 11:123]. The root "ghafala" in all its arrangements revolves around covering and concealment: from the sheath in which a thing is placed, so that it sees nothing of it and it sees nothing while it is within; from it comes "al-ghafla," the skin over the glans, and "al-ghufl," with a dammah, meaning land with no sign or mark; and a "dabba ghufl" is an animal with no brand, because the absence of a mark leads to ignorance of it, so it is as if it were in a sheath it does not look out of. From it also: "rajul ghufl," a man with no lineage in his reckoning, because that is closer to his being unknown. And "al-taghafful" is deception, meaning taking a thing without its being noticed. It has thus become clear that the aim of the surah is to describe the Book after wisdom and detail, by clarifying all the purposes for which it was sent down.

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: This surah is among what was related to him ﷺ of the reports of the messengers and the accounts of those before him, which contain the steadfastness bestowed in His words, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And We relate to you of the reports of the messengers that by it We strengthen your heart﴾ [Hud 11:120]. It is also among what was referred to in Surat al-An'am, as previously mentioned. It was singled out on its own and was not strung together with the stories of the messengers, although they are in one surah, because its content differs from those stories. Do you not see that those stories are about the sending of those mentioned before, peace be upon them, the manner in which their peoples received them, and the destruction of their deniers? As for this story, its essence is relief after hardship, and a presentation of the good outcome of patience. He, exalted is He, tested Ya'qub, peace be upon him, by the loss of his two sons, his sight, and the scattering of his sons. He tested Yusuf, peace be upon him, by the pit, the sale, the wife of the 'Aziz, the loss of father and brothers, and the prison. Then He tested them all with the spread of harm and scarcity of means: ﴿Harm has touched us and our family, and we have come with meager merchandise, so give us full measure and be charitable to us﴾ [Yusuf 12:88]. Then Allah rectified their condition with understanding, the gathering of their scattered, the restoring of their father's sight, the harmonizing of their hearts, the removal of what Satan had provoked, the deliverance of Yusuf, peace be upon him, from a plot he was subjected to, his being surrounded by protection, and his innocence before the king and the women. All of this resulted in beautiful patience and the majesty of certainty in the good reception of decrees through entrusting and submission, despite successive trials and long duration. Then, in the course of this glorious story, there came the repentance of the wife of the 'Aziz, her return to the truth, and her testimony for Yusuf, peace be upon him, to his freedom from everything that stains, which Allah had granted him. Then the 'Aziz chose him for himself, along with the wonders and lessons that flowed from this glorious story: ﴿Certainly in their stories is a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 12:111]. So this story stood alone in itself, and did not correspond with the stories of Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, Shu'ayb and Musa, peace be upon them all, and what happened to their nations. For this reason it was separated from them. He had already alluded, in a surah of its own, to the outcome of one who endured, was content, and submitted, so that believers would take heed of what is folded within that. He had also made clear to them, from what this surah has summarized, the allusion in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has promised those of you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession upon the earth﴾ [al-Nur 24:55], up to His words "secure." The story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, in its entirety, was most like the condition of the believers in their hardship at the beginning, their emigration, their being split from their people, and their scarcity of means, until Allah gathered their scattered. ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became by His favor brothers﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:103]. Allah bequeathed them the earth, supported them, and gave them victory, because of their noble faith and great patience. This is what necessitated the singling out of this story from those stories, and Allah knows best. As for its being mentioned after them, it is fitting for its state, and because it is news of the outcome of one who believed, took heed, and stopped at the limit set for him, so that what had befallen him did not harm him (p-12). It was not mentioned right after the stories of al-A'raf, because the remaining completion of those stories is what occurs in Surat Hud. Moreover, mentioning the states of the believers with those among the hypocrites who were with them, and their patience toward them, is something that must come first and be followed by this story in terms of the outcome of [patience] and the urging to it, as has passed. So it was delayed until after Surat Hud, peace be upon him, for the sake of this whole matter, and Allah the Exalted knows best. Furthermore, Surat Yusuf, peace be upon him, is also fitting to be mentioned right after His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, good deeds erase bad deeds; that is a reminder for those who remember﴾ [Hud 11:114], and His words: ﴿And be patient, for indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾ [Hud 11:115], and His words: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one nation﴾ [Hud 11:118], and so on, and His words: ﴿And say to those who do not believe: Work according to your position; indeed we are working﴾ [Hud 11:121], ﴿and wait; indeed we are waiting﴾ [Hud 11:122]. So reflect on that. As for its connection to the first, the remorse of the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and their acknowledgment of their wrongdoing and the excellence of Yusuf, peace be upon him, over them: ﴿Allah has preferred you over us, and indeed we were sinners﴾ [Yusuf 12:91]; and his pardon of them: ﴿No blame upon you today; may Allah forgive you﴾ [Yusuf 12:92]; and the remorse of the wife of the 'Aziz and her words: ﴿Now the truth has become manifest﴾ [Yusuf 12:51], and so on. All of this falls under the category of good erasing evil, and it is as if that were an example of what the believers know of good erasing evil (p-13). As for the connection of the surah to His words, exalted is He: ﴿And be patient, for indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾ [Hud 11:115], this is a command from Him, glorified is He, to His Prophet, peace be upon him, to be patient with his people. So it followed with the condition of Ya'qub and Yusuf, peace be upon them, and what happened to them and their patience, despite the long duration and the successive trials of Yusuf, peace be upon him, by the pit, separation from his father, and prison, until Allah delivered him in the most beautiful deliverance after the long hardships. Do you not see the words of our Prophet, when he mentioned Yusuf, peace be upon him, and bore witness to his lofty state and great patience, saying: "Had I remained in prison as long as my brother Yusuf remained, I would have answered the caller." So reflect on his excuse for him, peace be upon them both, and his testimony to the great rank of Yusuf, peace be upon them both: ﴿And We relate to you of the reports of the messengers that by it We strengthen your heart﴾ [Hud 11:120].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 3 (part 2 of 2):

When He said to him, ﴿And be patient, for indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost﴾ [Hud: 115], (follow) the condition of Ya'qub and Yusuf, upon them both be prayers and peace, among the doers of good. ﴿And We gave him Ishaq and Ya'qub﴾ [al-An'am: 84] — up to His saying ﴿And thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ [al-An'am: 84]. The verse has included the mention of Ya'qub and Yusuf, upon them both be prayers and peace, and our Prophet, upon him be the best of prayers and peace, was commanded to take them as examples in patience. He was told, ﴿So be patient as the steadfast of the messengers of determination were patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], and Yusuf, upon him be prayers and peace, is among the Ulu al-'Azm (the messengers of firm resolve). Then, the condition of Ya'qub and Yusuf, upon them both be prayers and peace, in their patience and in seeing the good outcome of patience in this world, along with what Allah prepared for them of great reward, is the most fitting thing for the condition of our Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, in enduring the Quraysh and in being separated from his homeland. Then this was followed by his victory over his enemy, the strengthening of his religion, the manifestation of his word, and his return to his city in a state which brought coolness to the eyes of the believers, and what Allah opened for him and for his companions. So reflect on this. What we have mentioned is clarified by the conclusion of the surah with His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿until when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied, Our help came to them﴾ [Yusuf: 110], the verse. The essence of all this is the command to patience and the good ends of the friends of Allah in it. As for the relation to His saying: ﴿And had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they will not cease to differ﴾ [Hud: 118], there is nothing more fitting for this nor more wondrous than the condition of virtuous brothers, sons of one father, from among the prophets of Allah, Exalted is He, and His righteous servants, in which there occurred among them such dispersion that Allah made it a lesson for those of understanding. As for the relation to the verse of warning, it is clear, and it is as if the speech, in effect, says, "Act according to your station, and wait; we will be patient over you for the duration of the patience of Ya'qub and Yusuf, upon them both be prayers and peace." Thus, by the grace of Allah, the reason for the revelation of this surah after the surah of Hud has been made clear. And Allah knows best. End.

ولَمّا تَمَّ ما أرادَ تَعالى مِن تَعْلِيلِ الوَصْفِ [بِالمُبِينِ] أبْدَلَ مِن قَوْلِهِ ”أحْسَنُ القَصَصِ“ قَوْلَهُ: ﴿إذْ﴾ أيْ نَقُصُّ عَلَيْكَ خَبَرَ إذْ، أيْ خَبَرَ يُوسُفَ إذْ ﴿قالَ يُوسُفُ﴾ أيِ ابْنُ يَعْقُوبَ إسْرائِيلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِما الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ ﴿لأبِيهِ﴾ وبَيِّنَ أدَبَهُ بِقَوْلِهِ - مُشِيرًا بِأداةِ البُعْدِ إلى أنَّ أباهُ عالِي المَنزِلَةِ جِدًّا، وإلى أنَّ الكَلامَ الآتِيَ مِمّا لَهُ وقْعٌ عَظِيمٌ، فَيَنْبَغِي أنْ يَهْتَمَّ بِسَماعِهِ والجَوابِ عَلَيْهِ، وغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِن أمْرِهِ: ﴿يا أبَتِ﴾ تاءُهُ لِلتَّأْنِيثِ (ta' al-ta'nith، أي تاء التأنيث) لِأنَّهُ يُوقَفُ عَلَيْها عِنْدَ بَعْضِ القُرّاءِ بِالهاءِ، وكَسْرَتُها عِنْدَ مَن كَسَرَ دالَّةٌ عَلى ياءِ الإضافَةِ الَّتِي عَوَّضَ عَنْها تاءُ التَّأْنِيثِ، واجْتِماعُ الكَسْرَةِ مَعَها كاجْتِماعِها مَعَ الياءِ، وفَتْحُها عِنْدَ مَن فَتْحَ عِوَضٌ عَنِ الألِفِ القائِمَةِ مَقامَ ياءِ الإضافَةِ.

ولَمّا كانَ صَغِيرًا، وكانَ المَنامُ عَظِيمًا خَطِيرًا، اقْتَضى المَقامُ التَّأْكِيدَ فَقالَ: ﴿إنِّي رَأيْتُ﴾ أيْ في مَنامِي، فَهو مِنَ الرُّؤْيا الَّتِي هي رُؤْيَةٌ في المَنامِ، (p-١٦)فَرَّقَ بَيْنَ حالِ النَّوْمِ واليَقَظَةِ في ذَلِكَ بِألِفِ التَّأْنِيثِ (alif al-ta'nith، أي ألف التأنيث) ﴿أحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا﴾ أيْ نَجْمًا كَبِيرًا ظاهِرًا جِدًّا مُضِيئًا بَرّاقًا، وفي عَدَمِ تَكْرارِ هَذِهِ القِصَّةِ في القُرْآنِ رَدٌّ عَلى مَن قالَ: كُرِّرَتْ قِصَصُ الأنْبِياءِ عَلَيْهِمُ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ تَمْكِينًا لِفَصاحَتِها بِتَرادُفِ السِّياقِ، وفي تَكْرِيرِ قِصَصِهِمْ رَدٌّ عَلى مَن قالَ: إنَّ هَذِهِ لَمْ تُكَرَّرْ لِئَلّا تُفْتَرَ فَصاحَتُها، فَكَأنَّ عَدَمَ تَكْرِيرِها لِأنَّ مَقاصِدَ السُّورِ لَمْ تَقْتَضِ ذَلِكَ - واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ.

ولَمّا كانَ لِلنَّيِّرَيْنِ اسْمانِ يَخُصّانِهِما هُما في غايَةِ الشُّهْرَةِ، قالَ مُعَظِّمًا لَهُما: ﴿والشَّمْسَ والقَمَرَ﴾ ولَمّا تَشَوَّفَتِ النَّفْسُ إلى الحالِ الَّتِي رَآهم عَلَيْها، فَكانَ كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: عَلى أيِّ حالٍ؟ وكانَتِ الرُّؤْيا باطِنَ البَصَرِ الَّذِي هو باطِنُ النَّظَرِ، فَكانَ التَّعْبِيرُ بِها لِلْإشارَةِ إلى غَرابَةِ هَذا الأمْرِ، زادَ في الإشارَةِ إلى ذَلِكَ بِإعادَةِ الفِعْلِ، وألْحَقَهُ ضَمِيرُ العُقَلاءِ لِتَكُوَنَ دَلالَتُهُ عَلى كُلٍّ مِن عَجِيبِ أمْرِ الرُّؤْيا ومِن فِعْلِ المَرْتى الَّذِي لا يَعْقِلُ فِعْلَ العُقَلاءِ مِن وجْهَيْنِ فَقِيلَ: ﴿رَأيْتُهم لِي﴾ (p-١٧)أيْ خاصَّةً ﴿ساجِدِينَ﴾ ]أجْراهم مَجْرى العُقَلاءِ لِفِعْلِ العُقَلاءِ].

Thus it is as if it were said: "What did his father say to him?" So it is said: ﴿He said﴾, knowing that his brothers would envy him because of what this vision indicates, if they were to hear it: ﴿O my dear son﴾, thereby showing his compassion toward him, and he emphasized the prohibition by making the idgham (assimilation) apparent, saying: ﴿Do not relate your vision﴾, that is, this one, ﴿to your brothers﴾. Then he gave the reason for the prohibition with his words: ﴿lest they devise a plot﴾, that is, lest they contrive ﴿against you a plot﴾, that is, one aimed specifically at you, so the lam is for specification (ikhtisas).

In the verse there is evidence that there is no prohibition on backbiting (ghibah) for the sake of giving sincere advice; rather, it is among the things that are recommended. Al-Rummani said: The ru'ya (vision) is the perception of a meaning in sleep in the manner of an imagined seeing, because the intellect is overwhelmed by sleep; so when a person conceives of a meaning, he imagines that he sees it. And Imam al-Razi said in al-Lawami': it is the quiescence of the outward senses from perception and sensation, and the movement of the inner faculties toward the perceptive faculties. For the human soul has outward senses and inward faculties; when the outward senses become still, the inward senses are employed in perceiving unseen matters. Sometimes one perceives them in the form they actually have, so it needs no interpretation; and sometimes one sees them in an imitative form suitable to them, so it needs interpretation. An example of the first is the vision of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he entered the Sacred Mosque; and the second is like the vision of Yusuf, upon him be peace, this one.

Al-Rummani also said: a true vision has an interpretation, while a false vision has no interpretation, and that is the end of his words. This applies to one whose heart sleeps, and those other than the prophets, upon them be peace.

Since it was the customary practice that the compassion of brothers prevents such things, he gave the reason for it, bringing him near, with his words: ﴿Indeed, Satan﴾, that is, the burnt and distanced one, ﴿is to man﴾, that is, to mankind in general, and especially to its great ones, ﴿a clear enemy﴾, that is, manifest in enmity and making it clear to everyone who has understanding; so he sows enmity by what he presents to them of the loss of fortunes through abandoning it. In the verse there is evidence that the matter of visions is problematic, so one should not relate it except to a compassionate, sincere advisor.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 6:

When Ya'qub, upon him be peace, knew from this vision what his son would attain of prophethood and kingship, he said: ﴿And thus﴾, meaning: your Lord has chosen you to be informed of this great vision, which indicates nobility and honour. He gave an example of what He has chosen you for by saying ﴿will choose you﴾, meaning: will select you and gather for you the highest of matters. ﴿Your Lord﴾, the One who nurtures you with kindness, for kingship and prophethood, ﴿and will teach you﴾ ﴿of the interpretation of events﴾ [of] dreams and other things, of the books of Allah, the practices (sunan) of the prophets, and the hidden meanings indicated by created beings, spiritual and corporeal, (p-19) because kingship and prophethood cannot stand except with knowledge and with the ultimate interpretation to which the meaning returns. This is the understanding of narrations (fiqh al-hadith), which is wisdom, because it is the manifestation of that to which its matter is ultimately directed, and on which its benefit rests; and its use is most frequent in regard to dreams. ﴿And complete His favour﴾ through prophethood ﴿upon you﴾ through justice and adherence to the upright path, ﴿and upon the family of Ya'qub﴾, meaning all your brothers and whoever of their offspring Allah wills, so that He makes their favour in this world connected with the favour of the Hereafter. This is because in this vision he expressed them by the stars guided by them. The word "al" (family) is used only for one who has standing and nobility, and its attribution is restricted to those who can speak. Al-Raghib said: As for "al al-salib" (the family of the cross), if its transmission is sound, it is anomalous; and "ahl" (people) is used for one who has no standing.  ﴿as He completed it upon your two fathers﴾

Since their existence did not extend into the past, he introduced the preposition and said: ﴿before﴾, meaning: [before] this time. Then he specified the two fathers by their grandfather and their father's grandfather, saying: ﴿Ibrahim﴾, meaning: with friendship (khullah) and other honours. ﴿and Ishaq﴾ with prophethood, and He made the prophets and the kings among his descendants. The completion of favour is the judgment that it endures in its purity, free from any defect that would diminish it.

Since this cannot be done except through knowledge encompassing all causes, so that from them what is suitable is established, and through wisdom by which He governs that cause so that (p-20) no other cause opposes it, and since the context called for knowledge to be mentioned first because of what was mentioned of the knowledge of interpretation, together with what preceded from His saying at the end of that surah: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Hud: 123], and the like of that at the beginning of this, he said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is All-Knowing﴾, meaning: perfect in knowledge, ﴿All-Wise﴾, meaning: perfect in wisdom, which is placing things in their most perfect positions.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 7:

When that happened, the listener anticipated what would occur between him and his brothers: would he conceal the vision from them or inform them of it? And under both possibilities, what would result? So He said, answering one who seems to have asked, "What was the matter with them?", opening the statement with the particle of anticipation and confirmation after the oath particle (lam al-qasam), as emphasis for the matter and as informing that it was in the most perfect manner: ﴿Certainly there was﴾, i.e., an occurrence that was in its most wise placement, ﴿in Joseph and his brothers﴾, i.e., because of this vision and what came of its interpretation and the causes of that, ﴿signs﴾, i.e., great indications, showing the Oneness of God the Exalted and the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and other things that the story contains, ﴿for those who ask﴾, [i.e.,] those who inquire about them, from Quraysh, the Jews, and others. These are also signs of God's greatness and power in the fulfillment of Joseph's vision (peace be upon him), his deliverance from those who plotted against him, his protection, and the elevation of his affair. By "his brothers" here is meant the ten who were from his father, and they are: Ruben and Simeon (with an initial letter bearing a dot above, i.e., shīn), Levi, Judah, Zebulun (with a zayn and a bāʾ), Issachar (with a hamza, a kasra, a yāʾ, a seen, and a khāʾ bearing a dot), Dan (with an unpointed letter), and Gad (with a jīm), between her and the kāf; Asher (with a hamza with a madda, a shīn bearing a dot, then a yāʾ, and an unpointed letter), and Naphtali (with a fatḥa on the nūn, a sukūn on the fāʾ, a tāʾ with two dots above, and a lām followed by a yāʾ). And his full brother Benjamin (with a ḍamma on the bāʾ). Thus he mentioned them in the Torah, and I have carefully recited their names as the scholars of it have done; this was previously discussed in al-Baqara with additional detail. And the āyah: the indication of the great matters that occurred; similar to it are ʿalāma (sign) and ʿibra (lesson), and ḥujja (proof) is more specific than them, because it is the reliable evidence that necessitates confidence in the soundness of the meaning in which there is wonder.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 8:

Having established that, he began with mentioning the verses that occur within the setting of this existence, saying: ﴿When they said﴾, i.e., that was when the brothers said, after he (Joseph) had related the dream to them and Satan had embellished (the matter) for them — as Ya'qub, upon him be blessings and peace, had suspected — swearing oaths, to indicate the utmost concern with this statement, and that it was among the things that moved them to the utmost degree of agitation. Or it is the emphatic lam of inception (lam al-ibtida'), confirming and verifying the content of the sentence: ﴿Surely Yusuf and his brother﴾, i.e., his full brother Binyamin, ﴿are dearer﴾ — and it is (used) in the singular, because the elative form (af'al) used with the comparative, whether masculine or feminine, is (used) in the same way for one and for more than one when it is not definite and not in a construct state — ﴿to our father than us﴾, i.e., he loves the two of them more than he loves us. And love (hubb) is an inclination that calls for willing good and benefit for the beloved, unlike desire (shahwa), which is the soul's inclination and its striving toward what contains its pleasure. ﴿And we are a band﴾ — while the situation is that we are — i.e., strong in ourselves, and some of us support others; as for the two of them, they are young children with no sufficiency in them. The "'usba" (band) is from ten to forty. So it is as if it were said: "Then what?" — on the assumption that the two of them are dearer to him. They said, emphasizing, because the state of their father in uprightness and guidance was a call to (make them) deny (it): ﴿Indeed, our father is in manifest error﴾, i.e., in going astray from the path of rightness in that matter, ﴿manifest﴾, in that he preferred the two of them over us. The nearness that calls for love is equal in all of us, since we are equal in sonship, and we have a distinction that requires our being preferred, namely that we are a band: we have from benefit to him, and defending him, and sufficiency, what they do not have. Abu Hayyan said: "Ahabb" is an elative (af'al al-tafdil), and it is formed irregularly from the passive participle (mafʿul), and for that reason it is governed by "ila" (to), because when the thing it is connected to is the agent in meaning, it is governed by "ila," and when it is the object, it is governed by "fi." You say: "Zayd is dearer to 'Amr than Khalid," so the pronoun in "ahabb" is the object in meaning, and 'Amr is the lover. And when you say: "Zayd is dearer in 'Amr than Khalid," the pronoun is the agent and 'Amr is the beloved, and Khalid, in the first example, is the beloved, and in the second example is the agent. He said: "Al-dalal (error) here is al-huda (guidance)" — related by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both — end of quotation.

When that had come about, and they understood that what most preoccupied their father with them was the love of Yusuf (peace be upon him), while the love of his brother was merely secondary, it was as if they consulted among themselves, saying: "This has been settled; so what will you do?" Then one of them said, or whoever Allah willed from among them: ﴿Kill Yusuf⟩. The original meaning of qatl (killing) is to cause movement to cease through stillness. ﴿Or cast him out to some land⟩. They connected the verb without a preposition, and they made the noun indefinite to indicate that it is an unknown, remote land in which he would perish. The speaker meant by this: if you refrain from directly killing him with your own hands.

Since the implied condition was: "If you do that," he answered him with his words: ﴿Your father's face will be free for you⟩, that is, exclusively for you, ﴿your father's face⟩, that is, his attention toward you, his turning to you, your intention (p-24) and your purpose. Since the people of religion do not neglect the reform of their religion, for it is the focal point of their affairs, they said: ﴿and after him you will be a people⟩, that is, you will be in a state of the utmost firmness; and since they knew that death is unavoidable, which prevents them from continuing into the future time, they introduced the preposition and said: ﴿after him⟩, that is, after Yusuf (peace be upon him), ﴿a people⟩, that is, possessing energy and strength to undertake affairs, ﴿righteous⟩, that is, deeply established in the quality of righteousness and steadfast upon a path that calls to wisdom, through the establishment of harmony among you and the winning of the father's love by greatly honoring him, and through repenting of a single sin which would be the cause of removing what compels the disease of envy, which entails a chain of sins of hatred, estrangement and enmity. Thus they resolved to repent before the sin was committed.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 10:

So it is as if it were said: "This is among the most astonishing of wonders, from any relatives at all, let alone brothers." Then what did they say upon hearing it? It is said: ﴿A speaker said﴾. Since the context is that the entire matter belongs to Allah, for He saves whom He wills by what He wills, the purpose was not directed to specifying the one through whom salvation came. So he spoke indefinitely, indicating that counsel of sincere advice must be given by whoever speaks it, and that a person should not belittle himself in giving sincere advice under any circumstances. ﴿A speaker﴾ then was specified to some degree, and it said: ﴿from among them﴾, that is, from among the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him. ﴿Do not kill Yusuf﴾, neither with your own hands nor by casting him into destruction. For killing is the greatest of the major sins after shirk. It is as if there was not in that region of theirs except one well, so he identified it and said: ﴿And throw him﴾. It is as if there was water in it and a place where one could settle, but there was no water in it. So he meant by his words ﴿into the darkness of the well﴾, that is, its depth, hidden from the eyes, for that is sufficient for the intended purpose. ﴿And if you do so, some travelers will pick him up﴾, the plural of sayyar, which is one who travels extensively. This is ﴿if you are indeed﴾ bound to be ﴿doing﴾ what you intend of removing him from his father so that his face may be free for you. And al-jubb: the well that has not been lined with stone, for its earth has been cut away from it until the water was reached. And from Abu 'Amr: this was before they became prophets.

Then it was as if it were said: "Indeed, this is good, inasmuch as it turned them away from killing him. Did they persist in it, or did one of them rise up to draw them away from it out of the impulse of kinship and the affection of blood-relation?" It was said: "Rather, they persisted, because they ﴿said﴾, employing the stratagem to reach him, asking in the manner of amazement, because he had sensed evil from them and was warning them about him: ﴿O our father, what is wrong with you﴾, meaning: what is the matter with you, in the state in which you ﴿do not trust us with Joseph﴾, "while" the situation is ﴿indeed we are sincere advisers to him﴾. Sincerity (nuṣḥ) is a sign of trustworthiness and its cause; for this reason they were paired in His saying ﴿a trustworthy sincere adviser﴾ [al-A'raf: 68]. Security (amn) is the calm of the soul in the absence of evil, and its cause is the prolonged respite in a matter that may be cut off by something disliked, so that deception by that respite occurs among the ignorant. Its opposite is fear (khawf), which is the (p-26) agitation of the soul at what is expected of harm. Sincerity (nuṣḥ) is the purifying of an action from a corruption that is intended; its opposite is deceit (ghish). The reciters agreed on dropping the vowel of nominative case in ﴿ta'manna﴾ and on assimilating its nūn after it was made quiescent, following the orthography; some of them with full assimilation, some with ishmām, and some with rawm, indicating the negation of any unease in his heart concerning him, upon them both be prayers and peace, regarding his safety from them, in the most eloquent manner, although they were worthy of his being at ease with them to the utmost degree of ease. Had the vowel of nominative case appeared with any of the reciters, this subtle and wondrous allusion to this point would have been lost.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 12:

When this was the place where it would be said: "For what purpose would that be?", they answered it: ﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾ to our pasture, if you send him [with us] ﴿he will enjoy himself﴾, that is: we will eat and drink in the countryside and expand in abundance, ﴿and he will play﴾, that is: we will do what the souls desire of the permissible things, leaving off seriousness (al-jidd), which is everything that involves hardship and toil, for that is what he went on with; ﴿and indeed we will be his guardians﴾, that is: thorough in guarding him. Abu Hayyan said: "Ghadan" is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), and it is an adverb of the future, applied to the day that follows your day and to the future time without restriction. The origin of "ghad" is "ghadaw," and its final letter was deleted. End.

(p-27) So it is as if it was asked: "What did he say to them?" It was answered: ﴿He said﴾. What he said did not increase their hearts' rancor, because what they had said to him was such that he would be delighted by it, since Yusuf, peace be upon him, was pleased with it. ﴿Indeed, it grieves me﴾, meaning a grief that is apparent and certain, as indicated by the clear pronunciation of the nun in "لَيَحْزُنُنِي" and the affirmation of the lam of commencement (لامَ الِابْتِداءِ, the emphatic lam). ﴿That you take him away﴾, meaning that the taking him away would be renewed in any form, because I cannot bear being parted from him, even for a moment. He opened for them a door through which they could argue when they carried out what they intended, by his saying, combining the two hardships of the inner self and the trial, [as they said] (مُؤَكَّلٌ بِالمَنطِقِ). ﴿And I fear﴾, meaning that if you take him away and occupy yourselves with what you mentioned, ﴿that the wolf will eat him﴾, meaning this kind of animal seems to have been abundant in their land. ﴿While you are heedless of him﴾, meaning specifically, ﴿ghafilun﴾, meaning deeply immersed in heedlessness, because of your preoccupation with what concerns you of the interests of pasturing.

Al-Huzn (grief) is the heart's state over what has happened of separation from the beloved, and it grows greater when the separation leads to what is hated. Al-Akl (eating) is cutting food by chewing, which is followed by swallowing.

Thus it is as if it were said: their coming with the like of this is a marvel. "So what did they say?" It is said: **﴿They said﴾**, answering the second matter in a way that softens the father regarding sending him, emphasizing so that his heart would be at ease, indicating the oath by its lam: **﴿Verily, if the wolf devours him, while we are a band﴾**, i.e., while the situation is that we are **"ʿuṣbah"** (a band), i.e., strong men, some of whom support others; and they answered the oath with what sufficed in place of the answer of the condition: **﴿Indeed, then we would surely be losers﴾**, i.e., if this is the case, we would be complete (p-28) in loss, because if we lose our brother, we are even more prone to losing our other possessions. And they turned away from answering the first matter, because it could only be answered with something that would stir his chest and make him know that they, on account of his preference in love, were in an extreme state of envy that cannot be described; and at least they would say: "What is the meanness in parting with him one day, and the generosity in parting with us every day?" And that is among the things that would stand between them and their aim.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 15:

So it is as if it were said: "This plot is great and a grave matter. What did their father do?" It is said: He answered their request and sent him with them. ﴿So when they had set off﴾, joining their departure ﴿with him and agreed﴾, that is, all of them, and each one of them agreed by resolving firmly and truly; and the agreement (ijma') upon an action is the resolve to do it when all the motives gather together. ﴿To put him﴾, and al-ja'l (putting, making) is the bringing about of that by which a thing comes to be in a state other than what it was; its equivalent is al-tasyir (rendering) and al-'amal (doing). ﴿into the depths of the well﴾. They did that without any obstacle. However, since this answer was extremely clear, because the situation indicates it, it was left out, for when they had agreed upon it, it is known that there was no obstacle for them to prevent it. Then He joined to this omitted answer, which is in the force of what is spoken, His saying: ﴿And We revealed﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿to him﴾, that is, to Yusuf, upon him be peace.

Since being saved from it was very remote, His saying ﴿You will surely inform them﴾ emphasized it for him, that is, you will inform them with a great information in a manner whose like is rare in its majesty, ﴿of this affair of theirs﴾, that is, what they did to you, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ — because of the loftiness of your station, the greatness of your authority, the remoteness of your condition from their imaginings, and the long period of time that changes appearances and alters forms and shapes — that you are Yusuf. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj, as transmitted by al-Rummani. Al-shu'ur (perception) is the apprehension of a thing, like a hair in its fineness, and from it come al-mashi'ir (the sensory organs) in the body. Yusuf, upon him be peace, was twelve years old when they threw him into the well, as said by al-Hasan. They said: The confirmation of this is that when they entered upon him seeking provisions, he asked for the drinking-cup, placed it on his hands, then tapped it and understood, and said: "Indeed this cup tells me that you had a brother from your father called Yusuf, and your father used to favor him over you, and you took him away and threw him into the depths of the well, and you told your father: 'The wolf ate him.'"

And when it was known that after this act there is nothing but excuse-making, he connected to the implied answer his saying: ﴿And they came to their father at nightfall﴾ — without Yusuf, upon him be peace — ﴿weeping﴾ — in the darkness of the night, lest their father scrutinize their faces when he sees them in the light of day, (faces) contrary to what they brought of excuses. It has been said: "Do not seek a need at night, for shame is in the eyes; and do not make excuse by day for a sin, lest you stammer in your excuse." The verse indicates that weeping does not prove sincerity, since pretence is possible. ﴿Weeping﴾: al-bukaa' (weeping) is the flow of tears from the eye at a state of sorrow.

So it is as if it were said: "If they weep, weeping is rightfully theirs, out of fear of God and compassion for the brother. But what will they say when their father asks them about its cause?" So it was said: ﴿They said, "O our father..."﴾.

Since they knew that he, peace be upon him, would not believe them, owing to the light of his heart (*nur al-qalb*) and the soundness of his discernment (*firasa*), and because of the suspicion they themselves had incurred, they emphasized their claim and said: ﴿Indeed, we went racing (*nastabiq*)﴾, meaning we brought about a race with the utmost eagerness on each of our parts. ﴿And we left Joseph﴾, our brother, ﴿by our belongings﴾, meaning by what was with us of the things we needed at that time, such as clothing, provisions, and the like. ﴿So the wolf ate him﴾, meaning his being left alone resulted in the wolf eating him. ﴿And you would not believe us﴾, meaning you would not accept us as truthful in our report, ﴿even if we were﴾, meaning even if it were a state innate to us, ﴿truthful﴾, meaning among the people of truthfulness and trustworthiness in your knowledge, (p-31) because you had never tested us in a lie, nor had you ever known from us anything of it, whether in earnest or in play.

When they knew that he would not believe them, for several reasons, among them his sound physiognomic insight through the light of the heart and the strength of his intuition; and among them that a lie in itself never lacks evidence of its falsehood; and among them that the doubter almost betrays himself, they resorted to a stratagem of emphasis, using something that would make their claim seem plausible. So God, exalted be He, said, relating about them: ﴿And they came upon his shirt﴾, i.e., Yusuf, peace be upon him, ﴿with false blood﴾, i.e., falsified blood. He used the verbal noun for it as an intensifier, because it does not correspond to reality. They claimed it was the blood of Yusuf, peace be upon him, but the reality was the blood of a young goat which they had slaughtered and smeared on the shirt. This is transmitted by al-Rummani from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and from Mujahid.

He said: "Blood" (dam) is a reddish, flowing substance which naturally runs in the veins of living creatures, and it has properties perceived by sight: it quivers, it is viscous, and it is smooth.

It is narrated that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, took the shirt from them and placed it over his face, and wept until his face was stained with the blood of the shirt, and said: "By Allah, I have never seen a wolf more gentle than this one today: it ate my son but did not tear his shirt."

There were three signs in the shirt: its indication of their lying; its indication of Yusuf's truthfulness, in that it was torn from behind; and the return of sight to his father through it.

It is as if it were asked: "Did he believe them?" It is answered: "No!" Because the custom in such a matter is that it does not devour him entirely, so something of him must remain by which it is known that it is him. Had it been so, they would have brought it to clear their names, and to bury it in their cemetery along with the rest of their forebears. He was able to demand this of them, but he knew that they had said this only after a firm resolve upon unbearable matters. So he feared that opening the inquiry would bring greater evils than the dreaded matter they had brought, as is shown by His saying after that: ﴿So search for Yusuf and his brother﴾ [Yusuf: 87], and the like.

It is as if it were asked: "Then what did he say?" It is answered: ﴿He said, "Nay, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you"﴾, i.e., he did not eat him, the wolf. Rather, ﴿sawwalat﴾ means "adorned and made easy," from as-sawl, which is relaxation. ﴿For you, your souls, an affair﴾, i.e., a great matter by which you have removed Yusuf. ﴿So patience is fitting﴾, i.e., there results from this grave calamity that there will be patience ﴿beautiful﴾ from me, which is that patience in which there is no complaint to creatures. ﴿And Allah﴾, i.e., the One encompassing in knowledge and power, ﴿is the One whose help is sought﴾, i.e., the One from whom aid is sought ﴿against﴾ bearing ﴿what you describe﴾ of the destruction of Yusuf, peace be upon him.

It should not be said that they combined the attributes of the hypocrite, namely: "When he promises he breaks it, when he speaks he lies, and when he is entrusted he betrays." This is because it occurred from them once, whereas the hypocrite does it constantly or in most of his states.

The two roots of sawwala, through their permutations, are: the five permutations of s-w-l, namely la-sa, sa-la, wa-sa-la, la-wa-sa, and sa-wa-la; and the five permutations of s-y-l, namely la-si, ya-sa-l, say-a-la, sa-li, and la-ya-sa. Both revolve around what one desires to obtain, and what it entails: pleasant living, adornment, coolness of heart, firmness, softness, treatment, deception, and constancy. From the hope for the desired thing comes as-su'l (with waw), and it may be spelled with a hamza, meaning "what is sought." Al-wasilah means rank and standing in the sight of a king. Al-Qazzaz said: it is said that tawassaltu and tawassaltu have the same meaning, and al-wasilah also means need. Wasala fulan means he sought a means of access. Al-lu'as means a claw. From action and treatment: tawassala bi-kadha means he drew near by such a thing. Al-lawas means eating; la'asa al-shay' fi fihi bi-lisanihi means he turned it in his mouth with his tongue. Walisat al-naqah fi mishyatiha talis wa lisanan means the she-camel struck from the neck in her gait.

From pleasant living: fulan fi salwah min al-'aysh means he is in a comfortable ease of life, i.e., a pleasantness that consoles him from worry. From this comes al-salwa, which is a well-known bird, and is also honey. Aslá al-qawm means they felt safe from the beast.

From adornment: sawwalat lahu nafsuhu kadha means his soul made such a thing appealing to him, so he sought it. From coolness of heart: salawtu 'an al-shay' means I forgot the thing when your heart abandoned it after it had inclined to it. Saqaytani minka salwah means you consoled my soul regarding you. Al-layas, with a vowel, means heedlessness. Al-alyas is the cuckold who has no jealousy, and the one of good character. Talayasa 'anhu means he closed his eyes to it.

From softness: al-salyu is the membrane in which the young is contained; it is a ya-root, and one says from it: sallaytu al-shah, like ridiy salī, meaning the ewe's membrane was cut. From it comes as-sawal, which is looseness in the joints of a sheep. Al-sahab al-aswal is the cloud that is loose because of the abundance of its water. Al-aswal means the relaxed one. From it comes laysa, the sister of kana, because when a thing increases in softness it may sometimes be counted as non-existent. From it comes sala, meaning flowed. Al-sa'ilah of the cheek is the one moderate in the bridge of the nose. Asala gharar al-nasl means he lengthened it. As-sillan, with a kasra, is the base of the sword's blade. As-sayyalah is a plant with long white thorns; when it is pulled out, milk comes forth from it; or it means what grows long of the samur tree.

From deception: al-wals, which is betrayal; al-muwalasah means flattery; and at-tawassul means theft.

From constancy: al-layas, with a vowel, and al-mutalayis mean the slow one, which is also from softness. Al-alyas is the one who never leaves his dwelling.

From firmness: al-layas, with a vowel, which is courage; he is alyas. Al-alyas is a camel that carries what is loaded, and a lion. Waqa'u fi salā jamal means a difficult matter, because a camel has no salā. The salā in the belly is cut off, like "balagha al-sikkinu al-'azm," the knife reached the bone. It is possible that from firmness also comes al-yasl, with a fatha and sukun, meaning a hand, i.e., a group of the manifest Quraysh; and al-basl, with a single bā', means the other hand. Lasa means he ate very vigorously.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 19:

When their scheme had been completed and they had kindled in their father [peace be upon him] the fire of grief, the soul turned to the news of Yusuf (peace and blessings be upon him), as indicated by His saying: ﴿You will surely inform them﴾ [Yusuf: 15], and so on. God, Exalted, then tells of that in its causes: ﴿And there came a caravan﴾, that is, a people traveling swiftly to the land in which they had cast Yusuf (peace and blessings be upon him) into its well. ﴿Then they sent their warid (water-seeker)﴾, that is, their messenger whom they send to take charge of the water and go to the well so that it may be drawn for them. ﴿So he let down his bucket﴾ into it, that is, he sent it into the well so that it would fill it. As for "dalla" (to lower), it means he brought it up full. Then Yusuf (peace and blessings be upon him) held onto it, and he drew him up. It is as if it were said: what did he say when he lowered the bucket for the water? Yusuf clung to the rope, and he raised him, and behold, there was a person most beautiful in appearance. It was said: ﴿He said﴾, that is, the warid informed his companions of the good news: ﴿O good news!﴾, that is, this is your time, so come forth. It is as if it were said: why did he call out "good news"? He said: ﴿This is a boy﴾, and he brought him to his group, and they rejoiced at him as he had rejoiced. ﴿And they concealed him﴾, that is, the warid and his companions, ﴿as merchandise﴾, that is, while he was, in their supposition, a commodity they would trade in. ﴿And God﴾, that is, the All-Encompassing in knowledge and power, ﴿is All-Knowing﴾, that is, of perfect knowledge, ﴿of what they do﴾, even though they concealed him.

Abu Hayyan said, and excellent was what he said: his clinging to the rope indicates his youth, for had he been eighteen or seventeen the rope would generally not have borne him. The word "ghulam" (boy) supports this, since it is applied to him literally from age two up to puberty, and it may also be applied to a full-grown man. [End.]

[p. 37] Since their delight in him, together with his beauty, dignity and splendour, made it likely that they would compete for him and bid up his price, God, exalted is He, informed us that they did not do this, so that it would be known that all of his affairs follow one pattern in breaking customary norms. He said: ﴿And they sold him﴾. That is, the caravan (al-sayyara) persisted and insisted in concealing him as merchandise, until they sold him to the Chieftain (al-'Aziz). The meaning of persistence is why He expressed it with *shara* rather than *baa'a* (sold). It is possible that *shara* here means *ishtara* (bought), i.e. the caravan bought him from his brothers ﴿for a price﴾, which is the exchange, in gold or silver, and it may be said of other things by analogy ﴿paltry﴾, that is, few.

The root *sh-r-y* is ya'i-radical in its three permutations (sh-r-y, sh-y-r, r-y-sh), waw-radical in its six (sh-w-r, sh-r-w, w-sh-r, w-r-sh, r-sh-w, r-w-sh), and hamza-radical in its three ('-r-sh, '-sh-r, r-sh-'). All revolve around *al-lujaja* (obstinacy), which is persistence in spreading out, and which entails the clarifying of that matter. Strength at times and weakness at others is entailed by it. Among its unrestricted uses: *sharaytu al-shay'* means I owned the thing by sale; *sharaytuhu* means I removed my ownership of it by means of it; likewise *ishtaraytu* in both senses. The noun is *al-shira'* with a long vowel, and it may be shortened. Thus persistence and spreading occur sometimes by removal and sometimes by acquisition. Whoever abandons one thing and clings to another has bought it. *Shaara-hu* (mutual trading) [*musharaa*]: he bargained with him. *Shara wa* (also *shara*) the thing: its like; its waw is substituted from a ya', as if taken from the substitute of the sold item, since one seeks equivalence in it. It is broader than what has no equal. *Shara* the lightning: it flashed out widely. Zayd: he became angry and persisted until he flared up in anger. The horse in its running: it reached its full extent. *Istasha al-rajul*: he became obstinate. *Al-barq*: it shone. *Al-mushara'a*: skill, [and argument] and bargaining. *Al-shir'a* (like *ghaniyya*): the way and the nature; and it seems this is the root meaning from which its branches stem, because nature is the likely cause of obstinacy. *Shara al-thawb* and *al-lahm* and *al-iqt* (curds): he spread them out, i.e. he placed them spread on a mat or something else so they would dry. *Shara fulanan*: he mocked him or humiliated him, as if he persisted with him until he subdued him. *Shara bi-nafsihi 'an al-qawm*: he went before them and fought on their behalf, or went to the ruler and spoke on their behalf. *Al-shara* (like *'ala*): the mountain, because of its height in spreading; the road, because of spreading in it; a road at Salma with many lions; a mountain in Tihama with many beasts of prey, either because they spread through it, or because the one who hides in it is the strongest and most stubborn of people. A mountain in Najd of the Tayy tribe, and the region; it is also read with a long vowel. *Ashra-hu*: he wearied him and inclined him, because of the spreading of what is in it. *Ashra al-jumal*: its wool split, i.e. its fleece. *Baynahum*: he incited them. *Shara al-ba'ir* in its walking: it hastened. *Shara al-faras* in its bridle: when he pulled it. *Al-shariyya* (like *ghaniyya*): among women, those who bear only females, as if they persisted in inclination with their nature, which is femininity, and were obstinate in it; or it returns to the weakness that accompanies need. *Al-mushtari*: a star because of its brilliance, and a bird because of the shining of its wing and its spreading. *Ashwarra*: he was agitated. *Shara zimam al-naqa*: its halter became much agitated; this is from spreading and from weakness. *Istasharat al-umur*: they grew and became great. *Shara jiluduhu*: small red pustules afflicted him, causing a burning and distressing itch, which generally arises in one outbreak and intensifies at night; as if it was named for its spreading over the whole body and its strength. *Tasharra al-qawm*: they scattered. *Tasharra al-sahab*: the clouds dispersed. *Al-shara*: the colocynth tree, or the colocynth itself; and the palm sprouts from the pit, as if its growth without human cause is obstinate. *Al-shiryan*: from the trees of bows, as if for its strength and its scattering of arrows when they are shot from it; and the singular of *al-sharayin* is the pulsing veins, because of their strength and spreading. *Shiyar* (with kasra): Saturday, because it is the first day on which creation began, as if creation spread from it. *Al-rish* (with kasra): feathers of a bird, well known, like *al-rash*, because it spreads over its whole body and it has the strength to spread them whenever it wishes; this is the cause of its welfare and its strength to spread in the air. From it: *al-rish* and *al-riyash*: luxurious clothing, abundance and livelihood. *Dhat al-rish*: a plant like *al-qaysum*. *Rasha al-sadiq*: he fed him, gave him drink and clothing, and improved his condition. *Kala rish* (like *hayyin* and *hayyin*): abundant in leaves. *Al-rish* (vowelled): abundance of hair in the ears and face. *Al-muraysh* (like *mu'azzam*): a shaggy camel. *Rashsha al-sahm*: he fletched it, i.e. he attached feathers to it at the notch, so that it thereby had the strength of spreading. *Rumh rashin*: a spear shaft, likened to feathers in its thinness. *Al-muraysh*: a weak man with firm loins. It is also: striped cloth, because of its variegation like feathers. It is also: a thin-fleshed person. A she-camel *muraysha*: thin-fleshed, because that is stronger for her in walking. *Al-muraysh* also: a litter fitted with leather, because that is the cause of its strength, and it has for it what feathers and sinew have. *Al-shiwar*, *al-shura*, *al-shara*: beauty, loveliness, appearance, clothing, fatness and adornment. *Istasha fulan*: he wore fine clothing, as if it came from feathers, and because it is generally bound with obstinacy and spreading. *Istasharat al-ibil* and took its *mishwar* (pasture-run): it grew fat. *Al-mishwar* (with kasra): the place where animals are displayed. *Shara-ha*: he broke it in, i.e. he spread her out so that she would be strong for what is required of her. *Shara al-'asal* and *istasharahu*: he extracted it from the honeycomb, for emphasis in that. *Al-shara*, with the first letter of the root vowelled with fatha and it may be kasra: honey. *Al-mishwar*: what one extracts with it. Whatever the animal leaves of its fodder: arabized; as if it was likened to what remains of the extracted honey which is not counted. Or its origin is *nishwar* with nun, then the mim was substituted for it because of their closeness; if that is so, it is from *nashr*. *Al-shuwar* (triptote): household goods, because they spread in the house. The man's member, his testicles and his anus, because of what spreads from each of them. *Shawara bi-fulan*: he did an act to him that causes shame, as if he persisted in that until he cut off his spreading in apology. *Tashawwara al-rajul*: he was embarrassed, as if he is the reflexive of *shawwartuhu*. *Shawara ilayhi*: he gestured, like *ashara*, because of the spreading of what he indicated. *Ashara al-nar*: he raised it. *Al-shawaran*: safflower, because of its brilliance. A mountain near the Aqiq of Medina, which has much rainwater, because of its strength in holding it and the strength of those who dwell in it in spreading in it. *Khayl shiyar*: fat and handsome horses. *Al-shura* (vowelled with damma): a fat she-camel, because of her strength in spreading; with fatha: a bashful woman, because of her spreading and height. *Ashartu 'alayhi bi-kadha*: I commanded him, for spreading in speech before the gesture, for reaching a decision; the noun is *al-mashura*; or it is from *al-ishara*, which is moving the hand or eyebrow or the like toward the one indicated. *Al-rashwa* (triptote): the bribe. *Rashahu*: he gave it to him; so it spreads the act, and none does that except one who is obstinate in the matter; it may be traced back to weakness. *Al-rA'ish*: the intermediary between the briber and the bribed. *Istarsha*: he sought a bribe. *Al-fasil*: the calf seeking suckling. *Arshiyat al-yaqtin* and *al-hanzal*: their threads, because they spread, and he likened them to *al-rasha'*, with kasra and the long vowel, which is the rope. *Al-rishan* (like *ghina*), the foal and the camel that stops, and the herder shouts: *irshu-hu*, or *arshihi, arshihi*, and it scratches its *khawran*, i.e. its dung, with its hand, and it runs. Ibn Faris said: *al-khawran* is the course of dung in the animal. *Arshá*: he did that. *Al-qawm fi dammihi*: they shared in his blood, because that is spreading. *Bi-silahihim fihi*: they thrust their weapons into it. *Al-rasha*: a plant drunk to aid walking. From its hamza-radical: *rasha'a*: he had intercourse; and no one is more obstinate than the one prepared for intercourse, and spreading is in it too. *Rasha'at al-zabya*: she gave birth. *Al-rasha'* (vowelled with fatha): a name for the gazelle when it grows strong and walks with its mother, so then it is fit for spreading and obstinacy in running. *Al-rasha'* also: a tree that rises above the height of a man, and a herb like *al-qarnuwa* (with qaf), as if it is intensely pungent, so it is likened to the obstinate, because *al-qarnuwa* is used for tanning. End of the hamza-radical.

*Washarha al-khashba bi-l-mi'shar*: not hamza-radical; a dialectal form of *ashraha*, when he sawed it, i.e. split it in two or more. *Al-washr* also: a woman's filing and thinning of her teeth, and it comes from strength, shining and separation. *Al-mu'tashira*: the one who asks that this be done to her. *Muwashshir al-'adadayn* (and it is hamzated): the tattooing; because his arms are like what is cut with notches. From its hamza-radical: *ashir* (with kasra), i.e. he was insolent, i.e. he despised morality and treated people as one who disdains them, so he wronged them and persisted in his arrogance. A she-camel *mu'ashsharr*: energetic. *Ashshara al-asnan*: he filed the teeth, likening them to the teeth of the saw with which one cuts wood and the like quickly; so it is like the act of the obstinate. End of the hamza-radical. *Wirash al-ta'am*: he took it and ate greedily, eagerly, and was greedy and eager for the thin edges of matters, because that does not happen except from persistence and obstinacy. *Wirasha fulan bi-fulan*: he incited him. *Wari'sha 'alayhim*: he entered while they were eating and did not leave. *Warish*: the name of a thing made from milk, because it spread from its original form. *Al-warash* (vowelled): a pain in the belly. *Ka-katif*: the energetic, light one among camels and others; and its feminine is with the ha'. *Al-tawrish*: incitement. *Al-wirshan*: a bird. From its hamza-radical: *al-arsh*, which is the blood-money, because one persists in seeking it and in being content with it, and it is what most concerns its affair. It is also bribery, and what a defect diminishes from a thing, said in the Qamus, because it is the cause of compensation and dispute; and between them is *arsh*, i.e. disagreement and dispute. *Al-arsh*: incitement and giving, because the giver overcomes himself, as if he disputed with himself and persisted until he overcame it. *Al-arsh*: character, because it is the source of obstinacy; it is said: I do not know which *arsh* this is? i.e. which character. *Al-ma'rush*: the created. *Aarish* (like *sahib*): a mountain. End of the hamza-radical. *Al-rawsh*: much eating, and little eating: opposites; and it is from persistence and the weakness that sometimes arises from persistence, along with its resemblance to feathers. A camel *rashin*: abundant in ear hair. From clarification: *shara al-dabba*: when he rode it at the display to its buyer; *shawwarahā*: he looked how its gait was, i.e. its course, or tested it to see what it has; or turned it over; likewise the slave-girl. *Istasha al-fahl al-naqa*: the stallion caressed the she-camel, looked at her to see whether she was in heat or not. *Istasha amr fulan*: he clarified it. *Al-mustashir*: one who knows the barren from others. It returns to persistence, because if not for it he would not know the matter. From weakness: *rashahu*: he flattered and courted him; *tarashsha-hu*: he was soft with him; *inna-ka lamustarrishin li-fulan*: you are obedient to him, following his pleasure; and it is from bribery. A camel *rashin*: weak in its loins; likewise a spear *rashin*, with ha'. *Rashahu al-marad*: the illness weakened him, as if it is from feathers. All of this returns, after reflection, to persistence, and God knows best.

The root *b-kh-s* in every order (*bakhasa, khabasa, sabakha, sakhaba*) revolves around scarcity, and it entails taking with the palm: *bakhasat-hu haqqahu*: it diminished him, making his right less than it was. *Al-bakhs*: gouging out the eye, which is a specific deficiency. *Al-bakhs*: land that grows without irrigation, as if because of the scarcity of what grows in it compared to irrigated land. *Al-bakhs*: unjust levy. *Sabbakhtu 'an fulan*: it lightened for him; *al-sabkha*: salty land, because of the scarcity of its growth and benefit; *sabbakhat al-qutn*: when she cut it, so its total becomes little; [and] *al-tasbikh*: what falls from a bird's feathers, because of its loss from it; *al-tasbikh*: deep sleep, because it diminishes its owner and lightens what is in him of heaviness. From that: *al-khabs*, which is taking with the palm, and it necessarily entails scarcity; from it the lion is called *al-khabis*, because of his taking what he wants with his palm. *Al-sikhab*: a necklace of cloves that has no jewel or pearl in it.

Because "al-bakhs" means a small, deficient amount, he (God) substituted for it, as an emphasis on the meaning, to belittle their opinion and to express wonder at their condition, the phrase ﴿dirhama﴾ (for a few dirhams), that is, not dinars, ﴿ma'dudah﴾ (counted), that is, fit to be counted, because there was no abundance of them, with which counting would be difficult. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that they were twenty dirhams. ﴿Wa-kanu﴾ (and they were), that is, a state that was like a natural disposition, ﴿fihi﴾ (regarding it), that is, specifically, rather than the rest of their goods, seizing the opportunity regarding it before it became known to them and it was taken from their hands, ﴿min al-zahidin﴾ (among those who were indifferent). That is, in complete indifference, to the point that they desired to be rid of him and sold him for a paltry price. Zuhd (indifference) is the turning of desire away from a thing toward what is better than it in the eyes of the one who is indifferent. This specifies that the pronoun refers to the caravan, because the state of his brothers regarding his affair was far beyond indifference by many stages. Had it referred to them, it would have said: "and they were among those who were distant from him or those who hated him," and the like.

(p-48) Since it was customary for a slave to be treated with contempt, God informed us that He honored him above this custom. He said, alerting us that his purchase took place in Egypt: ﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said﴾, meaning, the one who took him with great eagerness, and had they required it, he would have paid a high price for him. ﴿From Egypt﴾, meaning the well-known city. The expression is used in this form rather than a shorter one to draw attention to the fact that his sale was an injustice and that he had not entered anyone's possession at all. ﴿To his wife﴾, commanding her to honor him in the most emphatic way: ﴿Make his residence comfortable﴾, meaning the place where he stays. This is greater than an order to honor him personally. The meaning is: honor him greatly, such that he is treated with honor in everything connected to him, so that he will desire to remain with us. Since it was as if she had asked, "What is the reason for your instructing me about him in particular?", he began a new statement: ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾, meaning his condition is deserving and worthy that he should benefit us, and this is in the sense of the buyer's expectation. ﴿Or we may adopt him﴾, meaning with great eagerness if we find him fit, ﴿as a son﴾. So I am hopeful of that.

When God informed us of the beginning of his affair, and it was known that this came about because he had been established in people's hearts in a way that required their reverence, honor and exaltation, God informed us of the end of his affair, likening it to this known content. He said: ﴿And thus﴾, meaning just as We established Joseph by causing the caravan, the people of the desert, to be disinclined to him at one time, and by the honoring of his buyer and the rivalry over him at another time, ﴿We established Joseph in the land﴾ (p-49), meaning the land of Egypt, which, because of the abundance of its benefits, was as if it were the entire earth, through having dominion in it, so that he could rule with justice and with prophethood, ﴿and that We might teach him﴾, through Our greatness, ﴿the interpretation of events﴾, meaning by returning their outward appearances to their inner realities. Here God pointed to the one being likened without naming it explicitly, because of what the context indicates. He affirmed the establishment in the land so that it would indicate its necessary implication, which is sovereignty and the power to rule justly, and He mentioned teaching so that it would indicate what it necessarily implies, which is prophethood. Thus He indicated the necessary implication first through what it necessitates, and then the necessitating thing through its implication. This is like His saying: ﴿A company fighting in the way of God and another disbelieving﴾ [Al Imran: 13]. This is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which two contrasting elements are mentioned, each one's counterpart being omitted), or something close to it.

Since it is among the most wondrous of wonders that one who was empowered to be subjected to such actions should become established in a land where he was a stranger, looked down upon, alone, with no clan and no helpers there, God said, negating this wonder: ﴿And God is dominant over His affair﴾, meaning the Supreme Sovereign is dominant over the matter He intends. The outward reality of His command is evident to everyone who has insight. Jacob ordered Joseph, peace be upon them both, not to relate his dream out of fear for him from his brothers, but God's command prevailed until what he had warned of occurred. His brothers intended to kill him, but God's command prevailed over them. They wanted some of the caravan to pick him up so that his name would be erased, but God's command prevailed, his name became manifest and famous. Then they sold him so that he would be a slave, but God's command prevailed until he became a king, and they prostrated before him. Then they wanted to incite their father and to comfort his heart so that they might have his full attention, but God's command prevailed and exposed their deceit. The wife of the governor plotted against him to deceive him about himself, but God's command prevailed, and He protected him so that he did not intend evil. Rather, he fled from her as far as he could. Then she exerted her efforts to humiliate him and to place the accusation upon him, but God refused except to honor him and clear him. Then Joseph, peace be upon him, wanted the cupbearer to mention him, but God's command prevailed and made him forget to mention him until the appointed term God had set had passed.
