How many matters there were in this story and in others that point to the fact that there is no command other than His, glory be to Him! ﴿But most people﴾, meaning those who are in confusion, ﴿do not know﴾, because they do not reflect that He, exalted be He, is above every matter, and that judgment belongs to Him alone. They are occupied with looking at outward appearances, the causes that He establishes. Thus He, glory be to Him, is veiled from them by the veil of causes.

[The commentator] mentioned what preceded of the story of Joseph, peace be upon him, from the Torah (p-51). It says at the end of the second book of it: "Joseph, son of Jacob, was seventeen years old, and he used to tend the flock with his brothers. Israel loved Joseph more than his brothers, because he had been born in his old age, so he made him a coat of many colors. His brothers saw that their father loved him more than them, so they hated him and could not speak to him peaceably. He had a dream and related it to his brothers, and said to them: 'Hear this dream that I saw: I saw that we were binding sheaves in the field, and my sheaf stood upright, and behold, your sheaves surrounded it and bowed down to it.' His brothers said to him, 'Do you think you will reign over us and rule over us?' They hated him even more for his dream and his words. Then he had another dream and said: 'I have seen another dream: I saw the sun, the moon and eleven stars bowing down to me.' He related it to his father and his brothers, and his father rebuked him and said: 'What is this dream? Shall I and your mother and your brothers come and bow down to you on the earth?'" (p-52) "His brothers envied him, but his father kept these words in mind.

Joseph's brothers went out to pasture their flocks in Nablus. Israel said to Joseph, 'Behold, your brothers are pasturing in Nablus. Come, I will send you to them.' He said, 'Here I am!' His father said, 'Go and see how your brothers are and how the flocks are, and bring me word.' So Jacob, peace be upon him, sent him from the valley of Hebron, and he came to Nablus. A man found him wandering in the field and asked him, 'What are you seeking in the field?' He said, 'I am seeking my brothers. Tell me where they are pasturing.' The man said to him, 'They have left from here, and I heard them say, "Let us go to Dothan."' So Joseph followed his brothers and found them at Dothan. They saw him from afar, and before he came close to them they plotted to kill him. They said to one another, 'Here comes the master of dreams. Come, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits, and we will say that a wicked beast devoured him, and we will see what becomes of his dreams!' Reuben heard and rescued him from their hands, and said to them, 'Let us not kill a soul, nor shed blood. Rather, throw him into this pit that is in the wilderness, and do not lay your hands on him.' He intended to save him from their hands and return him to his father.

When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of the coat of many colors he was wearing (p-53), and they took him and threw him into the pit, which was empty and had no water. Then they sat down to eat bread. They lifted up their eyes and saw, and behold, a caravan of Arabs was coming from Gilead (in another version: from Jarsh), and their camels were laden with spices, balm and myrrh, and they were heading for Egypt. Judah said to his brothers, 'What profit is there in killing our brother and shedding his blood? Come, let us sell him to the Arabs, and let us not lay our hands on him, for he is our brother, our flesh and blood.' His brothers obeyed him. Then Midianite merchants passed by, and they drew Joseph up from the pit and sold him to the Arabs for twenty pieces of silver. They brought him to Egypt.

Reuben returned to the pit, and behold, Joseph was not in it. He tore his garments, returned to his brothers and said, 'The boy is gone! Where shall I go now?' They took Joseph's coat, slaughtered a young goat, smeared the coat with its blood, and sent it with those who came to their father, saying, 'We found this. Examine it: is it your son's coat or not?' He recognized it and said, 'It is my son's coat! A wicked beast has devoured my son Joseph completely!' He grieved for his son for many days. All his sons and daughters came to console him, but he refused to accept consolation and said, 'I will go down to the grave grieving for Joseph.' Thus his father wept for him. And the Midianites sold Joseph to Potiphar, the chief of the guards of Pharaoh." End of quotation. There is in it what contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and it can be interpreted. And God knows best.

ولَمّا أخْبَرَ تَعالى يُوسُفَ عَمّا يُرِيدُ بِيُوسُفَ عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ بِما خَتَمَهُ بِالإخْبارِ عَنْ قُدْرَتِهِ، أتْبَعَهُ الإعْلامُ بِإيجادِ ذَلِكَ الفِعْلِ دَلالَةً عَلى تَمامِ القُدْرَةِ وشُمُولِ العِلْمِ فَقالَ: ﴿ولَمّا بَلَغَ أشُدَّهُ﴾ أيْ مُجْتَمَعَ قُواهُ ﴿آتَيْناهُ﴾ أيْ بِعَظَمَتِنا ﴿حُكْمًا﴾ أيْ نُبُوَّةً (prophethood) أوْ مَلِكَةً يَكُفُّ بِها النَّفْسَ عَنْ هَواها، مِن حِكْمَةِ الفُرْسِ، فَلا يَقُولُ ولا يَفْعَلُ إلّا أمْرًا فَصْلًا تَدْعُو إلَيْهِ الحِكْمَةُ؛ قالَ الرُّمّانِيُّ: والأصْلُ في الحُكْمِ تَبْيِينِ ما يَشْهَدُ بِهِ الدَّلِيلُ، لِأنَّ الدَّلِيلَ حِكْمَةٌ مِن أجْلِ أنَّهُ يَقُودُ إلى المَعْرِفَةِ ﴿وعِلْمًا﴾ أيْ تِبْيِينًا لِلشَّيْءِ عَلى ما هو عَلَيْهِ جَزاءً [لَهُ -] لِأنَّهُ مُحْسِنٌ ﴿وكَذَلِكَ﴾ أيْ ومِثْلُ ذَلِكَ الجَزاءِ الَّذِي جَزَيْناهُ بِهِ ﴿نَجْزِي المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ أيِ العَرِيقِينَ في الإحْسانِ (excellence in good deeds) كُلِّهِمُ الَّذِينَ رَأسَهم مُحَمَّدٌ (ﷺ) الَّذِي أُسْرِيَ بِهِ فَأعْلاهُ ما لَمْ يُعْلَ غَيْرُهُ؛ وعَنِ الحُسْنِ: مِن أحْسَنَ عِبادَةَ اللَّهِ في (p-٥٥) شَبِيبَتِهِ آتاهُ [اللَّهُ -] الحِكْمَةَ [فِي اكْتِهالِهِ -]، والأشُدُّ: كَمالُ القُوَّةِ، وهو جَمْعُ شِدَّةٍ عِنْدَ سِيبَوَيْهَ مِثْلُ نِعْمَةٍ وأنْعُمٌ، وقالَ غَيْرُهُ: جَمْعُ شَدٍّ؛ قالَ ابْنُ فارِسٍ في المُجْمَلِ: وبَعْضُهم يَقُولُ: لا واحِدَ لَها، ويُقالُ: واحِدُها شَدَّ - انْتَهى. [قِيلَ -]: وهَذا هو القِياسُ نَحْوَ ضَبٍّ وأضَبُّ، وصَكٍّ وأصَكُّ، وحَظٍّ وأحَظُّ، وضُرٍّ وأضَرُّ، وشَرٍّ وأشَرُّ قالَ الرُّمانِيُّ: قالَ الشّاعِرُ:

هَلْ غَيَّرَ أنْ كَثُرَ الأشَرُّ وأهْلَكَتْ .... حَرْبُ المُلُوكِ أكاثِرَ الأمْوالِ

انْتَهى. واخْتَلَفُوا في حَدِّ الأشُدِّ فَقِيلَ: هو مِنَ الحُلُمِ، ورُوِيَ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُما أنَّهُ مِن عِشْرِينَ سَنَةٍ، ورُوِيَ غَيْرُ ذَلِكَ، والمادَّةُ تَدُورُ عَلى الصُّعُوبَةِ، وهي ضِدُّ الرَّخاوَةِ، ويَلْزَمُها القُوَّةُ، فالشَّدُّ عَلى العَدْوِ مِنها، وشَدَّ الحَبَلَ وغَيْرَهُ: أحْكُمُ فَتَلَهُ، والشَّدِيدُ والمُتَشَدِّدُ: البَخِيلُ - لِصُعُوبَةِ البَذْلِ عَلَيْهِ، والشِّدَّةُ: صُعُوبَةُ الزَّمانِ، وشَدُّ النَّهارِ: ارْتِفاعُهُ، وهو قُوتُهُ، وشَدَدْتُ فُلانًا: قَوَّيْتَ يَدَهُ ودَبَّرْتَ أمَرَهُ، وأشَدُّ القَوْمِ - إذا كانَتْ دَوابُّهم شِدادًا فَهم مُشِدُّونَ ضِدَّ مُضَعِّفِينَ.

(p. 56) When God informed that the cause of the blessing upon him was His favor to him, He followed it with its proof, saying: ﴿And she sought to seduce him﴾, meaning she turned him back from his affair, went around him with stratagems. It is a metaphor for deceit, which is the necessary meaning of *rāda yarūdu*, "to come and go." ﴿She in whose house he was﴾, who had complete power over him to the utmost degree, ﴿he being in the prime of youth﴾, ﴿sought to seduce him﴾, meaning a seduction that had no cause other than herself, because seduction cannot reach a person's self except after mixing with him. This is like saying, "This happened by his command." She went around him with every kind of trick, set for him the snares of deception, and remained for a time twisting around him from the crest to the flank. This is because the root *r-w-d / r-y-d* is both waw-based and ya-based in all its seven permutations: *rawada*, *dawara*, *warada*, *waydara*, *radā*, *ūrīda*, and *darā*. They all revolve around *dawarān* (rotation), which is returning to the point of origin. It necessarily implies intention, coming, approach, withdrawal, gentleness, delay, the employment of cunning, and good consideration. Sometimes it occurs without intention, so bewilderment comes from it, and that entails corruption and destruction. It is said: *dāra fulān yadūru* when a man walks in the manner of his creation. *Ad-dahr dawwārī* means "the age is revolving," because it turns with its people between elevation and abasement. *Ad-dawār* is a semblance of spinning in the head. *Dārrat al-qamar* (the halo of the moon) is well known. *Ad-dā'ira* is the circle. *Ad-dār* (p. 57) is the gathering of an open space and a building, because of the rotation of its construction, for turning within it, and for going out from it and returning to it. *Ad-dārī* is the sailor who manages the sail, which is the canvas, because he turns it on the mast of the ship, or because he keeps to the stern of the vessel. *Ar-rā'id* is the one who seeks pasture, that is, who goes and comes in search of it, because he has no fixed destination on the earth, as if he were turning within it. He who does not deceive his family, and every seeker of a need, is so described, as said by Ibn Duraid.

*Rāwadat ar-rajul* means she sought to make him do an act. *Rā'id ar-raḥā* is its handle, that is, the stick by which the millstone is turned and which the grinder grips. *Ar-rīyād* is the wandering of camels in pasture, coming and going. *Rādat al-mar'a* means the woman went back and forth among the houses of her neighbors. *Rāda wasādahu* means he did not settle. *Ar-rawad* is seeking, going, and coming. *Imshi 'alā rawad*, with a damma, means "slowly," and its diminutive is *ruwayd*. *Al-mirwad* is that with which one applies kohl, because it is turned within the eye, and it is also the iron piece that turns in the bridle, and the iron axle of a pulley. *Ad-dayr* is well known. It is said of a man who is the head of his companions, "He is the head of the monastery," as if it were from their turning to him. *Taraddaytu bir-ridā'* and *irtadaytu* (I wrapped myself in the cloak), as if from *al-idāra* (encircling). *Ar-ridā'* is also the sword, because one wears it at the place of the *radā* (the shoulder). *Ar-radayān* with fatha means a donkey walked between its droppings and its rolling-place. *Rādaytu fulānan* is like *rāwadtuhu*. *Raddat al-jāriya*, when a girl raised one of her legs and hopped on one, because the manner of her walking then resembles turning. *Ar-rīd* with kasra is the dust, because it seeks you, that is, it walks with you from the first of your life. From coming is *al-wurūd*, which is arriving at a watering place, of water or of a path. *Al-wārid* is one who goes to the water to draw from it, one who descends to the water to take from it. *Al-wird* is well known. The flower of every tree is a *wird*, because it is sought for smelling and other purposes, and it comes out of it, so it is *wārid*, that is, coming. It is also simultaneously rounded. *Al-warad*, with kasra, is the day of fever when it seizes its sufferer at a fixed time, because it comes to him, and it is also from rotation, because it revolves at that very time. All this is suitable for approach. From this: *arnaba wārida*, that is, a nose turned toward the rain-lock. *Ar-rayd* is the nose of a mountain, as said by Ibn Fāris. Ibn Duraid said: *Ar-rayd* is the protruding projection of a mountain, plural *ruyūd*. In the Qamus: *al-ḥayyid* of a mountain is a projection standing out like a wing. The brave man is called *wārid* because of his approach to everything he desires and his dominance over it. *Al-wariḍān* are two veins flanking the sides of the neck, the front ones, thick. *Al-wird* is a share of the Qur'an, because one aims at it in recitation, turns toward it, and is occupied with it. *Darayt ash-shay'* means I knew it, so you are turned toward it and arrive at it. *Ad-daraʾa*, with hamza, is a ring on which one learns thrusting and shooting. *Ad-durriyya*, with or without hamza, is an animal behind which the hunter of game conceals himself and so deceives it. It belongs to approach and deception. If someone says *banā fulān adwaran makānan*, that is, they relied on raiding and attack. *Ad-durriyy* resembles the *mudarra* of a bull, which is its horn, because one aims with it at a thing and approaches its target, improving it with it. *Mā adrī ayna radda?* means "Where did he go?" *Al-irwād* is delay in a matter. *Imshi ruwayḍan* means slowly, on gentle pace. *Ar-rādda* and *ar-rayda* are gentle winds, as if they come gently. From bewilderment, corruption, and destruction: *radiya ar-rajul* means the man perished, and *arda-hu Allāh* means God destroyed him. (p. 60) *Taradda fī hūwwa* means he plunged into a pit. *Radaytuhu bil-ḥijārah* means I struck him with stones. *Ar-raddāh* is a rock with which one breaks a thing. *Al-marādī* are the targets. From good consideration: *ardaytu 'alā al-khamsīn* means I exceeded fifty, because good consideration entails increase. *Arādahu ʿalā ghayrihi* means he surpassed it over another. The hamzated letters of this root will be explained in *sanurāwid* in this surah, God willing.

﴿And she locked the doors﴾, meaning she locked them many times, for additional strength. They said they were seven. *Al-ighlāq* is closing the door in such a way that opening it becomes difficult. ﴿And she said: "Come, you"﴾, meaning she prepared herself and made herself attractive ﴿for you﴾ specifically, so approach me and obey my command. The root, on the assumption that the *tā'* is original or added, in all its permutations, ya-based, waw-based, hamzated and unhamzated, revolves around *irādat imtithāl al-amr* (intending obedience to a command): *hayta laka*, with the last letter in any of its three vowels, and its first letter may take kasra, meaning *halumma* (come). *Hayyata tahyītan* means he shouted and called him. *Hāt*, with kasra on the *tā'*, means give me. So says the Qamus. *Al-muhāyāh* is a verbal reciprocal from it. *Al-hīt* is the obscure part of the land, as if it calls the man of resolve to stand upon its reality. *At-tīh*, with kasra, is pride and arrogance, so the one who is bewildered calls forcibly to obey his command. *Al-mafāzah* (the desert wasteland) overpowers its traveler, and going astray in the desert is naming a thing by the name of its place. From this: *tahā* meaning he was heedless. From this: *mada tihwā'un min al-layl* with kasra, meaning a portion of the night, because it is the place of heedlessness, or because it calls its watcher to sleep and its sleeper to wakefulness. This is according to the assumption that the *tā'* is original. As for the assumption that it is added, then *hā'a bi-nafsihi ilā al-ma'ālī* means he raised himself to high things, so he sees himself worthy of obeying her command. *Al-hawʾ* is aspiration and past command. *Al-hawʾ* also means opinion, and it is pronounced with damma. *Hu'tu bihi* means I rejoiced at it, and this only happens at doing what one desires, as if he had obeyed your command. *Hawiya ilayhi*, like *faraḥa*, means he intended. *Hā'a*, like *jā'a*, means he answered, that is, obeyed the command. *Hā'a*, with kasra, means *hāt*, and *hā'a*, like *jā'a*, means *hāk*, with the meaning of "take." *Al-hay'a* is the state and manner of a thing that calls to leaving it or adhering to it. *Tahāyawū* means they agreed. *Hā'a ilayhi* means he longed for him, as if he called him to see him. *Tahayya'a li-sh-shay'* means he took its form, as if he became receptive to the command or fit to obey his command. *Hayya'ahu* means he set it right. *Al-hay'* with fatha or kasra is the call to food and drink, and the call of camels to drink. *Iyhi*, with kasra on the hamza, is a word meaning he asked for more and sought to make him speak. With the *hā'* quiescent, it is a rebuke meaning "enough for you." *Hā'hā'a* means he laughed loudly in his laughter. This happens only with one who has obeyed his desire.

When she said what she said and did what she did, together with the power she had over herself and the authority she had over him, and his beauty and youth, it was as if it were said: "This is a station from which hardly anyone escapes. What then did he do?" It is said: ﴿He said﴾, that is, Yusuf, using judgment by knowledge, ﴿"I seek refuge"﴾, that is, I take refuge from this matter, ﴿in God﴾, that is, I cling to the fortress of Him who possesses the attributes of perfection, who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, and whose refuge is the one to whom one should hold fast and resort. Then he gave the reason for this in his words: ﴿"He is my Lord"﴾, that is, the Originator, the Manager, and the one who is good to me in every matter, so I hope for His goodness in this, ﴿"He has made my abode good"﴾, by placing in my heart a great station with your master, so that he entrusted me with all that he owns and put me in charge of everything he possesses. If I opposed my Lord's command and betrayed the one who made me a place of trust, I would be a wrongdoer, placing a thing in other than its place. This interpretation, along with its being more fitting for the righteous who are watchful, is better, because it implies counseling the Aziz. If we returned the pronoun to the Aziz, it would not imply piety.

Since it was known that the tongue of her state was saying: "And if it were wrongdoing, what then?" he said something whose implication was: "Then I would not prosper." He gave the reason with his words: ﴿"Indeed, the wrongdoers do not prosper"﴾, that is, they do not attain their aim at all, ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, that is, those who are deeply immersed (p. 63) in wrongdoing, which is placing a thing in other than its place, those who, on the assumption of the act, I would be counted among. How wonderful this is as a proof of His goodness, His wisdom, and His knowledge! For when he saw the slippery position, he hastened to cling to Him in whose hand is the dominion of everything. Then he recalled His favor to him, which obligates gratitude for it and keeps him far from slips. Then he recalled the station of wrongdoing and what it necessarily brings to its doer of grief at not prospering.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 24:

Since this act cannot be fully good unless it occurs at the height of desire and the surging of appetite, as is the nature of manhood, He said, exalted is He, in refutation of one who imagines the opposite of that: ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾, meaning she brought about hamm (hamm: firm intention and resolute determination directed at committing the act), and she had no barrier to it from religion, reason, or incapacity, so her pursuit intensified. ﴿And he desired her﴾, as is the nature of stallions when the means are abundant. ﴿Had he not seen﴾, meaning with the eye of his heart, ﴿the proof of his Lord﴾, which He had bestowed upon him of wisdom and knowledge; meaning he would have desired her, but since the proof was present before him in the presence of one who sees with the eye, the abundance of desire did not veil it, nor did the dominance of passion, so he did not desire at all, even though he was in the utmost readiness for that, because of the strength God had given him while he was in the age of youth. Had it not been for watchfulness, the abundance of motives would have led him to desire her; but the light of witnessing erased it altogether. This estimate is the one fitting to one of his station, and it is also what the style of these verses indicates, in making him one of the sincere and the virtuous from whom evil is averted, and that prison was more beloved to him than that, with the decisive evidence of the falsehood of what her words contained: ﴿What is the recompense for one who intended evil to your family?﴾ [Yusuf: 25] – the verse, concerning the mere intention. And the estimate of what was mentioned after "lawla" is necessitated in this particular construction of the Arabic idiom, for the omitted response after every conditional must have the meaning indicated by what precedes it. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿She would almost have disclosed it, had We not fortified her heart﴾ [al-Qasas: 10], meaning: she would have disclosed it. As for what has come from the early generation (al-salaf) that contradicts this, nothing of it has been authentically transmitted from any one of them, and the reports attributed to them, when gathered together, contradict one another and thus cancel each other out; and the Arabic idiom does not support any of them, because they estimated the omitted response of "lawla" as something for which there is no indication in the preceding or following speech. Imam Abu Hayyan drew attention to this, and Imam al-Razi preceded him to it, saying: "This is the view of the verifying scholars among the exegetes," and he elaborated on establishing the proofs for this in a way that delights the ears, and he placed first what indicates the response of the conditional, so that the first thing to strike the hearing would be what shows that he was at the utmost capacity for the act, and that nothing prevented him from it except knowledge of God. It is as if it were said: this affirmation is great. So it is said, as an indication that it is constant for him, as is the nature of infallibility: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning like that affirmation, We establish it in every matter ﴿that We might avert from him evil﴾, meaning the desire for fornication and other things, ﴿and immorality﴾, meaning fornication and other things. So it is as if it were said: why did He do this to him? Then it is said: ﴿Indeed he is of Our servants﴾, meaning those whom We have glorified with Our glory, ﴿the sincere ones﴾, meaning he is among those who are pure essence, not mixed with any impurity, and of their offspring also. This, together with the statement of Iblis: ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82] ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [Sad: 83], is a testimony from Iblis that Yusuf, peace be upon him, is free of hamm in this incident. The Imam said: "Whoever attributes hamm to him, if he is among the followers of the religion of God, let him accept the testimony of God; and if he is among the followers of Iblis and his soldiers, let him accept the testimony of Iblis to his purity." He said: "Perhaps they will say: we were the students of Iblis, then we surpassed him," as it has been said:

I was a youth from the army of Iblis, who rose
in the affair until Iblis became one of my soldiers.

If I had died before him, I would have been better than him after him
in the paths of sin, which he has not yet mastered.

(p-66) Then Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned his extreme resistance, in earnestly fleeing, as evidence of his sincerity and that he had not intended (the sin) at all. He said: ﴿And they raced to the door﴾, meaning they brought about a race with utmost eagerness from each of them: this one to flee from her, and that one to prevent him. The verb reached its object without "ila" (to), as evidence that each of them exerted the utmost effort in the race. So she caught up with him at the far door, although he had preceded her with the strength of manhood and the strong motive to flee to Allah. But her perfect devising of deceit, by the doors being locked, meant that he was busy opening them, so she seized him by the least part she could reach of his shirt, which was what was behind him, fearing his escaping. Her grip on him intensified while he turned away from her and fled from her; so he opened it and wanted to go out, but she prevented him and did not cease struggling with him until ﴿she tore his shirt﴾, and it was ﴿from behind﴾, meaning the back side of it. A piece was torn off and remained in her hand. ﴿And they found﴾, meaning they came upon, with the dust and the disordered state that did not befit them, ﴿her master﴾, meaning her husband. He did not say "their master" because Yusuf, upon him be peace, had not entered into slavery, as has passed, since a Muslim cannot be owned; he was the master. ﴿At the door﴾ at that moment, meaning the outer door, in a very strange manner. This is how this situation should be understood, because a master cannot open it, let alone reach anything else, since all were locked.

(p-67) When the listener knew that they found him in this state, it was as if it were said: "What then happened?" So it was said: ﴿She said﴾, hastening without shame or hesitation. "What" is negative, and it could also be interrogative: ﴿What is the recompense of one who intended﴾, meaning of you or of anyone else, whoever he might be, because of your greatness, ﴿evil to your family﴾, meaning even if it were other than adultery, ﴿except that he be imprisoned﴾, meaning placed in prison for a certain time so that he may be judged there as is fitting, ﴿or a painful punishment﴾, meaning lasting and established, other than imprisonment. Recompense is repaying an action with what is its due. This was her state at the moment of surprise. As for him, upon him be peace, he acted according to the noble manner: he kept silent to conceal her, and refrained from mentioning the indecency.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 26:

So it is as if it were said: "Then what did he say when she accused him with this?" It was said: ﴿He said, seeking to defend himself, not to expose her,⦾ "It was she"⦾ using the third-person pronoun, because he was too shy to face her with a sign or a second-person pronoun,⦾ ﴿she sought to seduce me away from myself﴾. He said this only when she compelled him to it by attributing to him betrayal. And his truthfulness in what he said, by my life, does not need any clarification beyond the state in which the two of them were: (p-68) that they were at the door. Had the solicitation come from him, they would have been only in her place, where she sits, which is the head of the house and its most honored spot. ﴿And a witness testified﴾. Since every fit person is sufficient as a witness, and there was no necessity to specify him, it said: ﴿a witness⦾ from her family﴾, meaning a great one, because a person of her household carries greater weight in testimony. He was an infant who spoke in his defense. Al-Rummani transmitted this from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with them. Likewise, a child from the people of al-Yamamah testified for the Prophet (ﷺ) during the Farewell Pilgrimage, on the day he was born, that he was the Messenger of Allah, and so he was called "Mubarak al-Yamamah."

The witness said: ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front,⦾ meaning, in the state of evasion,⦾ ﴿then she has told the truth,⦾ meaning, as becomes clear to you, ﴿"torn" (qadda),⦾ meaning cut completely,⦾ ﴿from the front (qubul),⦾ meaning from the side facing him of his body,⦾ ﴿then she has told the truth﴾. It is necessary to supply a verb of clarification, because conditional clauses carry their meanings only in the future, even if their wording is in the past.

Since her truthfulness is not decisive in preventing his truthfulness, he said: ﴿and he is of the liars.﴾ For had he been approaching her, while she was pushing him away from herself or fleeing from him, and he was following her and stumbling in his shirt, the tear would not have been in the front (qubul).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 27:

﴿And if it was﴾ i.e., as it appears to you, ﴿his shirt﴾ i.e., Yusuf, upon him be peace, ﴿torn from behind﴾ i.e., from the side of what was turned away from her. He put "qudda" (was torn) in the passive form because of the dispute about the one who tore it. ﴿Then she has lied﴾, and since it was so, her lying [about his intent -] to do evil does not confirm the truth of his intent toward her, [he said -]: ﴿and he is of the truthful﴾, because had it not been for his turning away from her and her advancing upon him, that would not have happened. So her master recognized the validity of this without doubt, because the meaning of "in" (inna) here is the conditional in the sense of affirming a matter which necessarily entails something else, not as an expression of doubt. He mentioned the sign of her truthfulness first because it is something her master loves, so on the surface it is a show of concern for her, but in reality it is a confirmation of her lying twice: the first by implication (bil-luzum), and the second by direct correspondence (bil-mutabaqa).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 28:

Since the meaning was "so he looked," he built upon it his saying: ﴿When she saw﴾, i.e., her master, ﴿his shirt﴾, i.e., Yusuf, peace be upon him, ﴿torn from behind, he said﴾ to her, having decided between his truthfulness and her lying, emphasizing it because of her denial: ﴿Indeed, it is from your scheming﴾, i.e., this accusation against him is from you, O women. Kayd (scheming, seeking to harm a person by what he dislikes) ﴿Indeed, your scheming is great﴾. The great (ʿaẓīm) is that which makes the measure of another fall short of it, in sense or in meaning. So he regarded it as great because it is subtler, finer and more hidden than the scheming of men, because Satan is more capable over them due to their deficiency (p-70), and their scheming, which is from the scheming of Satan, is the weakest of the weak in comparison with what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, arranges in nullifying it.

Then the Governor (al-'Aziz) said, commanding him (peace be upon him), dropping the vocative particle to indicate that his closeness to the heart was due to his state: "Yusuf, turn away from this." That is, withdraw entirely, passing beyond "from this." That is, make it like what you turn your face away from, toward the direction of aversion, by not mentioning it to anyone and not concerning yourself with it, for I have not been affected by you in any respect, since your innocence has become manifest. Then he turned to her and said: "And seek forgiveness" (wastaghfiri). That is, ask forgiveness "for your sin" (li-dhanbiki), that no punishment befall you from me or from God. He resumed explaining what he had alluded to with his words: "Indeed you were" (innaki kunti), that is, in an innate state (kawnan jibilliyyan), "among the sinners" (min al-khati'in), that is, those who are deeply immersed in error to the utmost degree of intensity. It is said: khati'a yukhti'u, when one sins deliberately.

When this contained the nobility of chastity (*al-'iffah*), which indicates the perfection of protection from sin (*al-'ismah*), and Allah the Exalted reinforced it with what indicates the loftiness of his beauty and the sublimity of his grace and gentleness, because custom holds that such beauty is a cause of a person's inclination toward someone, and so the motives to incline toward him are multiplied, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And women said﴾, that is, a group of women, since the news had spread. And since a city, the greater it is, the more intelligent its people are and the closer they are to wisdom, He said: ﴿in the city﴾, that is, the one in which the wife of the Aziz resided, ﴿the wife of the Aziz﴾. They attributed her to her husband, intending to spread the report, because the soul is more inclined to hear the reports of matters of great peril. *Al-'Aziz* is the one whose power makes him secure from being wronged, so *al-'izzah* (might) is more specific than mere power. They used the present tense in ﴿she seeks to seduce her young man﴾, that is, her slave, descending from the bed of the Aziz to his bed, ﴿from himself﴾, to convey that persistence in seduction had become for her like a natural disposition. *Al-fata* means the young man. Al-Rummani restricted it to the strong one, and said: al-Zajjaj said: "They used to call a slave *fata*, whether old or young, so there is a shared meaning in this." ﴿He has made her heart ache with love﴾, that young man, ﴿with love﴾, that is, from the direction of love. Al-Rummani said: *shaghaf al-qalb* is its covering, the membrane upon it. It is said: love entered the skin until it reached the heart. This is from al-Suddi and Abu 'Ubaydah. From al-Hasan, it is the inner part of the heart. From Abu [-] 'Ali, it is the middle of the heart. End. What is said in *al-Mujmal* and elsewhere is that it is the covering of the heart. A better explanation than Abu 'Ubaydah's is that his love became a *shighaf* for her, that is, a veil, that is, an enclosure surrounding her. As for *sha'afha* with the unpointed letter (ʿayn), its meaning is: it covered the *sha'afah* of her heart, which is its head near where the heart-veins are attached. Al-Rummani said: that is, it carried her in every direction, from *sha'f al-jibal*, which are the peaks of the mountains.

When that was said, it was as if it had been asked: "So what happened?" It was answered, and it was emphasized because whoever saw him would excuse her, and would be certain that if they had been in her place they would have done the same and would not have blamed her act: ﴿Indeed, we see her﴾, that is, we know her condition with a knowledge like sight, ﴿in clear error﴾, that is, encompassing her, ﴿manifest﴾, because she accepted for herself, after the honour of sovereignty, a descent from her station to the rank of a slave.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 31:

He indicated by the "fa" (so) that their speech reached her quickly, and so He said: ﴿So when she heard of their scheming﴾, i.e., the wife of the ʿAzīz. It is as if they intended by this speech that what the wife of the ʿAzīz did would be affected by it, so that they might see him; therefore she called it "scheming." ﴿She sent for them﴾ so that she might show them that for which they would excuse her, and their talk would thereby subside. ﴿And she prepared for them a reclining-couch﴾, i.e., she readied and brought forth for them that on which they might recline, of soft cushions and fine pillows. They came to her, and she seated them on what she had prepared for them. ﴿And she gave each one of them a knife﴾, in general, ﴿to cut with﴾, so that they might cut whatever food required cutting from what was brought to this gathering. Abu Hayyan said: It was said that it was meat, and they did not tear meat with their teeth; rather, they would eat it by slicing it with knives. Al-Rummani said: "So that they might cut fruit that was brought to them" — end. This is the outward reason for their coming, and its inner meaning is to establish the proof against them with what they could not repel, of what would be affected by that. ﴿And she said﴾ to Yusuf, her servant (ﷺ) ... (p-73) ﴿Go out to them﴾; he complied with what she commanded him, as is his habit [with her] in everything that involves no disobedience, and hastened to go out to them. ﴿So when they saw him﴾, i.e., the women, ﴿they greatly admired him﴾, i.e., they magnified Yusuf (peace be upon him) exceedingly, glorifying him as they would glorify their Lord. ﴿And they cut﴾, i.e., wounded themselves with many wounds, ﴿their hands﴾. Their blame became an excuse, and the doubling (of the verb) indicates multiplicity; it is as if the knife would fall upon the hand of one of them and cut it, so she would lift it from her hand by nature, then astonishment would overcome her and it would fall on another place, and so on. ﴿And they said: "Allah forbid!"﴾, i.e., a very great and extreme declaration of His transcendence, "for Allah," i.e., the Supreme King who possesses the attributes of perfection by which He created the like of this.

Since the purpose of this declaration of transcendence was to exalt him, he clarified it by their saying: ﴿This is not a human being﴾, because he surpassed humans greatly in beauty and turned away from desire without a cause, whereas we see that desire is prevented in him [because he was] in the utmost of strength and virility. It is as if it were said: "What then is he?" They said: "Indeed," i.e., "this" is not, in this beauty and loveliness, and they repeated the demonstrative to remove the possibility of error, ﴿but a noble angel﴾. This is because the natures have been disposed to attribute every surpassing quality of beauty, chastity and the like to the angels, even though they are unseen (p-74), just as they have been disposed to attribute the opposite of that to the jinn and the devils.

Then it was as if it were said: "What did the wife of the al-Aziz say to them?" So it is said: ﴿She said: "That is the one about whom you blamed me"﴾, i.e., the youth of very high rank, ﴿about whom you blamed me﴾.

When she knew that they had excused her, she said, emphasizing it out of delight in exposing herself in her love for him: "And indeed" — i.e., I say this while the case is that, by God, it has become certain that I ﴿sought to seduce him from himself﴾, i.e., so that I might attain him with what I desire. "But he remained chaste" — i.e., he established chastity and refusal against me, so his abstention grew firm, and I am not one who will turn back from him. Then she threatened him while he was listening, so that he would submit. She said to them, emphasizing because the state of her love makes it necessary to deny that she would do what harms the beloved: ﴿"And if he does not do what I command him"﴾, i.e., this youth in whom my excuse was established before you, ﴿what I command him﴾ [Yusuf 12:32], i.e., my command, ﴿he will surely be imprisoned﴾, i.e., he will be prevented from acting freely through confinement, with the least effort on my part. Since her resolve to imprison him was stronger than her resolve to inflict humiliation upon him, she emphasized it with the heavy nun and said: ﴿"And he will surely be among the debased"﴾ with the light nun, i.e., the humiliated. Or the addition in emphasizing the imprisonment is because it entails his removal, and the removal of the beloved is more deserving of denial than his humiliation. So the women said to him: "Obey her, lest she imprison you and humiliate you."

So it is as if it were said: "What did he say?" It was said: ﴿He said﴾, calling out to the One who had annihilated himself in witnessing Him from every witnessed thing, and defending himself against the whisperings of Satan that had come upon him concerning her beauty, her position and her wealth, and against the cunning of the women who varied their words in enticing and in threatening him. He knew that human strength is too weak to [bear -] such things except through a great support. He dropped the particle of address, as is the custom of those who are near to God: ﴿My Lord, the prison﴾, which encloses and prevents turmoil regarding what lies outside it, ﴿is dearer to me﴾, meaning less hateful to me, ﴿than that to which they invite me﴾, meaning these women, all of them, ﴿to it﴾, because he knew the evil outcome of disobedience after the swift passing of its pleasure. This expression indicates the utmost hatred for their compliance, for a prison is not ordinarily conceived of as something loved. Rather, the meaning is that if it were conceivable to incline toward it, my inclination toward it would be greater, but it is not conceivable to incline toward it because it is pure evil. Nevertheless, I prefer it over what they invite me to, because it is the lesser of two harms. The summary is that he used the word "love" for its opposite in this context, namely hatred, by way of what is called dalalat al-iltizam (implicative indication, indication by necessary entailment). It is as if it were said: "The prison is less hateful to me than that to which you invite me." That is the opposite of "ahabb" (dearer), whose meaning is "more loved," but the expression was transposed so that it would be like asserting something accompanied by its proof. For when he was made to compare two things in love, one of which is definitively hateful to him, it was understood with certainty that what is meant is that the hatred of this hateful thing is less than the hatred of the lesser one. Thus it was known with certainty that the lesser thing is more hateful than this one whose hatred is definite. The same applies to anything compared between two things in an attribute that prevents taking it in its literal sense, namely that the preferred item is in fact the opposite of it. And God is the Granter of success.

The du'a' (supplication) is the request for an act from the one being asked, and its form is like the form of the imperative, except that du'a' is addressed to one above you, while the imperative is addressed to one below you. ﴿And unless You turn away﴾, meaning, You, O Lord, now and in what is yet to come of time, ﴿their scheming from me﴾, meaning what has become confused of their deceit and their plotting, by which they intend wickedness, a stratagem to reach their aim through deception and delusion, ﴿I would incline﴾, meaning I would lean with a great inclination, ﴿toward them﴾, because of the natural inclination of the soul to such things with which the human being has been created. Whenever the fence of his protection is breached by one woman, her like will follow her, and the breach widens beyond the mender's ability to repair it. For this reason he said: ﴿and I would be﴾, meaning, in a state that is like an innate disposition, ﴿among the ignorant﴾, meaning those immersed in ignorance by committing deeds like theirs.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 34:

﴿So his Lord answered him.﴾ That is, the One who bestows favor upon him brought about, in a magnificent manner, the answering of his supplication, which was contained in this praise, because the generous one is satisfied with allusion instead of explicitness, as it has been said:

If a man praises you one day, the praise itself suffices him from your being asked.

And Allah, glorified and exalted is He, did this as an honoring of him and as a fulfillment of what had preceded from His promise in His saying: ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾ [Yusuf: 24], up to the end of the verse, ﴿so He turned away from him their plot﴾. Then He gave the reason for that in His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is the Hearing﴾, that is, of statements, ﴿the Knowing﴾ of hearts and intentions, so He answers whatever sincere intention is correct in purpose and good in resolve.

The Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 12, verse 35:

Since these matters were conducive to his elevation, and it was at that time the furthest thing from prison, had people been able to conduct their affairs according to the soundness of their intellects, God, exalted is He, informed that they opposed the caller to rectitude (al-sadad) and exchanged error (al-ghayy) for right guidance (al-rushd). This was because of His judgment that the prison was a great means of diverting their plotting (kayd) away from him and establishing his honour and power. So they did it, despite their knowledge that it was injustice and foolishness, in response to the dominant command of God and to manifest the exalted rank of Joseph by contravening customary practices again and again, and the demolition of the soundness of causes, one ball after another. Thus He said: ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ ("then") for this meaning, namely that they should have been at the utmost distance from his prison. ﴿بَدا﴾ ("it appeared"), i.e., it became manifest after being hidden, as is their habit, ﴿لَهُمْ﴾ ("to them"). Al-bada' in opinion (al-ra'y) is the changing of it because of the appearance of what had not previously appeared from it.

Since that manifestation occurred at a certain time of the age, they changed their opinion after it to another opinion. He introduced the preposition (al-jar) to indicate this, so He said: ﴿مِن بَعْدِ ما رَأوُا﴾ ("after they had seen"), i.e., their seeing ﴿الآياتِ﴾ ("the signs"), the decisive proofs of his innocence that necessitated his purity from the tearing of the shirt, the testimony of the witness, and other things.

Since the subject (fa'il) of "bada'" is an opinion (ra'y), He explained it with His statement, emphasising it, because one does not believe that a person would do what the preventive reason against it has become manifest to him: ﴿لَيَسْجُنُنَّهُ﴾ ("they would imprison him"), so he remained in prison ﴿حَتّى حِينٍ﴾ ("for a time"), i.e., until that rumour is forgotten and people show that if she had loved him she would not have striven to imprison him. It was said: that time was seven years. It was said: the cause of that was that she said to the Aziz: "This one has disgraced me among the people, and he is apologising to them and describing the matter as he likes, while I am confined. So either you permit me to go out and apologise as he apologises, or you make him equal to me in prison." Abu Hayyan said: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "He was commanded, so he was carried on a donkey and a drum was beaten before him, and it was proclaimed in the markets of Egypt that Joseph the Hebrew had intended his mistress, so this is his recompense, that he should be imprisoned!" Abu Salih said: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, did not mention this narration except that he wept. End of quotation. This is evidence for His statement ﴿إنَّ كَيْدَكُنَّ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, your plotting is great") [Yusuf: 28].

The Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi said in his book Lawami': In sum, all the states of Joseph, peace be upon him, are gentleness within harshness, blessing within the folds of affliction and calamity, ease within hardship, hope within despair, and deliverance after "no escape" (lat manas). The driver of destiny sometimes drives destiny toward what is decreed with harshness, and sometimes drives it with gentleness, and subjugation and harshness are more praiseworthy in outcome and less in consequence. End of quotation.

When he mentioned the prison, which was an obvious cause of humiliation, Glorified is He began to relate from his affair therein what its outcome was: that He made it a cause of honor. All of this is an explanation of his dominance over the matter and his being characterized by attributes of power, together with what this contains of a clarification that realized the faithful promise that had preceded for Yusuf, peace be upon him, and other than that of the judgment. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there entered﴾, that is, they imprisoned him as it had appeared to them, [p. 80] and there entered ﴿with him into the prison two young men﴾, the baker of the king and his cupbearer. It was reported to him that the baker intended to poison him, and he thought that the cupbearer had colluded with him in that. The word "ma'a" (with) indicates companionship and its establishment, so it indicates that the three entered the prison at one time, as Abu Hayyan said. When they entered the prison, Yusuf, peace be upon him, was good to his companions: he consoled their grieved, visited their sick, asked on behalf of their poor, guided them to goodness, and reminded them of God. So hearts inclined toward him and souls became fond of him, because of the goodness of his speech, the gentleness of his manner, and the virtue, nobility, and good character and form with which God had endowed him. There were people in the prison whose hope had been cut off and whose affliction had grown severe, and he continued to be gentle with them until they said: "May God bless you! How good your face is, how good your form is, and how good your speech is! Blessed for us has been our neighborhood with you. We do not wish that we were in anything other than this, because of what you tell us of reward, expiation, merit, and purity. Who are you, young man?" So he informed them of his noble lineage. The keeper of the prison said: "If I could, I would release your way! But I will be good to your neighborhood and generous to you." The two young men loved him and clung to him. So he said: "I beseech you both by God not to love me, for by God, no one has ever loved me without affliction entering upon me through him! My aunt loved me, and affliction entered upon me through her. Then my father loved me, and affliction entered upon me through him. [p. 81] Then the wife of my master [this] loved me, and affliction entered upon me through her. So do not love me." But they refused except to love him. It was as if it were said: "What happened to them both after entering with him?" So it was said: ﴿One of them said﴾ to Yusuf, peace be upon him. Perhaps the emphasis is either because their custom was joking, or because they had not seen anything, as al-Sha'bi said, and they only made this claim in order to test him: ﴿"Indeed I see myself"﴾ he narrated the past state in a dream: ﴿"pressing wine"﴾. Pressing ("'asr") is relying on what has moisture in it in order to extract from it, ﴿"wine"﴾, that is, grapes that would become wine. ﴿"And the other said"﴾, emphasizing the like of what passed: ﴿"Indeed I see myself carrying"﴾. Carrying is lifting a thing by means of a support for transporting it, ﴿"upon my head bread"﴾, that is, food prepared for eating with bread, which is the work of dough kneaded, spread out and pressed, in an oven over fire until it becomes fit for eating. ﴿"Of which the birds eat"﴾. The interpretation of the dream from the Torah will come later. It was as if it were said: "What do you want from informing us of this?" So they said: ﴿"Inform us"﴾, that is, inform us with a great informing, ﴿"of its interpretation"﴾, that is, what its matter returns to and becomes. It was as if it were said: "What makes you think that I know its interpretation?" So they said: ﴿"Indeed we see you"﴾, according to our knowledge of it, a knowledge that is like sight, that you are ﴿"among the good-doers"﴾, that is, among the two most excellent in the description of goodness in every matter you undertake. Therefore it occurred to us that you are good at interpretation, by analogy.

When he saw that they were discerning in matters, ﴿he said﴾, indicating that he knows that and something more subtle than it, so that they would accept his counsel concerning what is the most important matter for everyone, which is what the servants were created for, namely gathering upon God. This frees them to understand his speech and to accept everything he presents, since they need his legal opinion (iftaʾ). He confirms what they had described him with, of goodness, by what he followed up with, describing himself as possessing knowledge, seizing the opportunity for counsel while they are in this state of submission, with the greatest counsel one can give: commanding sincerity in the worship of the Creator and turning away from association (shirk). Therefore, whenever someone with knowledge is asked a question by anyone, he should precede his answer with counsel about what matters most to that person, and describe himself to him in a way that makes him desire to accept his knowledge, if the situation calls for that. This is not self-praise (tazkiyah) but a guidance to follow him in what brings one closer to God, so that he receives a reward like his. ﴿No food will come to you﴾, meaning while you are awake. By saying ﴿you will be provided with it﴾, which is built in the passive form for generality, he clarified that this applies specifically to the two of them and not to the people of the prison. ﴿Except that I will have informed you﴾, meaning I will have informed you with a great and magnificent information, ﴿of its interpretation (taʾwil)﴾, meaning of it and of what its affair will turn back to and return to.

Since the explanation covered the whole period between it and the food that preceded it, he removed the preposition and said ﴿before it comes to you﴾, meaning: I informed you that food of such and such a kind will come to you, and it will be a cause of such and such, for the causing effect that arises from the cause is the wealth.

When he described himself with the knowledge that would move every person of resolve to strive in the means by which he obtained that knowledge, so that he would become like him or come close to him, and it was a place where someone might say, "From where did you acquire that knowledge?", he answered, guiding to God and calling to Him in the best manner, with what souls incline toward, namely the hope for His bounty: ﴿That is [a part]﴾, meaning that great matter. He drew attention to the abundance of his knowledge by using partitive expression in his words ﴿of what my Lord has taught me﴾, meaning the One who brought me into being, nurtured me, and did good to me. I did not say it from soothsaying or astrology. It is as if it was said: why does no one other than you know it as you have been taught? So he answered, giving a reason for it and encouraging everyone who does as he did to seek God's bounty, emphasizing, to make known that this is a great matter that befits one like him to do: ﴿Indeed, I have abandoned the creed (millah) of a people﴾, meaning even though they were capable of attempting what they wanted, so they were able to harm me and imprison me after seeing the signs that testify to me. He drew attention to the fact that only one who does not reckon the consequence in any way would undertake such a thing. Then he said: ﴿who do not believe﴾, meaning they renew their disbelief because of their long-standing entrenchment in unbelief, ﴿in God﴾, meaning the Supreme Sovereign, whose affair is not hidden from anyone of understanding among the people of Egypt and others. Then he alluded to warning against the Day of Recompense, on which no one will avail another in anything, drawing attention to the fact that disbelief in it is what cuts one off from knowledge and from every good. So he said, emphasizing with a [great] emphasis, indicating that their affair should be rejected by everyone who hears it and should not be believed, because of the very clear evidences concerning the Hereafter that necessitate that no one deny it: ﴿and they, in the Hereafter﴾, meaning the abode to which gathering is unavoidable, because it is the locus of wisdom, ﴿they﴾, meaning in their inner selves just as they are in their outward appearances. The repetition of the pronoun points out that these people were singled out for this ignorance, while others have been guided. ﴿are disbelievers﴾, meaning they are deeply immersed in covering it up, so their hearts were darkened and they became forms without meanings.

Millah: the way of a group in which some of them protect others in religion. Its root is from al-maliylah, which is a fever that afflicts a person, as stated by al-Rummani. In al-Qamus: al-maliylah is the heat that lies dormant in the bone. He expressed it with "I abandoned" (taraktu) in place of "I avoided" (tajannabtu), even though he never engaged with that creed at all, as a way of making them comfortable and drawing them gently toward abandoning theirs;

Then he followed that with what points to the nobility of his lineage. He put forward his excellence by noting that he is from the house of prophethood and the mine of chivalry (futuwwa), so that this would be more conducive to his words being accepted, his arrows hitting their mark, and his aim being achieved. He said: ﴿And I have followed﴾, i.e., with utmost effort and desire, ﴿the religion of my fathers: Abraham﴾, the Friend of God, who is the grandfather of his father; ﴿and Isaac﴾, his son, a prophet of God, who is his grandfather; ﴿and Jacob﴾, his father, Israel: God. He is his father in truth. That is the tolerant monotheism (al-hanifiyya al-samha) (the ḥanīfiyya), which is inclining toward the evidence without rigid adherence to desire in any way. Al-Bukhari narrated in the Tafsir and elsewhere, from Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked: Who are the most noble people? He said: The most noble of them before God are the most God-conscious. They said: We are not asking you about this. He said: [The most noble of people is Joseph, the prophet of God, son of a prophet of God, son of a prophet of God, son of the Friend of God]. They said: We are not asking you about this. He said: Are you asking me about the mines of the Arabs? They said: Yes. He said: The best of you in the Jahiliyya are the best of you in Islam, when they gain understanding."

So it is as if it were said: What is that religion? He said: ﴿It was not for us﴾, i.e., it was not valid or proper in any way, because of the light of knowledge we possess, which has left us no confusion at all, ﴿to associate﴾, i.e., to renew at any time any part of association ﴿with God﴾, i.e., the One to whom all affair belongs, and he intensified the negation [so he said]: ﴿anything﴾, i.e., by what He prescribed for us of the upright religion, our religion was monotheism. Among the emphatic devices is the generality within the context of negation, so that this includes every thing: a rational being, a king, a human, a jinn, or anything else. Then he gave the reason for that by which it is known that just as this was obligatory upon them, it is obligatory upon everyone. So he said: ﴿That﴾, i.e., this negation was, or that prescribing of the ḥanīfiyya religion and its facilitation, and making the primordial natures (al-fiṭar al-ūlā) submissive to it and inclined toward it, is ﴿of the grace of God﴾, the Exalted in rank, the Great in measure, ﴿upon us﴾ specifically, ﴿and upon mankind﴾, who are our brothers in lineage, in general. So we and some of mankind have thanked God, and accepted what He graced upon us, and so we did not associate anything with Him. Grace (al-fadl) is the additional benefit beyond the measure of what is obligatory; every gift of God is grace, for nothing is obligatory upon Him. Therefore it was obligatory upon everyone to make monotheism sincere for Him, as gratitude for His grace, because the two proofs of reason and transmission converge that thanking the benefactor is obligatory. ﴿But most people﴾, [i.e., -] because of the turmoil they have with desire, have become blind to this obligation, so they ﴿do not give thanks﴾ for His grace by sincerity of action toward Him, and they associate with Him, being compelled by their primordial natures. Thus the verse is of the ihtibak (a rhetorical device where one element is mentioned and its counterpart is omitted): it mentions the negation of association first, which indicates its existence second, and it mentions the negation of thanks second, which indicates the omission of its affirmation first.

When He had set forth for them the proof of the true religion (al-dīn al-ḥanīfī), following the essence of creation, which is firmly established in minds: that God, exalted is He alone, is the Bestower of blessings, and therefore thanking Him is obligatory. After He had established for them the matter of His prophethood and the proof of it through what He told them of the unseen, and had called them to what was obligatory for them of tawḥīd (affirmation of God's oneness), which is Islam, while most of creation, except for the rare few, acknowledge the true God but associate with Him some of His creation, He followed this with the proof of mutual interference (burhān al-tamānu') against the corruption of every religion other than Islam, which all the prophets and messengers agreed upon, to confirm the evidence of transmission with decisive reason. [So he said], addressing them both by the title of companionship, with the particle used when something has a great impact on souls, in a place where affection is pure, sincere counsel is unmixed, hearts are cleared, and sincerity is deliberately intended in hope of deliverance: ﴿O two companions of the prison﴾. And ṣuḥba (companionship) is a constant attachment of specialization, like the companions of al-Shāfi'ī, for example, because of their constant attachment to his school; it is different from constant attachment of mere contact.

When their understanding was occupied by the call, he struck their hearing with a denial combined with an affirmation, and so he said: ﴿Are lords (arbāb) scattered (mutafarriqūn)?﴾ That is, gods (ālihah) that are ﴿scattered﴾, differing in their essences and realities, that you witness as needing a place, even though they are inanimate. Had they been living, their mutual interference would have been possible, which would lead to the possibility of each one's incapacity, which decisively shows that none of them is fit for divinity. ﴿Is better (khayr)﴾, that is, greater in the quality of praise and more deserving of obedience, ﴿or Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿the One (al-Wāḥid)﴾ in His essence, so He needs nothing at all, ﴿the Subduer (al-Qahhār)﴾ over everything, whose subjugation never ceases to recur forever. This is a proof with no error in it, as he thought. He (ﷺ) presented it in the form of a question to draw the listener's attention, having left the knowledge to him. He called them "lords" (arbāb) in accordance with their own claim, and likewise the comparative form (ukhayr/khayr) was used, because this is closer to fairness, as it is gentler in speech, and therefore more likely to be accepted.

When the answer to everyone who has understanding is "Allah is best," he indicated this by stating the matter firmly after that question. He denied their fitness for divinity before this possibility by their lifelessness, and on the supposition that they are alive, by their incapacity. So He said: ﴿What you worship﴾. Worship ('ibadah) is submission of the heart at the highest degree of submission. He showed the lowliness and baseness of what they worship by His words: ﴿besides Him﴾, that is, [Allah -] the One whose proof of mutual exclusion, which is the greatest proof, has been established for His divinity and for His exclusive possession of it, ﴿are only names﴾. He made clear what He intends and explained it by His words: ﴿that you have named﴾, that is, beings for which you invented names, ﴿you and your fathers﴾, with no meanings [in them -], because they have no spirits, let alone that they could possess in reality the meaning of divinity by which you named them. And if they had spirits, then divinity, which is absolute perfection that entails comprehensive knowledge and power, would still be negated from them in particular.

Since the purpose of the surah is to describe the Book as a clear exposition of guidance, and since negating the sending down was sufficient for clarity, because the worship of idols is false, and since the context was not one of disputation like that in al-A'raf, which would require obstinacy, procrastination, contention and prolonged argument, He said, negating the sending down in any manner whatsoever: ﴿Allah has not sent down﴾, that is, the One who encompasses all in knowledge and power,

﴿no authority﴾ for them, so no one has any command with Him regarding them. He intensified the negation and said: ﴿any authority﴾, that is, any proof by which one could gain power to magnify them. Thus the magnification of them was negated, whether for their own essence or for something else. The essential content of the argument is this: if they were living beings who could judge, they would not be fit for divinity, because their mutual opposition would make possible the incapacity of each of them, and that entails that none of them has fitness for divinity. But they are not living beings, so they are even more deserving of lacking fitness. Therefore it is known with certainty that there is no ruling for one who is subdued, and that everyone for whom a second is possible is subdued. From this is certainly concluded that rule belongs only to Allah, the One, the Subduer, and He has not ordered their magnification. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Rule belongs only to Allah﴾, that is, the One specially characterized by attributes of perfection. Rule (hukm) is the decisive settling of a matter according to what wisdom requires.

When rule was removed from others, and this was sufficient to make His unity obligatory, out of desire for what is with Him and fear of what is in His hand, He followed it, as confirmation of this and as binding upon them, with the statement that He has decreed it, so He said: ﴿He has commanded that you worship none but Him﴾, that is, O creatures, at any time and in any state, ﴿none but Him﴾, that is, He is the one whose command is executed, the one obeyed, the Judge.

When this proof was established in this clear manner, it was fitting to point to His excellence, so He indicated it with the particle of distance, to draw attention to the elevation of His station and the greatness of His rank, and He said: ﴿That﴾, that is, the greatest matter, which is His unity and His singling out from His creation, ﴿is the upright religion﴾ [that is -], which has no crookedness, so that deficiency could reach it from the side of its crookedness; its matter is manifest to whoever has a heart. ﴿But most people﴾, that is, because of the agitation they have with their desires, ﴿do not know﴾, that is, they have no knowledge, because they do not benefit from their intellects. So they are counted among dumb beasts, and for that reason they do not single out Allah in worship.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 41:

When his counsel was perfected and his standing was raised by his conveying to the two of them what was most important for them had they known it, namely its outcome in the everlasting life and the eternal exaltation, he turned to their need, to establish what he had mentioned and to confirm what he had settled. So he addressed them with the particle that indicates that what follows it is speech of great weight, so that their souls might gather to hear what is conveyed to them of the interpretation, and he said: ﴿O my two fellow prisoners!﴾, meaning, the prison, in which fortunes pass away, brokenness of the self occurs, and softness arises in the heart, so that affection is made pure within it.

Since the answer contained something that would grieve the baker, he left it general, so that each of them might suppose that he was the one who would be saved; if he compelled him to specify, that would be an excuse for him to depart from what is most fitting, so he said: ﴿As for one of you﴾, and he is the cupbearer, who will be released and will draw near, ﴿he will give his lord﴾, meaning his master whom he serves, ﴿to drink wine﴾ as he used to do. ﴿As for the other﴾, and he is the baker.

Since the one who has the capacity to be crucified is in fact the king, he built the verb for the passive in his saying: "he will be crucified" and perish, "and the birds will eat" — meaning that from his crucifixion it follows that the birds will eat ﴿from his head﴾. The verse is of the type of ihtibak: the mention of the one who is safe and near first, as a sign of the perishing, and the mention of the one who perishes second, as a sign of the safety first. Its explanation of the interpretation from the Torah will come later. It is as if it were said: "Look carefully at what you are saying!" It is related that they both said: "We saw nothing; we were only playing." So he said, indicating by the passive form the greatness of God and the ease of affairs for Him: ﴿The matter has been decreed﴾, and he explained it by his saying: ﴿concerning which you both inquire﴾, meaning you seek a ruling concerning it, acting upon the basis of the request for a fatwa; so you asked about its interpretation, which is the interpretation of your dreams, whether you were lying or telling the truth. I did not say it out of ignorance or error. How excellent is the placing of this firm knowledge to conclude the preceding verse, by negating knowledge from most people. And "one" (aḥad) is that which is specified from among the genitive noun by an indefinite, [for him,] like the attribute of the genitive noun; this is not the case with "some" (ba'ḍ), so one does not say: "I saw one of the two men" except with a man from among them, unlike "some." And fatwa is the answer by way of the meaning of the ruling, which is other than the answer by its cause; this was mentioned by al-Rummani. Perhaps their two visions point to what the king's vision points to: the juice indicates the green ears of grain and the fat cows, because it comes only from surplus; and the bread, which birds flew over and fates carried away with the spirit of its owner, points to the dry ears and the lean cows. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 42:

Since all knowledge is nothing in comparison with the knowledge of Allah, He expressed His knowledge by the word *al-zann* (supposition). It is also possible that *al-zann* is used in its proper sense, since he (Yusuf) said what he said after *ijtihad* (independent reasoning) based on indications. From this it is taken that it is permissible to be certain of what leads to a *zann* (a probable conclusion). So He said: ﴿And he said﴾, that is, Yusuf, peace be upon him, ﴿to the one who thought﴾, while being certain that he meant knowledge, because of His saying: ﴿the matter has been decided﴾ [Yusuf: 41]. It is also possible that the pronoun in *zanna* (thought) refers to the cupbearer. In that case it is used in its proper sense: ﴿that he would be saved from the two﴾, who is the cupbearer, ﴿Mention me to your lord﴾, that is, your master, the king of Egypt, by what you have seen of me of lofty character and purity of disposition, which indicate my distance from what I have been accused of. The meaning of "lord" here is other than its meaning in His saying: ﴿Are separate lords better?﴾ [Yusuf: 39]. So the cupbearer was saved and his companion was crucified, in accordance with what Yusuf, peace be upon him, had told them both. ﴿So Satan made him forget﴾, that is, the cupbearer, ﴿the mention﴾, that is, the one far from mercy, burned with the curse, ﴿of his lord﴾, that is, Yusuf, peace be upon him, ﴿before his lord﴾, that is, because of his reliance on him in that matter. ﴿So he remained﴾, that is, Yusuf, peace be upon him, because of this forgetting, ﴿in the prison﴾ from the time he entered until he left, ﴿for several years﴾, so that he would know that all causes take effect only through Allah, the Exalted. The real meaning of *bid'* (a few) is from three to nine. It is related here that it was seven.

He mentions what has passed of this story from the Torah (al-Tawrah).

After what has passed, it says: "Then the Midianites brought Joseph down into Egypt and sold him to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, from the hand of the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there. And [the LORD] was with Joseph, and he was a successful man, and he remained in the house of his master the Egyptian. His master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD made all he did prosper. So Joseph found favour in his sight, and became his servant, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put in his charge. From the time he made him overseer over his house and over all that he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake; the blessing of the LORD was upon all that he had in the house and in the field. So he left all that he had in Joseph's charge, and with him there he knew nothing except the bread which he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance."

After these things, his master's wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said: "Lie with me." But he refused and said to his master's wife: "Behold, because of me my master does not know what is in the house, and he has put all that he has in my charge. He is not greater in this house than I am, and he has kept back nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?" And although she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her, to lie beside her or to be with her. But one day he went into the house to do his work, and none of the men of the house was there in the house. She caught him by his garment, saying: "Lie with me." But he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house. When she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and had fled out of the house, she called to the men of her household and said to them: "See, he has brought among us a Hebrew to laugh at us; he came in to lie with me, and I cried out with a loud voice. But when he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment with me and fled and got out of the house."

She kept his garment by her until his master came home, and she told him the same story, saying: "The Hebrew servant, whom you brought among us, came in to me to laugh at me. But as I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment with me and fled out of the house." When his master heard the words of his wife, which she spoke to him, saying: "This is what your servant did to me," his anger burned. And Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were confined. So he was there in the prison. But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison. And the keeper of the prison committed to Joseph's charge all the prisoners who were in the prison, and whatever was done there, he was the one who did it. The keeper of the prison paid no heed to anything that was in Joseph's charge, because the LORD was with him. And whatever he did, the LORD made it prosper.

After these things, the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and his baker committed an offence against their lord, the king of Egypt. (In one copy, in place of "the baker," it reads: "and the chief of the cooks.") Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker (in one copy: "the cooks"), and he put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph was confined. The captain of the guard assigned them to Joseph, and he attended them. They continued for some time in custody. And they both dreamed a dream, each his own dream, in one night, each man with the interpretation of his own dream: the cupbearer and the baker (in one copy: "and the cook") of the king of Egypt, who were confined in the prison. When Joseph came to them in the morning, he saw that they were troubled. So he asked Pharaoh's officers who were with him in custody in his master's house, saying: "Why are your faces sad today?" They said to him: "We have had dreams, and there is no one to interpret them." Joseph said to them: "Do not interpretations belong to God? Tell them to me, please."

The chief cupbearer told his dream to Joseph and said to him: "In my dream, behold, there was a vine before me, and on the vine were three branches. As soon as it budded, its blossoms came out and its clusters ripened into grapes. Pharaoh's cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup, and I placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand." Joseph said to him: "This is its interpretation: the three branches are three days. Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore you to your office, and you shall place Pharaoh's cup in his hand as you did formerly, when you were his cupbearer. But think of me when it is well with you, and show kindness to me, and make mention of me to Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house. For I was indeed stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the pit."

When the chief baker saw that he had given a good interpretation, he said to Joseph: "I also had a dream: there were three baskets of white bread on my head. In the top basket were all sorts of baked food for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head." Joseph answered and said: "This is its interpretation: the three baskets are three days. Within three days Pharaoh will lift off your head and hang you on a tree, and the birds will eat your flesh from you."

On the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he made a feast for all his servants. He lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker (in one copy: "the cooks") among his servants. He restored the chief cupbearer to his office, so that he again gave the cup into Pharaoh's hand, but he hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had interpreted to them. Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.

— Translation of the passage ends here.

When the means that Yusuf (peace be upon him) had asked for was nullified, namely reminding the cupbearer of him, God, glory be to Him, brought about another means through which He would carry out what He willed of Yusuf's rule, and what He had decreed concerning the prostration of those whom the stars pointed to. So He said, indicating this: ﴿And the king said﴾. He is a person with power and wide reach, over whom governance and management are exercised. He spoke to his assembly, namely the magicians, the soothsayers, the *hazrah* (those who divine by reading signs in the body and the ground), the *qafah* (those who read traces and resemblances), and the wise men. He emphasised his words so that he would be known to be right in what he said, without being tested: ﴿Indeed, I see﴾. He used the present tense to narrate the situation, because of how greatly it alarmed him: ﴿seven fat cows﴾. *Simn* (fatness) is the increase of the body in flesh and fat. ﴿Which seven [lean ones] devour﴾, [i.e. -] cows ﴿lean﴾. *ʿAjf* (leanness) is the dryness of emaciation. [The verb] "and" "I see" [governs] "seven."

Since the interpretation of the dream is drought, famine and hardship, he attached the number to the plural of paucity, unlike what occurred in the context of multiplication in His saying ﴿it grows seven (p-99) ears﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261], so he said: ﴿green ears of grain﴾. [And] "I see seven" other "ears, dry," [Qur'anic wording:] "wheat over the green ones," so the dry ones prevailed over them. It seems he omitted this because the lean ones indicate it. *Sunbulah* (an ear of grain) is a plant like a reed bearing a cluster of orderly grains. It is as if it were said: "So what happened?" Then it was said: the king said: ﴿O assembly﴾, that is, the nobles and honoured ones whose sight is filled by their appearance and whose hearts are filled by their insight and their noble deeds. ﴿Explain to me﴾, that is, answer me and make clear to me, out of your nobility, with strength and penetrating understanding.

Since his intention was that they should not stray from the aim with their answer, nor go far from it, he expressed it with a word that conveys the sense of a time frame, and so said: ﴿in my dream﴾. And he restrained them from speaking without knowledge [by his words]: ﴿if you are able to interpret dreams﴾, that is, the kind of them, ﴿to interpret﴾. The *ʿibārah* (interpretation) of a dream is its explanation by crossing (*ʿubūr*) from its outward appearance to its inner meaning, as one "crosses" (*yuʿabbaru*) a river: from *ʿabara al-nahr*, i.e. he reached its bank (*shaṭṭ*), to its other bank. Similarly, the dream was "interpreted" (*ʾuwwilat*) when you mention its outcome, its return, which is the intended aim, by striking an example.

The root, with its six permutations, *ʿarraba*, *ʿabbara*, *raʿaba*, *rubaʿa*, *baʿara*, *bara*ʿa, revolves around passing from one place to another and from one state to another, and most of that is toward something better. Thus the Arabs (*al-ʿarab*) were so named because the basis of their affairs is relocation in search of good campsites. *Aʿraba* means to speak clearly, i.e. he spoke in the language of the Arabs and made his meaning plain, that is, he carried it from foreignness and ambiguity to clarity. *Aʿraba al-Furs* means when their Arabic became pure, as if they had passed the rank of mixed-breed to that of the Arabs.
