Likewise *al-ibil al-ʿirāb* (purebred camels). *Al-ʿurūbah* is Friday, because of its elevated status above the rest of the days. *Al-ʿurūb* is the laughing woman who loves her husband, shows him affection and displays this to him; it is also the disobedient woman toward her husband, because all of these are the conduct of the Arabs. They are the most passionate of people and the most able to win hearts with sweet speech, and they are the most disobedient and the most harsh when they wish. *Al-ʿarab* (with a vowel on the middle letter pronounced as "ʿarab") means vigour, because it is a movement away from laziness. *ʿArraba* (in the pattern of *fariḥa*) means to be vigorous and also to swell, because the swollen thing exceeds the form of others. *ʿArrabtu al-biʾr* means its water increased and rose. *ʿArraba* (in the pattern of *ḍaraba*) means to eat. *Al-ʿarabah* (with the middle vowel) is a river flowing strongly. *Al-nafs* (the self) is so named because of how often it moves through thought. *Al-ʿurbūn* is the sum by which a sale is secured, so it moves the goods from one state to another. *Istaʿrabtu al-baqar* means the cows desired the stallion, either from the *ʿurūb* (the loving woman toward her husband) or because desire is transferred to them from one state to another. *Taʿraba* means he lived in the desert among the Bedouins, who do not settle in one place but follow the rain. *ʿArūbāʾ* is the name of the seventh heaven, because it is elevated above all the heavens, as if it passed beyond all of them, and because its movement is a movement for all. *Al-ʿirab* (with a vowel on the first letter pronounced as "ʿirab") is the dry stalk of the wild grass, because it has become fit to be moved even by the blowing of the wind. *Al-ʿarabī* is a white barley whose ear has two rows, as if it were ascribed to the Arabs for its excellence. *Al-iʿrāb* is making a horse run and knowing the purebred Arab horse from the mixed-breed, because the state of ignorance of that passes to the state of knowledge. And [*iʿrāb* is] not making mistakes in speech, as if one thereby passed from foreignness to Arabic. *ʿArība al-rajul* (in the pattern of *iʿrāb* with a vowel on the middle letter) means he became overfull, and likewise a horse from fodder; and its stomach became corrupt; and his wound left a mark after healing. All of these transfer from one state to another. *Al-taʿrīb* is refining speech from error, as if one raised oneself to the Arabs. It is also cutting the fronds of the palm tree, because one moves them from their state to a better one. And that the animal should have its... [text damaged] then ... *Al-taʿrīb* and *al-iʿrāb* also mean what is ugly in speech, and condemning the speech of the speaker, as if it were a judgment that his Arabic has gone. Both also mean turning away from what is ugly, and that is bringing him into the qualities of the Arabs, which are the noble characters. Both also mean marriage, or allusion to it, because it moves a person from one state to another and from one action to another, in word and deed. *Al-taʿrīb* is also drinking much clear water, and acquiring a purebred Arab horse. It is said of a person: "ʿArīb," that is, someone who speaks clearly.

*ʿAbara al-ru'yā* means he explained it and reported what its matter would come to, as if he crossed its outward appearance to one of its inner parts. *ʿAbartu al-kitāb ʾaʿburuhu ʿabran*: I reflected upon it without raising your voice over it. *ʿAbartu al-nahr*: I crossed it from its bank (*ʿabr*), i.e. its side, to its other bank. *Al-ʿabar* is also the side, because one crosses from it and to it. *Al-maʿbar* is a boat by which one crosses the river, and a bank prepared for crossing. *ʿAbar al-qawm*: the people died. *Al-ʿibrah* (with a vowel on the first letter pronounced as "ʿibrah") is wonder; and (with a vowel on the first letter pronounced "ʿabrah") is a tear before it overflows, as if it had the force of flowing, or as if it repeats weeping in the chest, or sorrow without weeping, because that is the beginning of the flow of tears. In *Mukhtaṣar al-ʿAyn*: *ʿabrat al-damʿ* is its flowing, and *al-ʿabrah* is the tear itself.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 43 (part 2 of 2):

Al-ʿUbar (with a ḍamma, and it may also be vowelled ʿabar): the swelling of the eye, and the abundance of anything. It is also the plural of ʿābir (passing), because that is a crossing beyond the limit of paucity. Also, they permit whatever they wish. A majlis ʿabar (with kasra or fatḥa on the ʿayn) is one with many people in it, for the same reason. Also, it is fit for passing with its company from one state to another. A woman who is mustaʿbira (with the bāʾ possibly fatḥa) is one who is not favoured, meaning she is fit for the flow of tears. A she-camel ʿabr asfār (with the vowel possibly ḍamma, kasra or fatḥa) is one that is strong. ʿAbbarat ʿan al-rajul, meaning she spoke on his behalf, as if you crossed from his thought to the thought of the addressee. ʿAbarat al-danānīr taʿbīran means she weighed them without exaggerating their weight, as if you moved from ignorance of their quantity to supposition. Or ʿābir sabīl, meaning a passer-by. Al-Shiʿrā al-ʿUbūr is a star behind al-Jawzāʾ. Al-ʿUbūr is a jadhaʿa (a goat in its second year) of the sheep, because it has passed a year and is qualified to cross with the sheep and is counted among them. Al-ʿUbūr is also said of an uncircumcised man, because his glans is passing through his foreskin. A ghulām muʿabbir is a boy who has not been circumcised. A rajul ʿabar is one who is about to reach puberty and is not yet circumcised, meaning he is about to become an adult in this condition, namely that his glans is passing through his foreskin. ʿAbbara bihi al-amr taʿbīran means the matter became severe for him, as if he passed from a state of ease to hardship. ʿAbbarat bihi means it destroyed him. Al-maʿbara (with the letter shadda lightened) is a she-camel that has not given birth for three years, so that she is firmer for it, because she has become fit for riding over journeys. Al-ʿabīr is a kind of perfume, because its scent passes (far). Saffron also (is called ʿabīr), because its colour and scent pass (far). Al-ʿabrā is the Nile lote tree, because it grows along the bank of the river. Al-maʿbar among camels is one with thick wool, and among goats is one that has not yet passed (into adulthood), as if its wool passes the limit of its skin. A sahm muʿabbir and ʿabīr is one with many feathers, as if it has passed the limit of custom. Al-ʿubar (with ḍamma) is the bereaved woman, because she is fit for the sending forth of tears. Also, the clouds that move swiftly. Also al-ʿuqāb (the eagle), because of its strength in covering distances. A plant that is ʿabar is falsehood and vanity, because of how quickly it passes away. Raʿabtu fulānan means I frightened him, so he is marʿūb (terrified), because you moved him from security to fear. A sail rāʿib means a torrent that fills the valley. Rāʿib is also a land, from which come the rāʿibiyya pigeons, and pigeons too have the power of ʿubūr (conveying) messages from place to place. Raʿabat al-ḥamāma fī ṣawtihā tarʿīban means she raised her voice. Raʿabat al-sanām means she cut it. Al-Ruʿbūba is a piece of it, because it has passed its place. A jāriya ruʿbūba or ruʿbūb is a girl of good stature and complete, as if she has surpassed her peers in beauty. Al-Ruʿb are the short people, singular raʿīb or arʿab, a comparison with a piece of the hump. Al-Baʿr is the droppings of animals with hooves or cloven hooves, except domestic cattle, because they are dried (from ṭāʾ-kh-thā, to be dried in the sun), while wild ones pass (ṭabaʿ) baʿran, because it passes from its place without soiling it, so nothing of it remains on it. Al-Muʿabbir is its place. Al-baʿīr is the adult male camel or the young one, and it may refer to the donkey and every animal that carries (loads). In Mukhtaṣar al-ʿAyn: when the Arabs see a she-camel or a male camel from afar, they say "This is a baʿīr." When they recognize it, they say of the male "jamal" and of the female "nāqa." Al-baʿra (with the vowel tahrīk) is the glans, by comparison with it. Al-Rubʿ is the dwelling and the house itself, and the mahalla (encampment), because one goes out from it and enters into it, and therefore it is called mutabawwaʾ, because one returns to it, that is, one comes back. Rabaʿa yurabbiʿu means he remained. Arbiʿ ʿalā nafsika means wait for yourself, as if it is from al-rubʿ, that is, the dwelling, because one stays in it. Rabuʿa (when it became fertile) for moving from one state to another state. Hum ʿalā ribaʿātihim means on their former steadfastness and their original affair, as if it derives from the dwelling. Al-Rawbaʿ (like jawhar) is the weak and base one, as if that follows from remaining in a dwelling. Bahāʾ is one with a short hamstring, and a short man, as if it is a comparison with the rabʿa (the medium-height person) in the sense of mere shortness in contrast with the tall. Rubʿ al-ḥajar is lifting it. Al-ḥaml is lifting it onto the mount. Al-marbūʿ is one who is lifted up and relieved, because of the change of state in all of that. Al-murabbaʿa is a piece of wood with which one lifts the load. Al-murābaʿa is that two people take each other's hand and lift the load onto the mount, as if with the transfer it is derived from al-arbaʿa (four). It is also equalizing with the spring (al-rabīʿ). From it, the she-camel's hump became long, meaning she carried it. Rabīʿ al-shuhūr are two months after Ṣafar. Rabīʿ al-futūl are two: the one in which there are blossoms and truffles, and the one in which fruits ripen, for the transition in each of them. Al-Rubʿ (like ṣarad) is a young camel born in spring. A she-camel muraabbaʿ is one who has a rubʿ (a spring foal). Arbaʿa al-qawm means they became four, and entered into spring, and remained in the marbaʿ (spring pasture). Rabaʿat al-arḍ means the land received spring rain. Al-marābīʿ are the early spring rains. Arbaʿa al-rajul, when a child is born to him in his youth, as a comparison of youth with spring. A she-camel mirbāʿ is one whose habit is to give birth in the rabʿiyyat al-qayẓ (the autumn). Al-Rabʿiyya is the beginning of winter. Al-Rabīʿ is the rivulet, because of its flow and the growth of what is around it, and its plural is arbiʿāʾ. They lift the stone to test the strength. The fourth after the third, because it is beyond the group. A string or rope that is marbūʿ is twisted from four strands. Rabbaʿtu al-qawm urabbiʿuhum means I became their fourth. Al-Arbiʿāʾ is a day. Al-Mirbāʿ is a quarter of the spoils, which the chief used to take. Al-Rubāʿiyya (like thamāniya) is the tooth between the incisor and the canine, and its number is four. Every number that reaches four is rubāʿ, like thamān (eight). You say of the sheep in its fourth year, and of cattle and solid-hoofed animals in the fifth, and of the camel in the seventh: arbaʿat, as if one cannot pass in every kind from the limit of smallness to largeness except by this. Arbaʿa al-faras means the horse dropped its rubāʿiyya (its tooth). Ḥummā rubʿ comes on the fourth day. Rabuʿa al-rajul and arbaʿa, and this is the meaning of what the Qamus (the dictionary) said: rabbaʿathu al-ḥummā means fever took him every other day, because its second day is the fourth of its first day. Al-Rabʿa (with fatḥa) is the perfumer's jar, so that its scent may spread. The man between the tall and the short, with the vowel tahrīk, is like al-marbūʿ, because he passes the limit of each of them: this one toward tallness, and that one toward shortness. Irtabaʿa means he became a rabʿa. Al-Ribʿa (with vowel tahrīk) is the fastest running of camels. The distance between the stones of the cooking pot, because each of them crosses from the place of its companion. Arbaʿa māʾ al-rakiyya means it increased, so it passed its original place. ʿAlā fulān means he asked him, then went, then they returned to him. ʿAlā al-mar'a means he returned to intercourse with her. The people's camels in such-and-such a place: they grazed them and let them go to the water, coming whenever they wished. It is also possible that this is from the spring. Arbaʿat al-nāqa, when she closes her womb and does not accept water, as if she removed the ʿubūr, that is, moving from one state to another. Al-Rabīʿa is the helmet of arms, because it carries its wearer to safety. Al-Rawḍa, because the growth of plants in it passes the limit of the earth. Al-Murabbaʿ is the ship's sail, because it is the instrument of movement. Al-Murabbaʿ is a man of many marriages, because he passes from his former state, and because he sits between the four branches. Tarabbaʿa in his sitting, opposite of jathā (kneeling), either because he has become like the murabbaʿ (square), or taking from al-rubʿ (dwelling), because it is the sitting posture of one who remains in his house. Tarabbaʿat al-nakhīl means the palm trees broke and were cut, because of the change in their state. Istarbaʿa al-raml means the sand piled up, either because it passed from its first state, or from remaining in the rubʿ. Istarbaʿa al-ghubār means the dust rose. The camel for travelling: it became strong for it and endured. The man with the matter: he became independent and patient. Fulān yuqīmu rabbāʿat qawmihi means he manages the affairs and state of his people, that is, he moves them from one state to another. There passed from the sons of such-and-such a rubūʿ after rubūʿ, meaning living groups after living groups, either because that is a passing from house to house and state to state, or by omission of a noun, meaning people of dwellings, that is, residences. Al-Yarbūʿ is an animal like a mouse, either because of the intensity of its running, or because it makes two burrow exits and flees from whichever it wishes, so it is crossing and moving by power even if it is at rest. Al-Yarbūʿ is also the flesh of the back, as if it is compared to the animal. Baraʿa al-rajul (with three vowels) means he surpassed his companions in knowledge or other things, or he was complete in every virtue and beauty. This one is abraʿ than that one: more massive, because he passed its measure. Al-bāriʿ is the noble one with sound judgement. Tabarraʿa bil-ʿaṭāʾ means he gave generously beyond what was obligatory on him from his own self, as if he passed the rank of the obligatory. And God knows best.

In the verse is what the state of the scholars requires of the need of kings for them,

Then it is as if it were said: "What did they say?" It was answered: ﴿They said: "These are confused jumbles of dreams"﴾. That is, *aghlat* (mixtures), the plural of *dighth* (ضِغْث, with a kasra on the ḍād and a sukūn on the ghayn), which is a handful of grass mixing the green with the dry. ﴿Dreams﴾ means varied and confused, the plural of *ḥulm* (حُلْم, with a ḍammah on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn or ḍammah on the lām), which is *ru'yā* (vision). They qualified the dream with *adghāth*, which is a dream that is false, because it comes from the self's own talk or the whispering of Satan, and because it resembles mixtures of plants that have no affinity between them. A dream may sometimes come from the angel, and it is then true; sometimes it comes from Satan's distortion and confusions; and sometimes from the self's own talk.

[Then] they said: ﴿And we are not⦅...⦆﴾, that is, all of us, "with interpretation" (*ta'wīl*, the explanation or the outcome) of "dreams," that is, of confused dreams and others alike. They went to great lengths in the negation with their words "learned," so they deceived in more than one way. They gathered together, though it was a single dream, so as to make it confused jumbles with no meaning. They negated from themselves "absolute knowledge," which entails the negation of "knowledge of the particular," after they had framed their speech in this form, so as to give the impression that they did not know it except because it was confused jumbles. And Allah knows best.

The word *qawl* (قول, "saying") is speech that implies quotation when it is explained, so when it is stated that he said something, it requires a quotation of what he said. But when it is stated that he spoke, it does not require a quotation of what he spoke. The root *ḥ-l-m* (حلم), in all its permutations, revolves around turning a thing away from its true form, its habit, and what its natural disposition requires, as will come in Surat al-Ra'd in His words: ﴿Mighty in strength﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:13].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 45:

When this situation became a reminder to the cupbearer about Yusuf, peace be upon him, (p-111) Allah, glory be to Him, informed that he remembered him after his forgetfulness. So He said, turning away from the particle "fa" (then) to indicate that he was among those who were saved: ﴿And the one who was saved of the two said﴾, that is, the one who escaped from destruction, "from them both," that is, from the two companions of the prison, and he was the cupbearer. "And" the situation was that he "remembered" (idkara), with the unpointed dal, meaning he sought remembrance, with the pointed dhal, its form being ifta'ala. ﴿After a time﴾ of the periods, that is, long and gathered periods of time. ﴿I will inform you﴾, that is, I will inform you with a great information, ﴿of its interpretation﴾, that is, of the explanation of what this dream will ultimately mean, alone, as is the truth. The statement "So send me forth" follows from his words, that is, send me to Yusuf, peace be upon him, for he is the most knowledgeable of people, so send him to him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: The prison was not in the city.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 46:

He came to him, and the cupbearer who had been sent, after reaching him, called out to him with a near call, showing affection toward him: "Yusuf." He increased the affection with his words: "O truthful one (al-Siddiq)," meaning the one who is exceedingly truthful and who is believed in what deserves to be believed, by what we have tested of him and seen shining upon him. "Explain to us" (Aftina), meaning: mention to us the ruling "concerning seven" (fi sab'in), and he specified the number with the sound plural (jam' al-salamah), which is for the few, as has passed regarding what has passed, and he said: ﴿seven fat cows﴾, meaning which the king saw, ﴿which seven lean ones devour﴾, meaning from among the cows, ﴿very thin﴾, meaning extremely emaciated. "And" concerning "seven green ears of grain" (sunbulat), the plural of sunbulah, which is the gathering place of the grain from the crop, "green and" concerning seven "others" [meaning] of the ears, ﴿dry﴾. He framed the answer to the question in the manner of hope, either following the habits of sensible people in not deciding matters of the future, or because he regretted after sending (for the question) out of fear that the interpretation would be something he could not confront the king with, so he resolved to flee, on this assumption. Or, out of haste, to have Yusuf, peace be upon him, give the ruling so that he would hasten to return, since the people were in the utmost anticipation of him. So he said: ﴿Perhaps I may return to the people﴾ before some obstacle prevents me.

[And since their affirmation of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and their knowledge afterward of his virtue and their acting upon what he commanded them was conjectural, he said]: ﴿That perhaps they may know﴾, meaning, so that they would be hopeful of knowing your virtue, or what indicates it of good or evil, so that they would know, in every case, what they are able to act upon.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 47:

It is as if it was said: "Then what did he say to him?" It is said: "He said": its interpretation is that you will ﴿sow﴾, meaning you will bring about cultivation (al-zira'a). So it is a report of an unseen matter, and it is more fitting to the sense of the speech. It is possible that it is a report with the meaning of a command (p-113) ﴿seven years in succession﴾, meaning persistently and diligently (da'ibin mujtahidin). Al-da'b (persistence) is the continuation of a thing according to its habit. As your vision indicated by the pressing of wine, which does not occur except after sufficiency, and as the king's vision indicated by the fat cows and the green ears of grain, and the interpretation by this indicates that these seven years will be, as you know, among the most common conditions of time, in its middle, with fertility of one land and drought of another, and the water's inability over one plot and its flooding of another, as the word al-da'b indicated. Then he guided them to what they could strengthen themselves with against the evil that would come, so he said: ﴿what you reap﴾, meaning of anything, by means of that cultivation (al-hasd: cutting the crop after it has ripened) during those fertile [seven years], ﴿leave it﴾, meaning leave it in any case, ﴿in its ear﴾, so that it does not spoil by weevils or otherwise, ﴿except a little of what you eat.﴾ Abu Hayyan said: He indicated an beneficial opinion according to the food of Egypt and its wheat, which does not keep for two years in any manner except by the device of keeping it in its ear. End of quotation.

When he had completed the interpretation, he returned to the remainder of the dream's wording, and said: ﴿Then there will come﴾. And since the period of that coming was not one that encompasses the time of the interval, he used the preposition and said: ﴿after that﴾, i.e., after this great matter, which is the seven years in which you are doing this work, ﴿seven﴾, i.e., years, ﴿hard﴾ with a great famine. These are what the dream of your companion pointed to, the one whose provision was carried off by the birds and whose spirit traveled beyond what was decreed, and what the king's dream indicated with the lean cows and the dry ears of grain. ﴿They will consume﴾: he attributed the eating to them metaphorically, meaning the eating by their people, for the sake of affirming the eating. ﴿What you have stored﴾, i.e., by saving grain ﴿for them﴾. The word taqdim (ـتقديم, "advancing") means bringing something closer toward the front. He gave them good news that the hardship would end before what they had prepared was exhausted, and so he said: ﴿except a little of what you store up﴾. The word ihsan (إحصان, "storing up") means safeguarding, which is placing something in what is like a fortified stronghold. This is the interpretation of the dream.

Then He added to that by saying: ﴿Then there will come﴾, and He expressed the preposition for the like of what passed, saying: ﴿after that﴾, meaning the great drought, "a year" ('ām), which is twelve months. Its counterpart is al-ḥawl and al-sanah (year), and it is derived from al-ʿawm (swimming), because of the long swimming its people do in it. This was said by al-Rummānī. The expression of it [ʿām] rather than its synonyms is an indication that there will be in it, from abundance of rain by general irrigation, manifest fertility and abundant blessing, a great matter. Therefore He followed it with His saying: ﴿in it﴾.

And since what is longed for is relief, while it is well known that no one is able to grant it except Allah, He said, using the passive voice: ﴿the people will be granted relief﴾, from al-ghayth, which is rain, or from al-ghawth, which is deliverance. In the first sense it is permissible to form it from the triliteral and from the quadriliteral: it is said ghātha Allāh al-arḍ and aghāthahā, meaning He sent rain upon it. In the second sense it is quadriliteral only; it is said: istaghātha bihi fa-aghāthahu, from al-ghawth, which is of the waw root, and its meaning is the benefit that comes at the height of one's need, with the removal of harm. Al-ghayth is of the yā' root and is the rain that comes at the time of need. ﴿And in it﴾, that is, that good year.

And since pressing (al-ʿaṣr) for oils and other things can only be from its abundance, He said: ﴿they will press﴾, that is, they will extract the juices of things and their essences. It seems that from the ending of the dearth He took the beginning of the fertility, which the pressing indicates in the dream of the questioner (the prisoner), and the greenness and the ghee in the dream of the king, for it is the opposite of dearth, and every pair of opposites, the ending of one of them is inevitably the beginning of the other. So the messenger came and informed the king of that, and it pleased him and his heart was inclined to its truthfulness.

**Al-Biqa'i's commentary (*Nazm al-Durar*) on Surah Yusuf (12), verse 50:**

﴿And the king said﴾, meaning the one whose service al-Aziz was in, ﴿"Bring him to me"﴾, so that I may hear that from him and honour him. The messenger went to him to bring him to the king. ﴿So when the messenger came to him﴾, meaning Yusuf, peace be upon him, who was close in time to that event, ﴿[the messenger] with that message, and he was the cupbearer, [Yusuf] said to him﴾: ﴿"Return to your lord"﴾, meaning your master, the king, ﴿"and ask him"﴾ by saying to him, as a question, ﴿"What is the case of the women"﴾. He alluded to their deception against him without stating it explicitly, and he did not mention the wife of al-Aziz out of generosity and modesty. So he said: ﴿"who cut their hands"﴾, meaning: what is the report about them in their deception which (p-116) mixed with me, so that my trial became severe because of it? For they know that the wife of al-Aziz did not invite them except after their testimony that she had solicited me. Then she confessed to them that she had solicited me, and that I had disobeyed her in the strongest disobedience. So when he asks them, the truth will become clear, for your lord is ignorant of their affair.

Since this was a situation in which he would ask about the knowledge of his lord, may He be glorified, for that reason he said, resuming and emphasizing, because they had acted in that matter with ignorance, like one who denies the reckoning, which is the outcome of knowledge: ﴿"Indeed, my lord"﴾, meaning the one who manages me and does good to me in everything I undergo, whether hardship or ease, ﴿"is Knowing of their plot"﴾ against me when they invited me to obey the wife of al-Aziz. ﴿"And I shall not leave the prison until your lord knows what has been hidden from him of their affair, which my lord knows"﴾, so that my innocence may be manifested before the assembled witnesses concerning what they have charged me with, [namely] imprisonment, which by its nature occurs only for a crime. And if my innocence is not made manifest, the speech of the envious will not cease concerning me, and they will be on the verge of striving to lower my standing with the king, and [also] so that they do not say: "He did not remain in this prison except for a great sin," in which case there would be a kind of shame that is not hidden. In this is evidence that striving to clear one's honour is good, indeed obligatory. He framed the speech as a question to the king about their affair, not as a request that he investigate their affair, because asking a person about knowledge of something he does not know stirs him up (p-117) and inflames him to search for it, unlike asking him to investigate on behalf of someone else so that that other person may know. So by this he intended to urge him to strive in the inquiry until he knows the truth, so that he would then accept everything he related to him. And *al-kayd* is: scheming in order to bring harm.

"Bal" was explained in this way because its root is *yā'iyyah* in its five permutations: *balā*, *bayala*, *labbā*, *layaba*, *yalaba*; *wāwiyyah* in its six permutations: *bawala*, *balawa*, *walaba*, *wabala*, *lawaba*, *labawa*; and *mahmūzah* (hamzated) in its four permutations: *laba'a*, *ba'ala*, *abala*, *alaba*. All of these revolve around *al-khulṭah al-muḥīlah al-mumīlah* (mixing that changes and inclines). It seems that its essential meaning is *al-balā'* in the sense of testing, examining and trying, and it occurs in good and in evil; that is, he mixed him with something by which the hidden matter of his condition becomes known. Al-Qazzaz said: "*fitnah* occurs specifically in evil, and *balā'* is a blessing, from your saying *abላytuhu khayran* (I did him a good turn) when you do a favour for him." Some of the meanings of the root were mentioned earlier in [Surah al-Anfal]. *Nāqah balawa safar* and *balā safar* means a she-camel worn out by travel, when she was strong enough to endure it. *Al-Balwā* is *al-baliyyah* (calamity). *Ableytu fulānan 'udhran* means I came between myself and him with what there is no blame in, i.e., I mixed with him something that removed blame. *Al-Baliyyah* is a beast that used to be tied in the Jahiliyyah at the grave of its owner, not fed nor watered until it died. It is said: "The people are *bi-dhī balā* and *bi-dhī baliyān*," meaning scattered, as if its essential meaning is that (p-118) a person of intense mixing came upon them and separated them. *Balā al-shay'* (with kasra, *balā* as a short form and *balā'* extended) means it wore out and perished. *Buliya fulān bi-kadhā* (passive) and *ibtalā bihi* mean it befell him. *Al-bawl* means a man's offspring, a large number, bursting forth, and the opposite of excrement; there is no doubt that each of these, when an animal mixes with it, changes its state. *Al-bāl* means concern, thought and worry; from this, in my view, comes *mā bālaytu bihi* (I did not care for it), i.e., I was not concerned with it; likewise *mā ubālīhi bālatan*, which is a verbal noun from it, and *lam ubāli bihi* and *lam ubal*. But they inverted it from *bāwaltu bihi*, so that it would not be confused with *al-bawl* (urination), and God knows best. Their essential meaning is: I did not employ my *bāl*, which is my thought, in it, even if he applies his thought to my affair, i.e., he is too insignificant to think about his affair. And it is known that thought is the locus of the inclining mixing. *Al-bāl* is also the plough-handle used in working the land, because of the hardship of the work with it. *Al-bāl* is also a thick fish called "camel of the sea," because whoever it mixes with, it changes his affair. *Al-bāl* also means prosperity of life and condition. *Al-bālah* means a flask, as if it were from *al-bawl*, (p-119) a saddlebag, and a perfume container. *Al-walab* means connection; *lubtu al-shay'* means I joined it; *walaba huwa* means he connected, entered and hastened. *Al-wālib* is the one going off in his direction, as if grief mixed with him had impelled him to that. *Walaba al-zar'* (the crop) means when it produced *wālibah*, which are shoots that sprang from its roots. *Al-wālibah* means the offspring of a people and the offspring of property. *Al-wālibah* also means quick-growing plants. *Lāba yalūbu* means he became thirsty. *Al-lābbah* means *al-ḥurrah*, a place of large, black, connected, hard, fine stones; whoever mixes with it, it tires him and makes him thirsty, and by it black camels gathered together were named, and also *al-ṣammān*. *Al-lābbah* also means the dewlap of a camel, which is something like the lung that a camel brings out from its mouth when it is agitated, as if it were what had agitated it. *Al-malāb* is a kind of perfume and saffron. *Al-mulawwab*, like *mu'aẓẓam*, of iron means the wrapped part. *Al-lūb* (with ḍamma) is the piece that turns in the pot, because it changes what is in the pot by its turning. [*Al-lu'āb*] also means saliva. *Al-ab* means his camels became thirsty. *Al-labwah* is the female lion. *Al-wābil* is heavy, intense, violently falling, large-drop rain. *Al-wābilah* is the offspring of camels and sheep, (p-120) the head of the upper arm which is in the socket, and what has wrapped around the thigh's flesh. *Al-muwābalah* means persistence. *Al-mībal* is a braid of hide assembled on a stick with which camels are struck. *Wūbila al-ṣayd* means a swift, intense pursuit; *bi-al-na'jah* and *bal-lah shadīdah* means a strong desire of a ewe when she seeks the stallion. *Al-wabāl* means severity and evil consequence, and it is from severity and heaviness; and he was afflicted by *wabal al-jū'*, i.e., severe hunger. *Al-wabīl* is a disagreeable pasture. *Istawbalat al-arḍ* means when the land does not agree with your food, even if you are fond of it, and it is from *al-wabīl*, which is food that one does not desire. *Al-wabīl* of punishment means severe. It is also a stick, the club of a launderer with which he beats clothes after washing, a small stick with which the bell is struck, and a bundle of firewood. *Balā* is a particle by which a question is answered when it enters upon a negative statement, turning it into an affirmation, unlike *na'am*, which answers an affirmative statement. *Balā* also occurs in negation without a question; one says: "You did not give me a dirham," and you reply: "Balā" (Yes, indeed). *Liba* from food, like *riḍā*, means he ate much of it. *Al-lubāyah* (with ḍamma) is the *amṭā* tree. *Al-layāb*, with the yā' preceding, weighs like *saḥāb*, meaning less than a mouthful. *Al-yalab* (p-121) with fatḥa on the lām, means a shield; it is also said *al-daraq*, and armour of hides, or hides sewn one to another, worn on the head only. It also means the greatest of anything, and skin. *Al-abīl*, like *amīr*, means a stick. *Al-ḥazīn* in Syriac means the chief of the Christians, or the monk, or the owner of the bell; it is a form with a short 'ayn, which implies that its hamza is an extra letter, while the Qamus's form implies that it is original. On both estimates it is from the axis of the root, for whoever a stick mixes with is changed, and likewise the chief. *Mahmūzat al-labā'* like *ḍil'*, is the first milk, and it is the most deserving of things to be transformed. *Alba'a al-faṣīl* means the young camel asked for the nipple of the she-camel's udder so that it might suckle the colostrum. *Labi'at wa hiya mulbi'*, means the colostrum fell into her udder, and that does not happen except through what mixes with her, so it transforms that from her. *Al-labḥ* with fatḥa is the first drink, and it is more intense than what is in the middle in mixing and transformation. *Bahā'* is a lioness, and her mixing transforms the males of her kind, and others, by causing them to shun her; likewise *al-labwah* (p-122) with wāw. *'Isharun mulābī* (pregnant she-camels, like *mala'iq*) means their birth has drawn near, and this is clear in transformation. *Labi'at al-shāh waladahā wa alba'athu* means she nursed it with colostrum. *Labi'at al-shāh wa talba'athā* means she milked her colostrum. *Al-ba'īl*, like *amīr*, means small and weak, *ba'ul* (like *karuma*); it is said *ḍa'īl ba'īl*. *Al-ibl* (with two kasras, and the bā' may be sukūn) is a known thing; it is a singular that falls on the plural, not a plural nor a collective noun; its plural is *ābāl*. The transformation in its mixing through riding, carrying and other things is clear. *Al-ibl* also means the cloud that carries rainwater, and it is evident in that. *Ta'abbala 'an imra'atihi* means he refrained from having intercourse with her, from removal. *Nasaka*, i.e., he refrained from the mixing of the transforming world. *Bi-al-'aṣā* means striking with a stick, and whoever a stick mixes with, it transforms him. *Abala al-'ushb ubūlan* means it grew tall, so camels could seize it, and it is clear in transformation. *Al-ibālah*, like *al-ijjānah*, is a piece of birds, horses or camels, or a succession of them; whoever sees any of that transforms him from his state. *Ka-amīr* means a stick, the chief of the Christians, or the monk, or the owner of the bell; all of this is clear in transformation. *Al-ubul* (with ḍamma on the bā') is a bundle of grass, and its mixing transforms what eats it. *Al-ibālah* (like *kitābah*) means politics, and it is in the extreme of transformation for whoever is mixed with it. *Al-ablah* (like *farḥah*) means need and request, and it is well known in that. And it is blessed in camels. He does not *ya'tabil*: he does not persist in tending camels nor does he do well in that trade, or he does not persist mounted on them, i.e., he is quick to be affected and transformed by whoever mixes with them. *Ta'bīl al-ibl* means fattening them, i.e., mixing them with what transforms them. *Al-ibla* (with kasra) means enmity, and its transformation is known. With ḍamma, *al-'āhah*, a blight, and it is likewise. With fatḥa or with taḥrīk, it means heaviness, unwholesomeness, and sin, likewise. *Ta'bīl al-mayyit* means eulogizing him, i.e., praising him after his death, and it stirs grief for him. It came in his *ibālah* (with kasra), and *ubbiltuhu* (with two ḍammas and a shadda): his companions. There is no doubt that whoever comes thus transforms whoever comes to him. *Ḍaghatha 'alā ibbālah* like *ijjānah*, and with lightening: *baliyah 'alā ukhrā*, or *khiṣb 'alā khiṣb*, as if it were an opposite, and it is clear in transformation. *Abilat al-ibl ta'bulu wa ta'būlu ubūlan wa abalan*: they were satisfied, i.e., they sufficed with green herbage instead of water. *Al-rutub* (with two ḍammas) is green from herbs and trees, or a group of green grass. *Al-ubūl* (p-124) is staying in the pasture. There is no doubt that whoever mixes with that, it transforms him. *Allaba ilayhi al-qawm* means the people came to him from every side, and that is transforming. *Allaba al-ibl* means he drove them. *Al-ibl* means the camels were driven and some of them gathered together. *Al-ḥimār ṭarīdatahu* means he drove it violently, and gathered, and assembled, and hastened, and returned, and transformation is evident in all of that. *Al-samā'* means its rain continued, i.e., it transformed the land and its people. *Al-ta'lab*, like *tha'lab*, means a gathering of us and wild asses and wild goats, and it is *bahā'*. Whatever is like that transforms what it mixes with. *Al-ilb* (with kasra) means weakness. It is also a tree like citron, a poison, and that is evident in transformation. With fatḥa it means the vigour of the water-carrier, the inclination of the soul towards desire, thirst, planning against an enemy from where he does not know, musk of a young kid, poison, violent expulsion, the intensity of fever and heat, and the beginning of the healing of a boil. All of these are evidently transformative. *Rīḥ alūb* means a cold wind that stirs up dust. *Rajul alūb* means quick to draw out the bucket, or energetic. Whoever mixes with him, transforms him. *Hum 'alayhi alb wa ilb wāḥid* means they are gathered against him in injustice and enmity, and that is transformation beyond doubt. *Al-ulbah* (with ḍamma) means hunger; with taḥrīk it is *al-yalabah*. *Al-ta'līb* means incitement and corruption, and all of that is evident in transformation. Likewise *al-mi'lab* (for the swift one), and *al-alb* means pure, and it is transformative. *Al-alab* (with taḥrīk) is *al-yalab*, and it has passed that it is the shield, and God knows best.

When Yusuf, peace be upon him, had said that and refused to leave the prison before the matter was made clear, the messenger returned to the king and informed him of what he had said, peace be upon him. It was as though it were asked: "What did the king do?" It was said: He (the king) said to the women, after gathering them: ﴿What was your affair﴾, that is, your great matter; and his saying ﴿when you sought to seduce Yusuf from himself﴾ means: you deceived him with trickery, cunning and evasion. ﴿Yusuf from himself﴾ is evidence that his innocence was established for everyone who knew the story. So the king and some of the people, although they knew of the women's seduction and his chastity, did not know whether the seduction was from all of them or from some of them. It was as though it were asked: "What did they say?" It was said: They schemed in their answer when he asked them about the evil they had done with him; they turned away from it and answered by denying any evil on his part, peace be upon him. That is because they said ﴿حاشَ لِلَّهِ, "Far be God [from such a thing]"﴾, that is, seeking refuge in the Supreme King and declaring Him far above this matter. Thereby they gave the impression of their own innocence from it. Then they explained this seeking of refuge by saying, in wonder at his chastity, which they had never seen the like of, and no thought entered their minds that it could belong to a human being, however great his station: ﴿We knew nothing against him﴾, that is, Yusuf, peace be upon him. They went to great lengths in the denial, saying ﴿any evil﴾, thereby singling him out for innocence. This is as was mentioned earlier at the words of the chiefs ﴿confused dreams﴾ [Yusuf: 44]. This is the answer to the king, whose vision dazzles and whose wrath is feared, so it was the custom of the land not to speak plainly, lest the speech be free of the possibility of doubt, leaving room for escape from it, and worship of kings, except for those whom God wills among them.

When that was complete, it was as though it were asked: "What did the woman who was the origin of this matter say?" It was said: ﴿The wife of the ruler said﴾, openly stating the reality of the situation: ﴿Now the truth has become manifest﴾, that is, it has come to its clearest form and was cut off from falsehood by its appearance. From: ḥaṣṣa sha'rahu, when he completely shaved it so that what was beneath it appeared; and from it comes ḥiṣṣah, a portion of a thing. Its counterpart is kabba and kabkaba, and kaffa and kafkafa, so this is an intensification of the root, indicated by the derivation; this is the view of al-Zajjaj, as stated by al-Rummani. Al-Razi agreed with him in al-Lawami', and said: al-Azhari said: it is from ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ba'ir, when the camel's pads left their marks in the ground as it knelt, until its traces became clear in it. ﴿I sought to seduce him﴾, that is, I deceived him, and she sought to seduce him ﴿from himself﴾. She emphasized what she had made plain, praising him and denying every evil, by saying, emphasizing it because of her earlier denial: ﴿And indeed he is among the truthful﴾, that is, of the most upright in this description, in attributing the seduction to me and clearing himself. All the women testified to his innocence, and nothing of the evil that could be attributed to him had occurred from him. So whoever attributes to him after that any intention or anything else is merely following desire concerning a prophet among the sincere.

(p-128) When the matter became clear, the king ordered that Joseph be brought to him, so that he might make use of him in what was entrusted to him by the king. However, since the vindication of al-Siddiq (the truthful one) was more important than that, and it was the purpose of sending back the messenger, he placed the remainder of the discussion about it first, so that his speech on his own innocence would be connected to the speech of the women about it. What shows that this was his speech is the wisdom contained in it, which no one else in that age would know. So he said, based on what is estimated: when the messenger returned to Joseph, peace be upon him, and informed him of the women's testimony to his innocence, he said: ﴿That﴾, that is, this great moral conduct in my steadfastness in prison until the truth became manifest, ﴿so that he [the Chief] may know﴾ with firm knowledge ﴿that I did not betray him﴾, that is, in his household or in anything else, ﴿in his absence﴾, that is, while each of us was absent from the other. And "so that he may know" by her confession, while she was in security and ease, and by my steadfastness while I was in a place of constraint and fear, that which by its nature cannot remain hidden from everyone whom God has not strengthened with a spirit from Him. ﴿Indeed God﴾, that is, the One who encompasses all attributes of perfection, ﴿does not guide﴾, that is, does not make successful and does not grant success in any way, ﴿the schemes of the betrayers﴾, that is, those who are deeply immersed in betrayal. Rather, He necessarily brings about a cause that reveals the betrayal, even if the betrayer strives to conceal it. Betrayal (khiyanah) is opposing the truth by breaking a general covenant; its opposite is trustworthiness (amanah), and treachery (ghadr) is breaking it in a particular matter. The meaning is that, since I was innocent, God made my affair upright, made my outcome lead to great good and complete innocence; and since the other was a betrayer, God caused him to confess to it.

(p-129) Since that might lead to self-admiration, he said: ﴿And I do not declare myself innocent﴾, meaning, with a great declaration of innocence, ﴿my soul﴾ from absolute error, even if success (tawfiq) and divine protection (ismah) have overcome it. That is, by my declaration of innocence concerning what preceded, I did not intend merely the purification of the soul (tazkiyah lil-nafs). He gave the reason for not declaring innocence with his saying, emphasizing it against the denial of most people, or because their following of their desires is the act of one who denies the act of the commanding soul, ﴿Indeed, the soul﴾, meaning this type, ﴿is certainly one that commands evil﴾, meaning intensely so, ﴿evil﴾, meaning this kind always, due to its nature being inclined to that at every time, ﴿except that which﴾, meaning at the time when, ﴿my Lord has shown mercy﴾, by restraining it from commanding it, or by concealing it through restraining it from doing it after it had been inclined to commanding it; or, except those souls upon which my Lord has shown mercy, so they do not command evil. Then he gave the reason for this with his saying, emphasizing it to repel the suspicion of one who thinks there is no repentance for him: ﴿Indeed, my Lord﴾, meaning the One who is good to me, ﴿is Oft-Forgiving﴾, meaning abundant in concealing sins, ﴿Most Merciful﴾, meaning abundant in honoring whomever He wills.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 54:

When he had completed what he had previously mentioned, which is of greater importance, namely the innocence of the truthful one (al-Siddiq), and the king had learned of his innocence and what follows from it, in accordance with what was in the king's heart regarding bringing him to himself, he followed it with this, conjoining it to what was in its sequence of his saying ﴿"What was your business when you sought to seduce Yusuf?"﴾ [Yusuf: 51], so he said: ﴿And the king said﴾. He stated it explicitly and did not rely on a pronoun, out of dislike for ambiguity, because of what intervened between it and the reply of the wife of al-'Aziz, which was part of the speech of Yusuf, peace be upon him. Had all of it been her speech, he would have relied on the pronoun and would not have needed to bring it out. ﴿"Bring him to me, that I may take him exclusively for myself"﴾, meaning: I will seek and secure his exclusive service, ﴿"for myself"﴾, meaning: he will have no partner in him, cutting off the hope of al-'Aziz regarding him and removing the supposition that he would return him to al-'Aziz. Perhaps this is what Yusuf, peace be upon him, intended by remaining in prison until the matter was made clear, fearing that he might return to al-'Aziz and the woman would return to her former state, so the trial would increase.

Since the sense is: the king's messenger returned to him and informed him that the king had asked the women [and they said] what had passed, and ordered that he be brought so that he might take him exclusively for himself, Yusuf, peace be upon him, said what had preceded of those profound wisdoms, and answered the king's command. He came to him after he had prayed for the people of the prison, saying: "O Allah! Turn the hearts of the righteous toward them [and let not the news conceal them]." He wrote on the gate of the prison: "These are the abodes of affliction, the graves of the living, the houses of sorrows, the testing of friends, and the gloating of enemies." Then he bathed, cleaned himself, put on new clothes, and set out toward him. The phrase is conjoined with "fa" (then) to indicate his haste in this, the saying: ﴿"So when he spoke to him"﴾. The king witnessed in him what he witnessed of the majesty of prophethood, the beauty of ministry, the qualities of leadership, and the signs of felicity, ﴿"he said"﴾, emphasizing (mu'akkidan) the establishing (tamkinan) of his words, to repel one who might suppose that after prison and what approximates to it, he would not be raised to such an elevated rank: ﴿"Indeed, you are today"﴾. He expressed it with what denotes the present for the great strangeness of the matter, also to establish the speech, so he said: ﴿"with us, established (makin) and trustworthy (amin)"﴾. Makin means one of great standing (mukna), from makanah, a state by which its possessor attains his purpose. Amin means trustworthy, from amanah, a state by which breach of covenant is safe. It is said that the king used to speak seventy tongues [so he spoke to him in them, and he expressed them all; then he invoked the king in Hebrew, and the king did not understand it, so he asked him: "What is this tongue?" He said: "The tongue of] my fathers," and it greatly impressed him,

Then it is as if it were said: "What did the Righteous One (al-Siddiq) say?" So it was said: "He said" what it was incumbent upon him to strive for in the welfare of religion and of the world: "Appoint me" as keeper "over the treasuries of the earth," meaning the land of Egypt, which, because of the abundance of its goodness, is as if it were the earth itself. Then he gave the reason for it with what is the aim of kings, which they hardly ever attain, so he said: "Indeed I am a guardian" — meaning capable of managing what is entrusted to me — "knowing" — meaning possessing thorough knowledge of the ways of its welfare and of its development. Thus he informed them of the two faculties of preservation and understanding that God had gathered in him, together with what preservation requires of strength and trustworthiness, for the salvation of the servants from the evil that awaits them, so that this would be a cause of turning them away from the false religion to the true religion. (p-132)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 56:

When he had asked about what preceded, he said, informing that he was answered by God's subjugation of [the king] to him: ﴿And thus﴾, that is, and in the same way as We established Joseph in the land by placing in the heart of the king affection and sound belief, and in the hearts of all the people, and in the same way as he asked for the establishment, "We established" (makkannā), that is, by Our greatness, ﴿for Joseph in the land﴾, that is, absolutely, and especially the land of Egypt, by the king's appointing him over it, ﴿to settle﴾, that is, to take a dwelling to which he returns, from bā'a, meaning "to return" (idhā raja'a), ﴿therein wherever he wills﴾, by the success of all his aims, since all of it came under his authority. [This was] so that the souls of the people of the kingdom and of those whom he appointed through his hand would remain secure, so that the reward is merited and a good remembrance is achieved, along with what increases him in elevation of rank and grandeur of station. It is as if it were said: Why was this? He said: For two reasons. The first is that to Us belongs the whole matter, "We bestow" (nuṣību) in a manner of exclusivity ﴿with Our mercy﴾, by Our greatness, ﴿whom We will﴾, from those who deserve it in your view and otherwise. We are not asked about what We do, and We willed that Joseph attain this. The second is that he is a doer of good who worships God, having passed away from all other than Him, and We ﴿do not waste﴾ (p-133) in any way ﴿the reward of the doers of good﴾, that is, those who excel in that quality, even though it is within Our right to do otherwise.

Abu al-Qasim 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd al-Hakam related at the beginning of the Conquest of Egypt, via al-Kalbi, from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: The messenger came to him and said: "Remove the clothes of the prison and put on new clothes." He was thirty years old that day. When he came to him, he saw a young lad and said: "Does this one know my dream, when the magicians and soothsayers do not know it!" He seated him before him. Then he said: 'Uthman, that is Ibn Salih, and others in their narrations said: When he questioned him and conversed with him, he became great in his eyes, and his matter became grand in his heart. So he gave him his ring and appointed him over what was behind his door. He returned to Ibn 'Abbas and said: The drum was beaten in Egypt that Joseph was the king's deputy. And from 'Ikrimah: Pharaoh said to Joseph: "I have given you authority over Egypt, except that I want to make my chair four fingers taller than yours!" Joseph said: "Yes."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 57 (part 1 of 2):

Since this is something that people greatly esteem in this world, and its honour is not truly counted unless it is joined to the bliss of the Hereafter, he drew attention to what he has in the Hereafter, compared to which this is nothing. So he said, emphasising the disbelievers' denial of it: ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better﴾. Since the wording of the rulings in a general manner, attaching them to attributes that make the matter either desirable or fearful, is more excellent and more eloquent, (p-134) he said: ﴿for those who believed﴾, meaning they brought this attribute into being, ﴿and were mindful﴾, meaning by their natural disposition they constantly produce fear of God and take precautions against Him, a continuous production. This is among the greatest of their portions and highest of their rank, as was explained earlier, which indicates the perfection of his faith and piety.

Since it is well known that one who has these attributes carries out what he is entrusted with in the most complete manner and looks into it in the best way, it is as if it were said: he made him the king over the treasuries of the land, and he managed them by what God commanded him and taught him, until the affair was set right, goodness came, and evil departed. He omitted this only to indicate it through its implications, from the story of his brothers, which is the principal aim in itself, as will come. It has been understood from this story that the prevailing character of Egypt is baseness: hostility toward the stranger, exploitation of the weak, and submission to the strong. For they wronged him by imprisoning him after his innocence was established. Then he pardoned them and did good to them by what preserved their lives, then freed them after he had enslaved them, and returned their wealth to them after he had stripped it by what he had of grain. They repaid him for that by enslaving his children and the children of his brothers after him, and inflicting the worst torment upon them. The clearest proof that this is the character of the land is that when the Children of Israel left with Moses, peace be upon him, and God delivered them from all that humiliation and honoured them with the great signs and the Manifest Book that God honoured them with, they, every one of them, were few (p-135) who broke their covenants, daring to commit what cannot be borne. When he commanded them from God with a command, they turned away from it, as this has passed concerning the Tawrah (the Torah) in [al-A'raf and al-Baqarah] and other places. So God punished them with wandering in the desert, and He used to call them the crooked generation, because He knew the badness of their natures, until everyone who had grown up in the land of Egypt died. Then their children obeyed the commands until they possessed the lands that God had promised [their fathers]. This is mentioned in the Zabur (the Psalms) of Dawud, peace be upon him, in more than one place. Among them, in Psalm ninety-four: "Come, let us bow down and kneel and submit before the LORD our Maker, for He is our God, and we are the people of His pasture and the sheep of His hand. Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts and provoke Him as at the provocation in the wilderness, where your fathers tested Me, though they had seen My works. For forty years I loathed that generation and said: they are a people who go astray in their hearts, and they have not known My ways; so I swore in My wrath that they would not enter My rest. Our fathers in Egypt did not understand Your wonders, nor did they remember the multitude of Your mercies when they provoked You at the sea, the Red Sea, as they went up from it. Yet You saved them for Your name's sake, to make Your mighty power known. You rebuked the Red Sea and it dried up; You led them through the depths as through a desert. You delivered them from the hand of the enemy and redeemed them from the hand of the hater. The waters covered their enemies, and not one of them remained. Then they believed His words and sang His praise. Soon they forgot His works and did not wait for His counsel. They lusted exceedingly in the wilderness and tested God in the desert. He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their souls. They provoked Moses in the camp and Aaron the holy one of the LORD. The earth opened and swallowed Dathan and covered the company of Abiram. Fire blazed in their assembly; the flame burned up the wicked. They made a calf in Horeb and worshipped the molten image. They exchanged their glory for the likeness of an ox that eats grass. They forgot God their Saviour, who had done great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, and awesome things at the Red Sea. He said He would destroy them, had not Moses His chosen stood before Him in the breach to turn away His wrath, lest He destroy them. They despised the pleasant land and did not believe His word, and murmured in their tents and did not heed the voice of the LORD. So He lifted His hand against them to overthrow them in the wilderness, and to scatter their seed among the nations and disperse them through the lands, (p-137) because they joined themselves to Baal of Peor and ate sacrifices offered to the dead, and provoked Him by their deeds. A plague broke out among them suddenly. Then Phinehas stood up and interceded, and the plague was stayed. That was reckoned to him as righteousness, from generation to generation for ever. They provoked Him also at the waters of Meribah, and it went ill with Moses on their account, for they embittered his spirit, so that he spoke rashly with his lips. They did not destroy the nations that the LORD had commanded them, but mingled with the peoples and learned their works. They served their idols, which became a snare to them. They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons, shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, which they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan, and the land was polluted with blood. They were defiled by their works and played the harlot by their deeds. So the anger of the LORD burned against His people, and He abhorred His inheritance. He gave them into the hand of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them, and they were subdued under their hand. Many times He delivered them, but they rebelled against Him by their counsels, and were brought low by their iniquity." Here ends the quotation. Yet if you reflect, you will find that God exalts the stranger whom they humiliate, grants him good fortune and establishes his glory, as He did with Yusuf, peace be upon him, after prison, and with the Children of Israel after enslavement, (p-138) and He is the best Protector and the best Helper!

So let the one who dwells in it beware lest its character prevail over him, so that he becomes characterised by all of that: lack of zeal, hatred of the stranger, boldness in falsehood through flattery and sycophancy, cowardice in truth, complete abasement before tyrants, and [stammering] in speech. Rather, let him constantly train himself with God's commands, bring himself to obedience to them, follow His Messenger and love him, look into his biography and the biographies of his followers, and yearn for all of that, until it becomes a nature for him that strips him of the nature of the land, as the worshippers of it and its people of piety and asceticism did. May God protect us from the evils of our souls and the sins of our deeds, and we ask Him to seal our lives with righteous deeds and to make us among those upon whom there is no fear, ever.

He mentioned what came after what was previously mentioned of this story from the Tawrah. He said: "When two years had passed, Pharaoh had a dream: he seemed to be standing by the bank of the river, and behold, seven cows came up out of the Nile, fine-looking and fat-fleshed, and they grazed in the reed-grass. Then seven other cows came up after them from the Nile, ugly-looking and lean-fleshed, and they stood beside the fat cows on the bank of the river. The ugly, lean cows ate up the seven fine-looking, fat cows." (p-139) Pharaoh awoke from his sleep, then slept again and dreamed a second time: seven ears of grain came up on one stalk, full and plump, and behold, seven ears, thin and blighted by the east wind, sprang up after them. The thin ears swallowed up the seven full ears. Pharaoh woke, and his dream troubled him. In the morning his spirit was troubled, so he sent and called for all the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men, and he told them his dream, but there was none who could interpret it for Pharaoh.

Then the chief cupbearer spoke before Pharaoh and said: "I remember my faults today. Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put me in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, me and the chief baker, and we both dreamed a dream on the same night, each of us according to the interpretation of his dream. There was with us there in prison a young Hebrew, a servant of the captain of the guard, and we told him, and he interpreted our dreams for us, giving each of us an interpretation according to his dream. And as he interpreted for us, so it came to pass: I was restored to my position, and the other he hanged."

Pharaoh sent and called Yusuf, peace be upon him, and they brought him quickly out of the prison. He shaved his hair, changed his clothes, entered, and stood before Pharaoh. Pharaoh said to Yusuf, peace be upon him: "I have had a dream, and there is no one to interpret it for me; and I have heard concerning you that you hear a dream and interpret it in the best way!" Yusuf, peace be upon him, answered Pharaoh and said: "Is it perhaps that you think I answer Pharaoh with peace (salam) apart from the command of God, exalted is He?"

Pharaoh said to Yusuf: "In my dream I seemed to stand on the bank of the river, and behold, seven cows came up out of the river, fine-looking and fat-fleshed, and they grazed in the reed-grass. Behold, seven other cows came up after them, wretched, ugly-looking, and very lean-fleshed, the like of which I have never seen for leanness in all the land of Egypt. The lean, weak, ugly cows swallowed up the first seven fat cows, and they entered their bellies, yet it could not be seen that they had entered, and their appearance was as ugly as before. Then I awoke. (p-141) I dreamed again: seven ears of grain, fine and full, on one stalk, plump and beautiful, and behold, seven thin ears blighted by the east wind sprang up after them. The thin, weak ear swallowed up the seven full, fine ears. I told this to the magicians, but I found no one who could make it clear."

Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to Pharaoh: "The dream, O Pharaoh, is one. God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do. The seven fine cows and the seven fine ears are seven years: good. The dream is one. The seven lean, weak cows that came up after them, and the seven thin ears blighted by the east wind, will be seven years of famine. This is the word I spoke to Pharaoh. God has displayed what He is determined to do, and behold, seven years are coming in which there will be great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt. After them will come seven years of famine, and all the plenty will be forgotten in the land of Egypt, and the famine will consume the land, because the hardship that follows will be very grievous. The dream was repeated to Pharaoh a second time because the matter is fixed by the LORD, and God is hastening to bring it about."

"Now let Pharaoh look for a discerning and wise man and set him over the land of Egypt. Let Pharaoh appoint officers over the land to take a fifth of the produce of Egypt during the seven years of plenty. Let them gather all the food of these good years that are coming, and store the grain under Pharaoh's authority, and keep the corn in the cities. Let the food be kept in reserve for the people of Egypt against the seven years of famine that are to befall the whole land of Egypt, so that the land may not perish through famine."

So this word pleased Pharaoh and his servants. Pharaoh said to his commanders, "Is there anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God dwells?" Then Pharaoh said to Yusuf, peace be upon him, "Since God has made you aware of all this, there is no one as perceptive as you. You are the one empowered over my household. Through your command and word about me, the whole people will accept [your authority]. I am greater than you only in the pulpit." Pharaoh said to Yusuf, "Look, I have appointed you over the whole land of Egypt." Pharaoh took his ring from his little finger (p-143) and placed it on Yusuf's little finger, peace be upon him. He clothed him in garments of linen, put a collar of gold around his neck, and had him mounted on one of his conveyances. He proclaimed before him, "This is a lord and one empowered, and his authority extends over the whole land of Egypt." Then Pharaoh said to Yusuf, peace be upon him, "I have commanded that no one in the whole land of Egypt may gesture with his hands or step with his feet without your order."

Pharaoh named Yusuf "Clarifier of Hidden Things" (Muwaddih al-Khafaya). He married him to Asinat, the daughter of Qutifira', the imam of Iskandariyya (Alexandria). In another version, [the text reads] Hibr Wan. Yusuf, peace be upon him, went out as governor over the whole land of Egypt. Yusuf was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh, and he then toured the whole land of Egypt.

The land yielded abundantly throughout all seven years of plenty. He filled the storehouses and gathered the grain into the villages. He gathered the wheat of every village's fields and what surrounded them, and he stored it there. Yusuf, peace be upon him, stored from the granaries (p-144) an amount like a sand dune, and in another version, like the sand of the sea, very great, until counting it became impossible and it became uncountable.

Two sons were born to Yusuf, peace be upon him, before the year of famine began. Asinat, the daughter of Qutifira' Hibr Wan (in another version, the imam of Iskandariyya), bore him these sons. Yusuf, peace be upon him, named his elder son Bakr Manshā, because he said, "God has made me forget all my hardship" (in another version, "my suffering") "and all that happened to me in my father's house." He named the other Afrathim, and said, "Because God has made me abundant in the land of my servitude." Then the years of plenty that had been in the land of Egypt ran out, and the years of famine began, just as Yusuf, peace be upon him, had said. Hunger was in the whole land of Egypt, and bread could not be found in the whole land of Egypt, so all the people of Egypt went hungry. The people cried out to Pharaoh for bread. Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, "Go to Yusuf, peace be upon him, and do everything he orders you to do." (p-145)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 58:

Since the meaning, as has preceded, is: he (Yusuf) was given charge of the treasuries of the land, then the years of plenty came and he managed them with what Allah had taught him; then the years of drought came and they parched the entire land of Egypt and what bordered it of the lands of al-Sham and others. So he brought out what he had stored of grain for seven years, gradually, little by little, as "the All-Knowing, the All-Wise" had determined for him. The people heard of this, and they came to obtain grain from him from every direction. ﴿And the brothers of Yusuf came﴾, the ten of them, for this purpose, and their father swore by Binyamin, the brother of Yusuf on his mother's side, who was with him. He indicated his facilitation of their admission by the particle fa' [in "fa-qala"]: ﴿So they entered upon him﴾, meaning, because he used to attend to affairs personally, as is the practice of capable and resolute administrators who trust no one else with them. ﴿So he recognized them﴾, because he had been anticipating their arrival, knowing the drought in their lands and having set his resolve upon them, in addition to his knowing their appearances in their clothing [and otherwise], and no great change had come over their condition [in his eyes].

﴿And they did not recognize him﴾, because of his having parted from them as a youth. The firmness of their non-recognition is established in that they described him by it, since he had not occurred to their minds due to the long time elapsed, together with the change in his appearance through age, and what was added to him of retinue, servants, clothing, the state of the land, the dignity of the king (p-146) and the might of the sovereignty, and other things by which the familiar is not recognized and by which one feels estranged from what is known, in accordance with what the Exalted said: ﴿You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs while they do not perceive﴾ [Yusuf: 15].

Al-dukhul (entering): moving into an enclosure. Al-ma'rifah (recognition): the mind's clear apprehension of a thing, such that if it were witnessed it would distinguish it from other things that do not share its particular attributes.

Since the sense is equivalent to saying: they asked him for provisions, and he sold them after questioning them about their affair, saying to them, "Perhaps you are spies?" and asking them about their entire condition. They informed him about their father and their brother from him, so that he would know their righteousness and not suppose that they were spies, [the text] joins to this His saying: ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾, that is, Yusuf, upon him be prayer and peace, ﴿with their provisions﴾ which they had come for, and he had been generous to them. The jihaz (provisions, the goods prepared for transport) is the choicest of goods carried from one land to another. ﴿He said﴾, that is, to them: ﴿Bring me a brother of yours﴾, O company, ﴿from your father﴾, who comes with a message from your father, the righteous man, so that I may believe you; or, they had asked him for a load for their brother, so he showed that he did not believe them and requested that he be brought so that he might give him [his share], for he used to distribute food according to what was sufficient. Then he encouraged them by holding out hope of the like of the kindness he had shown them, for he had given them good hospitality. So he said, affirming to them [what they had seen from him]: (p-147) ﴿Do you not see﴾, that is, do you not know with a knowledge that is like seeing, ﴿that I give full measure﴾, that is, I always complete it in accordance with what truth requires, ﴿and I am the best of hosts﴾, I place each thing in its first place.

When he had encouraged them, he also instilled fear in them, saying: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me﴾, that is, your brother, on the first visit you make, ﴿then there will be no measure for you﴾. And he made them aware that he would not withhold it from them for any other reason, so he said: ﴿Nor shall you come near me﴾. And despite all this, it did not occur to them that he was Joseph.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 61:

So it is as if it was said: "What did they say?" It was answered: ﴿They said: "We will seek to get him from his father"﴾, meaning with a promise that is not broken, when we arrive. ﴿From him his father﴾, meaning: we will speak to him about it, dispute the matter with him, devise a way to win him over, act gently in this, and spare no effort. Then they emphasized this, after the verbal sentence introduced by the particle *sīn* (the future marker), with a nominal sentence stressed by two emphasis particles, so they said: ﴿And indeed we will surely do it﴾, meaning: we will do what he has commanded and we have undertaken it.

It was already explained at ﴿and she sought to seduce him﴾ [Yusuf: 23] that the root (*māddah*, the consonantal base of a word), whether it is of the *yāʾ* type or the *wāw* type, with *hamza* or without *hamza*, revolves around the notion of circulation (*dawarān*). Among its necessary implications are intention, approach, withdrawal, gentleness and delay. The non-hamzated form has already been explained. As for the hamzated form, from it comes *daraʾahu* (*dara'ahu*), meaning he pushed him away, because the one pushed back is returned to the place from which he came. [*al-mudārāʾa* (mutual pushing back)] means pushing away and disputing in general, i.e., whether it is done gently or harshly. Then the word became common and was restricted to the sense of gentleness. Pushing necessarily entails that the one pushed lands suddenly in a place he did not intend. From this comes *daraʾa ʿalaynā*, meaning he came out upon us unexpectedly. Al-Qazzaz said: its origin is from the saying of the people: "The torrent came *daraʾan*," meaning some of it pushes other parts of it, and it is the kind that comes from a place one does not know about. *Indaraʾa fulān ʿalaynā bi-l-sharr* means: he brought evil upon us from a direction we did not know. *Al-darʾ* means defiance (*nushūz*), and it comes from pushing. *Kawkab durriʾ* means a blazing, glittering star whose light pushes one part against another. From it comes *darʾat al-nār*, meaning the fire shone. *Indaraʾa al-ḥarīq* means the fire spread. *Daraʾa al-shayʾ* means he spread out the thing, because a spread-out thing is never free of pushing. *Tadāraʾū* means they pushed one another in dispute.

*Daraʾa al-baʿīr* means the camel had a swelling (*ghudda*), and with the swelling there is a tumor on its back. A female camel is *dāriʾ*, meaning afflicted with a swelling, because the swelling is bound to pushing; it does not part from it by the saddle, the riding, or other things. Every protrusion on the body has this characteristic. From it comes *al-darʾ*, meaning a piece of a mountain that is bright. A female camel is *mudriʾ*, meaning she let down milk and loosened her udder at the time of birthing, as if she pushed both of them out. *Iddaraʾat al-ṣayd* (on the pattern of *iftaʿalat*, the reflexive form) means she took a decoy for it. [The word *durriyya* (decoy) has already been mentioned under the *wāwī* (*wāw*-type) roots. From it comes *iddaraʾtu fulānan*, meaning I relied on him.] *Al-darʾ* also means inclination and crookedness, because it is suitable to be pushed so that it may stand straight. A road with *durūʾ* is a road of bends and ravines, i.e., cracks. So it is as if it pushes its rider away from the right direction. *Tadarru'an ʿalayhim* means they behaved arrogantly toward them, because that does not occur without pushing back, like defiance. Pushing also requires strength. From it comes *rajul dhū tadarruʾ*, meaning a man of protection and strength. *Radda'ahu bi-kadhā* (with the letter *rāʾ* placed first, i.e., *rādda*) means she made it a strength for him and a pillar that defends him. *Al-radʾ* means help, support, and a heavy load, because it pushes to keep balance. *Radaʾa al-ḥāʾiṭ* means he propped up the wall. *Radaʾahu bi-ḥajar* means he struck him with a stone, because when it hits him it pushes him away. *Al-ibil*: he took good care of them, because that does not happen without pushing away (what harms them). *Arda'a al-sitr* means he let down the curtain, by pushing it from the place where it was. *Arda'a al-walad* means he calmed and comforted the child, thus pushing away his worry. *Arda'a al-shayʾ* means he made it settle, as if to remove the pushing. Likewise *ardaʾahu*, meaning he corrupted it, either because he did not push for it by taking good care of it so he corrupted it, or because he pushed too much until it went bad. From this comes *ardaʾa*, meaning he did something bad, i.e., he did a corrupt deed that is not good. It seems that from this comes *al-udra* (with *ḍamma* on the first letter, and it may be pronounced with the vowel silent or moved), which is the enlargement of the two testicles in men and horses.

From pushing back comes *taraʾʾadati al-ḥayya*, meaning the snake shook as it glided and raised its head; and *al-rīḥ* (the wind), meaning it was agitated. It is as if some of it pushes others. From it comes *raʾd al-ḍuḥā*, meaning its rising, and *taraʾʾada al-ḍuḥā*, meaning the morning rose. Likewise *al-jāriya al-raʾda* and *al-ruʾd* (with *ḍamma*), meaning the delicate one. Al-Qazzaz said: she is the one swift in youth with good nourishment. Ibn Duraid said: *jāriya raʾda* (without hamza) means one who often comes and goes. When you say *jāriya ruʾda*, she is the delicate one. When it is explained as coming and going, it is from the circulation that is the basis of the root; when it is explained as delicate, it is from the agitation that necessarily accompanies it. *Ghuṣn ruʾd* (with *ḍamma*) means a moist branch, and it is of this same derivation. Al-Qazzaz said: I think the delicate girl was only called *ruʾd* from this. *Taraʾʾada* means he swayed in luxury. *Zayd* (a man's name, used here as an example) stood up and a tremor seized him. *Al-ghuṣn* (the branch) means it cast shade. *Al-ʿunuq* (the neck) means it bent. All of this comes from circulation and what necessarily accompanies it of agitation.

*Riʾd al-insān* means his friend, because he pursues him and circles around him. *Al-raʾda* means the root of the beard, which is the base from which the teeth grow, and it is the bone in which the two ends of the jaws turn, adjacent to the temples. From gentleness and delay comes *al-rūda* (with *ḍamma*), which is *al-tuʾada* (patience, deliberation).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 62:

When Allah (glorified and exalted be He) informed us that He had encouraged them (the brothers) regarding the matter of their brother through speech and had warned them, He informed us that He had encouraged them toward him through action, so He said, conjoining it to His earlier saying to them: ﴿And he said﴾, i.e., Yusuf (peace be upon him), out of compassion for his brothers and desiring to advise them concerning what they had asked of him: ﴿to his servants﴾, i.e., his young men (ghilman).
