The root of fata (youth, servant) is the strong young man, and its explanation will come at the words of the Exalted: ﴿They said, "By Allah, you will not cease remembering Yusuf"﴾ [Yusuf: 85]. ﴿Put their merchandise﴾, i.e., what they had set aside (bada'ahu, meaning they cut it off) from their wealth for trade, and which we took from them as the price of their food that we had given them. ﴿into their saddlebags﴾, i.e., their sacks (`udul); and the rahl is what is prepared for travel, whether a container or a mount. ﴿That perhaps they will recognize it﴾, i.e., their merchandise; he used the particle of certainty (la'alla, "perhaps") as an expression of optimism for them regarding safety, or (as an expression of) supposition, or (as an expression of) knowledge through revelation. So He said: ﴿when they return﴾, going back ﴿to their family﴾, i.e., knowing that it is precisely the same, which I returned to them as a kindness [to them], and they will be certain of this, and will not suppose that Allah has replaced it for them with its like, in view of their condition and out of honor to their father, and they will recognize this blessing as coming from me. ﴿That perhaps they will return﴾, i.e., so that their state and the state of whoever returns to us, once they recognize it, will be (such that) they return it out of scrupulousness, or for the sake of obtaining grain with it if they have no other, or out of hope for the like of this. He did not hasten to make himself known to them and to bring joy quickly to his father, because that is ordinarily not possible, owing to the profound wisdoms and firm planning that will come; and the use of the particle fa' (then/so) indicates their haste in returning, so He said:

﴿So when they returned﴾, that is, the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him, ﴿to their father﴾, what they had seen (of the generosity of the Truthful One, their need for him, and their clearing of themselves of being spies) moved them to say, ﴿"O our father..."﴾

Since the harm to them was an absolute prohibition, they constructed the verb in the passive voice in their statement, ﴿"The measure has been withheld from us"﴾, concerning ﴿our brother Benjamin﴾, who was given his camel's load in his absence, and ﴿for all of us, after this time, if we do not take him with us, so that our truthfulness may become evident"﴾. Withholding (al-man') is the creation of something by which a capable agent is prevented from acting.

Its opposite is empowerment (al-tasliT). As for incapacity (al-'ajz), its opposite is capacity (al-qudrah). ﴿So send﴾, that is, by means of removing this withholding, ﴿with us our brother﴾, for if you send him with us, ﴿we will measure﴾, that is, for himself, just as each one of us measures for himself. This is according to the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i (p-153) with the yā' (of the third person), while according to the reading of the majority, with the nūn (of the first person plural), it is to be understood as: ﴿the provision which the Chieftain has allotted﴾, from the grain (al-mirah), and it is a load for each one.

They reinforced what preceded of their conduct toward Yusuf, peace be upon him, which necessitates suspicion of them, so they said: ﴿"And indeed we will be its guardians"﴾, that is, specifically him, ﴿"guarding him"﴾, that is, against any harm reaching him, until we return him to you, being exceedingly diligent in this attribute. It was as if it were said: What did he do in this matter after they had acted (as they did), since he sent Yusuf, peace be upon him, with them? It is said: He resolved to send him with them, but he manifested his turning to God Most High regarding his affair, not being content with their emphatic pledge to guard him, because of what had preceded from them of the like concerning Yusuf, peace be upon him, namely that

﴿He said: "Shall I entrust him to you, except as I entrusted his brother to you before?"﴾ That is, will I now accept from you, and in the future, your giving me security regarding him in a way that would sadden me, a security that is "over him", meaning Binyamin, ﴿except as I entrusted you with his brother﴾, meaning in the past, ﴿Yusuf﴾, peace be upon him.

Since Yusuf, peace be upon him, had not known any treachery from them before what they did to him, and since his entrusting [Binyamin] to them was only for a short time, the prepositional phrase [in the verse] establishes the meaning: ﴿before this﴾. You had given your utmost assurance, yet you did not keep him safe for me nor return him to me. Security (al-amn) is the calm of the heart in the safety of the self. So in this matter I trust no one with him except God. ﴿God is the best guardian﴾, that is, the One who encompasses all in knowledge and power, better than you and better than anyone else. "And He" (wa-huwa), that is, inwardly and outwardly, ﴿is the most merciful of the merciful﴾. (p-154) So He is more merciful to me than to afflict me with him after my calamity with his brother.

They wanted to empty what they had brought of provisions. "And when they opened" (i.e., the sons of Ya'qub, peace be upon him) "their goods" — that is, their containers which they had carried from Egypt — "they found their merchandise" — that is, what they had with them from Canaan for purchasing food.

Since the thing that gladdens is the mere return, he constructed the statement in the passive: "it has been returned to them." Wijdan (finding) is the appearance of a thing to the self through a sense or what stands in for it. So it is as if it was said: "What did they say?" Then it is said: "They said" — that is, to their father — "O our father, what" — that is, what thing — "do we seek?" — that is, what do we want? It is as though he said to them: "What is the news?" So they said, by way of explaining that and as an emphasis on the request to take their brother along: "This is our merchandise." Then they explained the content of the indication with their saying: "It has been returned to us." Is there any honour beyond this?

Since the implied meaning was: "we will return with it to him with our brother, and our sincerity and truthfulness will become evident to him," [he built upon it his saying]: "and we will bring provisions for our family" — that is, we will bring them food supplies by our returning to him; and mirah (provisions) are the foodstuffs carried from one land to another — "and we will guard our brother," so that nothing befalls him of what is feared for him, as a confirmation of the promise to guard him and an explanation that there is no harm in his journey. And what indicates what is in the Torah — that he had kept one of them imprisoned so that they would bring their youngest brother — is his saying: "and we will gain an extra camel's load" — that is, the total of what we will bring after returning to him will be twelve loads, one load for each of us, and for the one who was imprisoned two loads, for his two trips, the first and the second. That is because he would give only one load per head. So it is as if he had not given them, for what he had equipped them with, other than nine loads. So it is as if it was said: "Will he grant you that in this crisis?" They said: "Yes, because 'that is an easy measure'" in comparison with what we have seen of the nobility of his character, the vastness of his kingdom, and the grandeur of his resolve.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 66:

So it is as if it were said: "What did he say to them?" It is said: ﴿He said﴾, that is, Ya'qub (peace be upon him), ﴿"I will never send him﴾, that is, Binyamin, ﴿with you﴾, that is, at any time, ﴿until you give me﴾ a covenant. The verb "tu'tunni" is from ill-itha' (giving), which is the bestowing of something so that it reaches the one who takes it. ﴿a solemn covenant﴾, which is a firm, binding pledge.

Since his intention was a covenant sanctioned by the Lord, and a covenant sanctioned by the Lord is one that is made by His names, because He, glorified is He, permitted it and commanded that trust be placed in it, it is as though it came from Him. So he said: ﴿in God's name﴾, that is, by the Supreme King, with mighty oaths: "By God, you will surely bring him back to me" from al-itya' (bringing), which is coming in every state, ﴿unless﴾ in the state of ﴿you are encompassed﴾, that is, a calamity from among the calamities befalls you, which you have no power to withstand, ﴿entirely﴾, so that you all perish from the last of you to the first. All of this is an addition to the strengthening of the covenant, because of the calamity that had befallen him through Yusuf (peace be upon him), although reliance in his protection is in fact upon God. This is of the same kind as "tie it and trust [in God]." So they agreed to him in (p-156) all that he asked. ﴿When they had given him their covenant﴾, that is, his sons gave him their pledge, ﴿he said: "God﴾, that is, the One who possesses all attributes of perfection, ﴿is witness over what we say"﴾, meaning He is the one able to fulfil it, the one in whose hands the disposal of it is hoped to be for good, not you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 67:

When he was permitted to take him out with them, God followed that report about his command to them to take precautions against calamities, because they were eleven men, brothers, people of beauty and stature, and they had become somewhat well known among the Egyptians because of what had passed between them and Yusuf, peace be upon him, in the first visit of words. So they were liable to have eyes fixed upon them and fingers pointed at them, and thus be struck by the evil eye. He had not instructed them on the first visit, because they were unknown, along with the people being preoccupied with the drought they were in. So He said, relating about him: "And he said," that is, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, to his sons when they wanted to travel: ﴿O my sons﴾, warning them against the evil of envy and the evil eye. ﴿Do not enter﴾ when you come to Egypt ﴿from one gate﴾ of its gates. The "one" in its absolute sense is that which is not divisible; as for the restricted one, by its application to a described thing such as "one gate," it is that which is not divisible within the meaning of that described thing. ﴿And enter from separate gates﴾, and be cautious lest they be closely joined or very near one another, so He said: ﴿separate﴾, that is, a great separation. This is the ruling of precaution, so that they would not be struck by the evil eye, as transmitted by al-Rummani from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, and al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. For the evil eye is real, and it is part of the decree of Allah, and our Law has come with that. In the Two Sahihs and others, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The evil eye is real." In another narration in Ahmad and Ibn Majah: "The Shaytan is present in it, and the envy of the son of Adam." In Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The evil eye is real. If anything were to outrun the decree, the evil eye would outrun it. And when you are asked to wash, then wash." In Abu Nu'aym's al-Hilyah, from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet said: "The evil eye can bring a camel into the cooking pot and a man into the grave." In Abu Dawud, from Asma' bint Yazid, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "It only overtakes the rider and throws him down." In Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, from Asma' bint 'Umays, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "If anything were to outrun the decree, the evil eye would outrun it." Imam al-Razi said: The source of the evil eye striking is the evil soul's imagining the destruction of the one it strikes. The meaning of this has already been mentioned in the narration of Ahmad and Ibn Majah from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, together with the presence of the Shaytan. This precaution is of the kind of taking up the causes that are commanded, because they are from the decree, not of the kind of guarding oneself against the decree, as Muslim, Ahmad and Ibn Majah related from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak, and in each there is good. Be keen on what benefits you, seek help from Allah and do not feel helpless. And if something befalls you, do not say: 'If only I had done such and such,' but say: 'Allah decreed, and He does what He wills.' For 'if only' opens the work of the Shaytan."

Its meaning, and Allah knows best: act the act of the strong, and do not act the act of the helpless. That is, look carefully, reflect deeply and take your time until you know the sources and the outcomes, so that you leave nothing that may benefit you in the matter you are facing, and that would harm you only by doing it; and do not leave a matter that could harm you without abandoning it and guarding against it with all your effort. For when you do that, [and if a matter from Allah comes contrary to your wish, you are worthy of not saying to yourself, "If only I had done such and such"], for you have left nothing undone. But if you act the act of the helpless and abandon firm resolve, how soon you may be reached through the abandonment of the causes, and how close you are to saying what opens the work of the Shaytan, "if only."

When he feared that from this command of his there might come to some minds the notion that caution averts the decree, he negated that, clarifying that he intended nothing but the taking of causes as Allah commanded, and that the matter after that is up to Him: if He wills, He causes the causes to produce their effects, and if He wills, He nullifies those causes and establishes causes that oppose them, and the feared outcome results from them. So He said: ﴿And I cannot avail you﴾, that is, I cannot repel, ward off, or substitute ﴿against Allah﴾, that is, against some part of the command of the Supreme King. He generalized the negation, saying: ﴿in anything﴾, that is, if He wills for you, whether you are scattered or gathered. This is the ruling of the decree. Then he gave the reason for that by his saying: ﴿Surely the judgment﴾, that is, there is no judgment, which is the decisive settlement of the matter according to what wisdom calls for, ﴿except Allah's﴾, that is, the One to whom the whole command belongs; no one other than Him can escape any of His will or flee from any of His decree. And for this meaning, namely that no cause benefits at all except by Allah, Allah sent down the basmalah conjoined with the letter of causation at the beginning of His Book, and commanded it at the beginning of everything. Abu Nu'aym related in al-Hilyah, in the biography of our Imam al-Shafi'i, with his chain to him and then to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he addressed the people one day and said in his sermon: "The most wondrous thing in man is his heart, and it has sources of wisdom and their opposites. If hope strikes it, greed makes it foolish. If greed stirs it, covetousness destroys it. If despair possesses it, grief kills it. If anger befalls it, rage intensifies. If it is made happy by contentment, it forgets caution. If fear reaches it, sorrow occupies it. If a calamity strikes it, impatience breaks it. If it gains wealth, richness makes it rebellious. If need seizes it, trial occupies it. If hunger exhausts it, weakness keeps it seated. If excess of satiety overwhelms it, fullness chokes it. So every shortfall in it is harmful, and every excess [in it] is corrupting." He said: Then a man among those who had witnessed the Camel with him stood up and said: (p-161) "O Commander of the Faithful, inform us about the decree." He said: [A deep sea, so do not enter it." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, inform us about the decree." He said: "A dark house, so do not enter it." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, inform us about the decree." He said]: "The secret of Allah, so do not burden yourself with it." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, inform us about the decree." He said: "As you insist, it is a matter between two matters: neither compulsion nor delegation." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, so-and-so says by capacity, and he is present with you." He said: "Bring him to me!" They brought him, and when he saw him he drew his sword about four fingers' width and said: "Is the capacity you possess with Allah or apart from Allah? Beware of saying either of them, lest you apostatize and I strike your neck!" He said: "Then what shall I say, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "Say: I possess it by Allah, who if He wills, gives it to me as possession."

And it will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, in [Surat al-Hajj] at ﴿Surely Allah does what He wills﴾ [al-Hajj: 18], what relates to this.

When the whole matter was confined to Him, glory be to Him, it became necessary to refer every matter to Him and to confine regard to Him. So He said, alerting to that: ﴿In Him﴾, that is, in Allah alone, to whom judgment belongs (p-162) alone, ﴿I have put my trust﴾, that is, I have made Him my trustee, and I am content with whatever He does. ﴿And in Him﴾, that is, in Him alone, ﴿let the trusting trust﴾, that is, those who are firm in the door of trust, for that is among the greatest obligations: whoever does it prospers, and whoever neglects it fails.

Then, Allah (exalted is He) confirmed what Ya'qub had said, affirming what he had indicated of his conviction, so He said: ﴿And when﴾. Its connection with the conjunction "wa" (and) indicates that they did not hasten to return on this occasion out of fear that he would say to them: "What you have has not been fully spent, so that you would be forced to exchange it," and the time was one of gentleness, not one of expansiveness. ﴿They entered﴾, that is, the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him, upon their arrival in Egypt, ﴿from the gate their father had ordered them﴾, that is, by it, ﴿from separate gates.﴾ They said: Egypt had four gates. ﴿That entry did not avail them﴾, that is, it did not ward off or repel anything, ﴿against Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King whose command none can repel. He intensified the negation and said: ﴿anything﴾, as was mentioned in the words of Ya'qub, peace be upon him: "except a need" (ḥājah), that is, something other than a complete need, ﴿within the soul of Ya'qub﴾, which was entering as he had commanded, out of compassion for them. "He fulfilled it" — Ya'qub — and brought it forth from himself to his sons, and they acted upon it according to his wish. Thus that sincerity availed them against their father's disobedience only, [for they were tested on this journey with a great matter from which they found no escape, namely being accused of theft and the detention of their brother from them].

Abu Hayyan said: In this is evidence for those who claim that "lamma" is a particle of obligation for an obligation, not a temporal adverb meaning "when"; for if it were a temporal adverb, it could not have been governed by "ba'da" (after) with the negative "ma" — end of quote.

Since this may have given the impression that there is no benefit in taking precaution, Allah, exalted is He, pointed to its refutation by praising Ya'qub, peace be upon him, urging imitation of him in taking the means while holding the belief that the matter is in the hand of Allah. So He said: ﴿And indeed he﴾, that is, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, [together with] his command to his sons of this, ﴿was certainly a possessor of knowledge﴾, that is, of understanding of the two rulings: the ruling of obligation and the ruling of decree, and awareness of the two realms is great, ﴿for that which﴾, that is, for that which ﴿We had taught him﴾ of the foundations of the religion and its branches. It is also permissible that the meaning be: he was a possessor of knowledge because of Our teaching him.

So they followed him in taking precaution in pursuing the means, while believing that they have no effect except as the One, the Subduer, enacts them. By this estimation it becomes clear that the exception is connected. The purpose of presenting it in the form of an exception (according to those who take it as disconnected) is to indicate the greatness of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and that what he commands is worthy of being effective, because it is from the command of Allah; for if everything availed by the decree of Allah, then what he pointed to would have availed. "Yughnī" has been explained as "yadfa'u" (repels) because the root *gh-n-y*, in whatever order, revolves around residence (iqāmah), so *aghnā* carries the sense of negation, which is the sense of repelling. Its explanation: *ghinā* in the sense of "resided," "lived," and "met"; *maghnā al-dār* is the place of settling; and residence entails sufficiency and wealth, since the poor man is troubled and restless, while the rich man (*ghaniyy*) — like *ilā*: to marry; when he opens it, it extends; and the noun is *ghaniyyah* with a *ḍammah*. This is because marriage necessarily entails residence. *Al-ghāniyah* is the woman who is sought but does not seek, or the woman who is rich in her beauty and needs no adornment, or the young married woman, or the chaste young woman, whether she has a husband or not; such a woman remains at home and is brief in her tents. *Aghnā ʿanhu ghinā fulān* means: he took his place and filled his role; its literal meaning is that he made the residence of something passing beyond him, so the object is elided. Thus if one says, for example, "So-and-so suffices for me in war," the meaning is: he sufficed for me the striking of heroes or the severity of war, [i.e.] he removed the residence of that from me, making it pass beyond me. There is no doubt that the meaning of that is repelling it from me, and likewise everything of this kind, and whatever has the *ghinā* of that, i.e., its residence and undertaking. It also entails — from the residence which is the pivot and the sufficiency which is its cause — *al-ghinā* (with a kasrah and mad), which is melodious singing with the voice; *al-ghinā* is also sand (*al-ramal*) because of its settling; *ghaniya bi-l-mar'ah* means he composed love poetry about her; *ghaniya bi-Zayd* means he praised or satirized him; these are all necessary consequences of residence and sufficiency; and from it *ghinā al-ḥamām*, the cooing of doves, which is a sound; and *naghā* — like *ramā* — means he spoke words that are understood, because that calms the mind from anxiety. From it is *munāghāh*, which is addressing a child with what pleases him; *naghaytu ilayhi naghyatan*, meaning I cast a word to him; and *al-naghyah*, like *al-naghmah*, is the first news before you verify it, from calling the part by the name of the whole; *nāghāhu* means he drew near to him; from it "the wave reaches up to the sky" (*yunāghī al-samā'*) means it rose; *nāghāhu* means he rivaled him, i.e., opposed him; and *al-mar'ah*: he courted her, i.e., conversed with her — all of these are necessary consequences of residence. *Al-ghayn* is a voiced, elevated letter of the alphabet, as if, by its strength, it resides in its place of articulation, not shaken from it, like *al-rā'* and the airy letters and others. *Al-ghayn* is thirst, because it is the origin: heat requires it, and quenching is an occurrence. *Al-ghayn* is cloud, because of its residence in the air. *Al-ghaynah* is land, because it is a place of residence; and thickly interwoven trees without water are likewise a place for that, because they are shady and there is no water in their land preventing benefit from any of their shade. *Al-ghaynā'* is green of trees, and a well; and with the short vowel, *Ghayn*: the peak of Thabir from the seven mountains — because all of that is a place of residence; perhaps the peak of this mountain has many trees, so it returns to the tree. *Al-aghyan* is tall, either as a comparison to the mountain peak or to the tree. *Al-ghānah* is the ring at the head of the bowstring on the bow. *Ghayna ʿalā qalbihi* means it covered over it, i.e., he set a veil over it so that it became like the sky relative to the cloud; from it *ghayna ʿalayhi* — when desire overwhelms him and he is clothed, or he swoons, or *al-rayn* (the rust of nature and defilement) surrounds him. *Al-ghīnah* with a kasrah is pus and what flows from the dead; it is as if from the removal of residence. Likewise *al-ghīn* with a kasrah is for a place of much fever; and *ghānat nafsī taghīn* means my soul became nauseated; *al-ibil ghāmat* means the camels contracted a disease like the *qallāb*, except that it does not kill — end of quote.

Since it might be thought that everyone is like this, i.e., knows what he knew, Allah, exalted is He, negated that by saying: ﴿But most of mankind﴾, that is, because of the confusion they have, ﴿do not know﴾, that is, they are not people of knowledge [of what We taught them], due to their turning away from it, and they exhaust their powers in concern for what has been guaranteed to them of worldly affairs, and in overcoming their upright, sound natural disposition by returning it to what desires and appetites call to, until no healing from any creature remains in it.

When He, exalted is He, had reported their entry into the city, He reported their entry for their need of Yusuf, upon him be peace, and so he (the narrator) said: "And when they entered upon Yusuf," that is, his sons, upon him be peace, "into Yusuf's presence" in this second visit, "he drew his brother to himself," that is, his full brother Binyamin, after they had said to him: "This is our brother whom you ordered us to bring, and we have brought him." He said: "You have done right, and you will find that [provision] with me." Al-iwa' is to draw oneself close by making one's place a place of comfort. The reason for his drawing him to himself was that he commanded that every two of them should eat separately, so Binyamin was left without a companion, and he said: "This one will eat with me." Then he said to him privately: "Every two of you [shall lodge] in one of the five houses which I have assigned to you, and this lone one will be with me in my house." This separation agreed with what their father had commanded them regarding entering separately. It is as if it were asked: "What did he say to him? Did he inform him of his own identity, or did he conceal that from him as he had done with the rest of his brothers?" So it was answered: "Rather, he said," informing him, "for there is no reason requiring concealment from him, as will be explained," confirming what the brother had of denial because of the long absence, the change of circumstances, and the cutting off of hope from him: "Indeed, I am your brother," Yusuf. Then he made the following a consequence of that, saying: "So do not grieve" (fa-la tabta'is), that is, do not bring upon yourself distress, which is aversion and sorrow, "because of what they used to do" (bima kanu), that is, all the other brothers, being firmly established in it, "doing" (ya'malun), what would distress us, even though they claimed that they had built that action upon knowledge. We have gathered for him the best of what togetherness can be, so do not inform them of anything of that. Then he filled their sacks for them as they had wished.

And it seems that in the first instance as well, in their provisioning, he was seeking to learn about their affairs over a long period without their noticing. For this reason he did not join it with a *fa'* (the particle of immediate sequence). In this second instance, he hastened their provisioning deliberately, aiming to be alone with his brother, without any watcher, by means of the stratagem he had devised. Therefore the *fa'* appears in His saying: ﴿So when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾, meaning, with the swiftest and best provisioning. This is supported by "*When Our command came*" in the stories of Salih and Lut, peace be upon them both, as passed in Surat Hud, peace be upon him. ﴿He placed﴾, meaning, either himself or by one he commanded, ﴿the drinking-cup (al-siqayah)﴾ that belonged to him, which is a vessel from which he drinks, ﴿in his brother's baggage﴾, his full brother, so that he might by this trick keep him with himself, while knowing that the Seer would not judge him a thief on this account, given the possibility that the goblet had been planted in his baggage without his knowledge, as had been done with their merchandise the first time. As for one who is not a Seer, the harm of this notion taking root in his mind is considerable, but it is slight compared with the benefit that results from it: the bringing together of his brothers with Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the removal of their estrangement from him through his brother's remaining with him, as will come with further explanation. This is alongside the certainty of clearing him (the brother) from suspicion soon. Thus it falls under the category of *irtikab akhaff al-darrayn* (choosing the lesser of two harms). Then he delayed them until they set off, and then he sent for them and they were detained. ﴿Then﴾, meaning, after their departure and their going far along the road, ﴿a crier cried out﴾, meaning, announced to them by calling, ﴿saying﴾, loudly, even though they were very near to him, as indicated by the omission of the particle of address: ﴿O caravan!﴾, meaning, O its people. He emphasised this because of their denial: ﴿Indeed, you are thieves!﴾, meaning, this is established for you without doubt, in reality, by what you did regarding Yusuf, peace be upon him, or figuratively, in that you are doing the act of a thief, as will be explained shortly. Moreover, this call was not from the speech of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and it is possible that it was not by his command, so that it would need correcting. Rather, its speaker understood it from his words, peace be upon him: "*My goblet is with the caravan*," or it may be that they took the goblet, so go and bring him to me, or them, and the like, which is true in itself. ***Al-'ir*** (the caravan) is the convoy that carries the loads; its original meaning is donkeys, then it became common until it was applied to any caravan, by way of likeness to them. The verse has contained an explanation of what the gentle handling of the pursuit of an aim requires, namely the setting up of the means that lead to it and prompt it, with a fair outward appearance and a true inward reality, something whose placement is hidden from many people and whose manner is obscure to them, because it is more effective for it and more successful in attaining what is sought from it.

(p-170) It is as if it were said: "This is a grave accusation; what did they say in answer to it?" So it was said: ﴿They said﴾ in reply to those who overtook them, "and" the situation being that the children of Israel "had come forward." It indicates—that those who overtook them were a group, with the crier being one of them, as is the custom of people of standing when they are sent on an important errand—by the plural in His saying ﴿against them﴾, i.e., against the group of the king: the herald and others, ﴿"What is it that you have lost?"﴾ of what it is possible for us to take.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 72:

﴿They said: "We miss﴾ — it seems the water-measure (al-siqaya) had two names, so here they used the expression ﴿the king's goblet (suwa' al-malik)﴾. Al-suwa' is the cup from which one drinks. ﴿And for whoever brings it﴾, i.e., produces it and returns it without search or trouble, ﴿a camel's load﴾. It is pronounced with a kasra (hijl): a measure of goods prepared to be carried on the back. As for haml in the belly, it is with a fatha. ﴿And I stand surety for it﴾, i.e., I guarantee and am responsible, I will pay it to him. The use of the singular pronoun at one point and the plural at another is evidence that the thief was one person, and that the act was attributed to all of them because of their approval of it. The verse also clarifies what the state of a person's bewilderment requires: being careful about the matter, and not hastening to say what is not permissible.

Thus it is as if it were said: What did the brothers of Joseph say? It is said: ﴿They said﴾, the words of one who is innocent, ﴿By God﴾, that is, the Greatest King, so they swore an oath joined with the particle "ta" (tā'), because it is in it that wonder (ta'ajjub) generally occurs. Al-Rummani said: Since it was rare among the particles of oath, it was assigned to the rare of meanings, and [the rare of meanings] is something one wonders at. He also said: It is a substitute for the waw, and the waw is a substitute for the ba', so it is a substitution of a substitution, and for this reason it is weak in inflection with the rest of the nouns. Then they emphasized their innocence by saying: ﴿Certainly you know﴾, that is, by what you have tested of our trustworthiness before this, in our two comings, ﴿that we did not come﴾, and they emphasized the negation with the lam, saying: "to cause corruption" (li-nufsida), that is, to bring about corruption ﴿in the land﴾, and "and" ﴿certainly you know that we were not﴾ [that is, in any way whatsoever] ﴿thieves﴾, that is, described with this attribute at all, by what you have seen of our circumstances: that one who returned our merchandise which we found in our saddlebags, and other things you have witnessed of the nobility of our conduct, along with our knowledge that it is a creation of ours that is not made by craft, which becomes apparent to some intelligent people with the least reflection.

So it is as if it were said: "What did those from the side of the Vizier say?" It was said: "They said" — a word confident that it [the cup] was among their belongings: ﴿What, then, is the penalty for it﴾, that is, the cup, ﴿if you are liars﴾ in your disclaiming of theft. And al-jaza' (recompense) is the requiting of an action with what it deserves of good or evil.

﴿They said﴾, confidently, from them, about their innocence, and informing of the ruling they held: "Its recompense" (that is, the cup, *al-ṣuwāʿ*) "from." Since the lesson lies in the act of finding itself, they put the verb into the passive, saying ﴿it was found in his baggage﴾. Because they were certain of their innocence, they attached the ruling to the mere finding and not to the theft. They then emphasized this with their words ﴿so its recompense is that very thing﴾, meaning nothing else. Thus it was as if it were said: "Is this a matter you have just now invented, or is it a legislation prescribed for you?" So they said ﴿Thus﴾, that is, [rather], it is a *sunnah* (established practice, custom) for us, like that severe recompense, ﴿We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, that is, those who are always wronging; we punish them for their theft. (p-172)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 76:

Then he searched their bags, ﴿so he began﴾, meaning that as a result, the caller (al-mu'adhdhin) or someone else who had been ordered to do so began ﴿with their bags﴾.

Since there was no intervening interval between opening their bags and opening the bag of his brother that could be counted as a separation, his beginning with their bags extended over the time between them. So he did not use a particle of sequence, but said ﴿before the bag of his brother﴾, meaning his brother Yusuf's full brother, peace be upon him, to avoid suspicion. ﴿Then﴾ [meaning after searching their bags and taking care in doing so] ﴿he brought it out﴾, meaning he caused the drinking cup (al-siqaya), which had earlier been said to have been placed in his brother's bag, to be brought out ﴿from his brother's bag﴾.

Since this was a great stratagem for seizing his brother under their own judgment, despite the covenant their father had taken from them, Allah, exalted is He, magnified it by pointing to it with the demonstrative of distance and attributing it to Himself, [and so He said]: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning like this great stratagem, ﴿We devised for Yusuf﴾ specifically, by teaching it to him, as a recompense to them for their scheme against Yusuf, peace be upon him. For this reason We arranged all the means that raised Yusuf, peace be upon him, and compelled (p-173) his brothers, who had plotted against him, by what they thought would nullify his affair, to come to him, until the last of these was their passing judgment upon themselves by what they had judged. Then He gave the reason for this by saying: ﴿He could not have taken his brother﴾, or it is a resumptive explanation of the stratagem. He emphasised the negation with the lam, saying: ﴿to take his brother﴾.

Since the taking could occur in various ways, he restricted it by saying: ﴿under the religion of the king﴾, meaning the king of Egypt, in a particular state among the states, because the penalty for theft among them was other than this. ﴿Unless Allah wills﴾, meaning He to whom the whole affair belongs, that is, by a cause He establishes, such as this cause, which is the judgment of the thief and his people upon themselves. In that case, the king would have nothing but to leave them free with what they had judged against themselves.

The root "sariqa" (s-r-q), with its four permutations sariqa, saqara, qasara, and qarasa, revolves around overpowering that burns and pains. It is sometimes with heat, sometimes with cold, and sometimes with other things. Accompanying it are strength and weakness, abundance and scarcity, and deception, and so concealment and night come about. From the general sense of overpowering comes al-qasr, which is domination and subjugation. Ibn Duraid said: al-qasr is taking by force and oppression. Al-qaswara is the lion, and al-'aziz is like the qaswar, and the hunters among the hunters, whose singular is qaswar, (p-174) and a plain plant, as if game abounds in it so that the qasawira frequent it. Qaswar al-nabt means it grew abundantly. The rakaz of the people, meaning their faint voice and sound, because hunters speak in whispers. Al-saqar in the language is a variant of al-saqr, for a bird that hunts. Qasr is the mountain of al-sarat, as if it were a place of hunting, subjugation, and domination. Al-qaysari is the abundant, because it entails overpowering. It is also a kind of dung beetle, as if it was named for general abundance and for the harm it causes by what it endures of filth. Al-qaysari is also a camel that is large, or hard, or huge and strong. A camel qurasiyya, with a damma and a lightened ya, is huge. Al-qirs, with a kasra, is the small gnats. Al-qaswara is also, among boys, a young man who is strong. The archer is so called because he is fit to overpower, and qaswar also means the hunter in general. It entails deception and concealment, and from it comes al-qaswara, which is the middle of the night, or its beginning, or most of it, because it is the place of concealment and overpowering. From it comes al-saraq, which is taking in secret. The phrase of al-Qazzaz is "in stealth and heedlessness." Saraqa, like fariha, means he hid. Al-sawariq are the projections in the bed of a lock, because of their strangeness and the obscurity of their matter, or because they strip away the act of theft by preventing the thief from opening the lock. Al-mustariq is the one who listens while hidden. Insaraqa 'anhum means he slipped away to leave. Deception and concealment entail a kind of weakness. From it comes: his joints were stolen, meaning they became weak, like fariha. Al-mustariq is the deficient, weak in creation. Insaraqa means he became languid and weak, either from this or from the stripping away, because whoever becomes languid or weak refrains from theft and harm. Qusur al-rajul means he grew old, and from it come al-qaris and al-qarib, meaning the ancient. Mustariq al-'unuq means its short one, as if something had been stolen from it, and he steals a look at it, that is, he seeks its inattention to look at it. Tasrraq means he stole one thing after another. Sarraqa, like sakkara, had the name al-Habbab, and he bought two riding beasts from a Bedouin, then seated him at the door of a house so that he would come out to him with their price. He went out through the other door and fled with them. So the Prophet (ﷺ) named him Sarraq, and he did not like to be called by anything else. Al-saraq, with a fatha and a sukun in the middle, is the finest silk, [or] the white silk, or silk in general, a Persian arabicised word whose origin is sirruh. Al-Qazzaz said: its meaning is good, because (p-176) it is fit to be targeted for theft by reason of the lightness of its load and the great value of its price. Al-sirqin is arabicised from sirkin, and it is possible that it comes from weakness. Perhaps the arabicised word is outside the root's origin, because it has no origin in Arabic. From harm by heat comes al-saqar: the heat of the sun and its harm. It is said: the sun saqarat him, with sin and sad, when it pained his brain. From it derives saqar, which is the name of one of the levels of Hell. Al-saqar is leading the way to the sacred precinct. Al-saqar is what flows from the dates, named from the cause, because heat caused it. Al-qawsara, which is al-qawsara, is a basket for dates, and both may be lightened, because dates are placed in it, and from them may come al-saqar. Al-saqir is the disbeliever, and the one who curses those who do not deserve it, because of the great harm, or because of the deserving of being in Saqar. Al-saquur is the heat and the iron with which a donkey is branded. From harm by cold comes al-qars, which is intense and cold frost, and al-qars, which is moved, is the coldest and densest frost. Al-qaras, with movement, is what is solid. Aqras al-'ud means he froze its water. From it comes al-qarid, for fish that has been cooked and left until it has solidified. Qarasa al-ma' means it froze. Al-bard means it became intense, like qarisa, like fariha. The family of qararis is said. It is said: nabat qarras, like sahab, a mountain of cold places or hills in the region of al-sarat. We made the water cold: baradnahu.

Once this is established, the correction of the caller's words, ﴿Indeed you are thieves﴾, if one considers overpowering in concealment, then there is no doubt that they are characterised by that, because they took Yusuf from his father, peace be upon them both, in this state. If one considers the general sense of taking in [concealment], then applying that to them is metaphorical, because with them, at the time of his calling to them while they were walking away, was something that was not theirs. They were carrying it away in concealment. That is, you in this state are doing the act of a thief. The first sense is strengthened by His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive﴾ [Yusuf: 15], and His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿With whomever we find our property with him﴾ [Yusuf: 79], as will come later.

Since Yusuf, peace be upon him, was only able to do this through the height of his rank, his firm establishment, and his elevation, after he had been in a state of humiliation among them, that was a matter of wonder. So Allah, exalted is He, said, turning to the station of speaking to strengthen the speech with the station of the third person and of speaking, and to increase the sense of the greatness of this act by framing it in the form of majesty, alerting one who might be heedless: ﴿We raise﴾, meaning We raise for Ourselves from greatness. The original would have been "his degrees", but He generalised it because that is more indicative of greatness and more fitting to its appearance (p-178). He said, alerting that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had suffered such degradation as he thought would not be lifted after it: ﴿degrees, whomever We will﴾, meaning through knowledge.

Since the cause of elevation is superior knowledge of causes, and that is because if creatures strove to lower someone and set for him every cause they knew and were able to, and Allah willed the opposite, He would, by His knowledge, bring about a single cause if He willed, nullifying all those causes and decreeing his elevation. Allah, exalted is He, drew attention to this by saying: ﴿Above every possessor of knowledge﴾, meaning among creatures, ﴿is one All-Knowing﴾, of great knowledge, whose greatness of knowledge minds cannot comprehend, nor can understandings imagine. He causes such causes that the causes of scholars fall short and the minds of discerning intellects are bewildered. He is Allah, exalted is He, as al-Rummani transmitted it from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and al-Hasan, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Thus the tanwin is for magnification.

ولَمّا تَمَّ ذَلِكَ، كانَ كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: إنَّ انْتِزاعَ أخِيهِمْ مِنهم - بَعْدَ تِلْكَ المَواثِيقِ الَّتِي أكَّدُوها لِأبِيهِمْ - لِداهِيَةٍ تَطِيشُ لَها الحُلُومُ، فَماذا كانَ فِعْلُهم عِنْدَها؟ فَقِيلَ: ”قالُوا“ تَسْلِيَةً لِأنْفُسِهِمْ ودَفْعًا لِلْعارِ عَنْ خاصَّتِهِمْ ﴿إنْ يَسْرِقْ﴾ [If he steals], فَلَمْ يَجْزِمُوا بِسَرِقَتِهِ، لِعِلْمِهِمْ بِأمانَتِهِ، وظَنِّهِمْ هَذا الصُّواعَ (ṣuwāʿ, the drinking cup) دَسَّ في رَحْلِهِ وهو لا يَشْعُرُ، كَما دَسَّتْ بِضاعَتُهم في رِحالِهِمْ (p-١٧٩) وإنَّما أوْهى ظَنَّهم هَذا سُكُوتُ أخِيهِمْ عَنِ الِاعْتِذارِ بِهِ، عَلى أنَّهُ قَدْ ورَدَ أنَّهم لامُوهُ فَقالَ لَهُمْ: وضَعَهُ في رَحْلَيِ الَّذِي وضَعَ البِضاعَةَ في رِحالِهِمْ ﴿فَقَدْ سَرَقَ أخٌ﴾ [then a brother has stolen] أيْ شَقِيقٌ ﴿لَهُ﴾ [of his], ولَمّا كانَ ما ظَنُّوهُ كَذَلِكَ في زَمَنٍ يَسِيرٍ، أدْخَلُوا الجارَ فَقالُوا: ﴿مِن قَبْلُ﴾ [before] يَعْنُونَ يُوسُفَ عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ (peace be upon him)، وذَلِكَ أنَّهُ قِيلَ: إنَّ عَمَّتَهُ كانَتْ لا تَصْبِرُ عَنْهُ، وكانَ أبُوهُ لا يَسْمَحُ بِمُكْثِهِ عِنْدَها، لِأنَّهُ لا يَصْبِرُ عَنْهُ، فَحَزَمَتْهُ مِن تَحْتِ ثِيابِهِ بِمِنطَقَةِ (minṭaqa, belt) أبِيها إسْحاقَ عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ وكانَتْ عِنْدَها، ثُمَّ قالَتْ: فَقَدْتُ مِنطِقَةَ أبِي، فاكْشِفُوا أهْلَ البَيْتِ، فَوَجَدُوها مَعَ يُوسُفَ عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ، فَسَمَحَ يَعْقُوبُ عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ حِينَئِذٍ لَها بِبَقائِهِ عِنْدَها ﴿فَأسَرَّها﴾ [So he kept it hidden] أيْ إجابَتُهم عَنْ هَذِهِ القَوْلَةِ القَبِيحَةِ ﴿يُوسُفُ في نَفْسِهِ﴾ [Joseph within himself] عَلى تَمَكُّنِهِ مِمّا يُرِيدُ بِهِمْ مِنَ الِانْتِقامِ.

ولَمّا كانَ رُبَّما ظَنَّ ظانٌّ أنَّهُ بَكَتْهم بِها بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ، نَفى هَذا الظَّنُّ بِقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿ولَمْ يُبْدِها﴾ [and did not reveal it] أيْ أصْلًا ﴿لَهُمْ﴾ [to them]، فَكَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: فَما قَوْلَتُهُ الَّتِي أسَرَّها في نَفْسِهِ؟ فَقِيلَ: ﴿قالَ أنْتُمْ شَرٌّ مَكانًا﴾ [He said, "You are worse in position"] أيْ مِن يُوسُفَ وأخِيهِ، لِأنَّ ما نُسِبَ إلَيْهِما مِنَ الشَّرِّ إنَّما هو ظاهِرًا لِأمْرِ خَيْرٍ اقْتَضاهُ، وأمّا أنْتُمْ فَفِعْلَتُكم بِيُوسُفَ شَرُّ مَقْصُودٍ مِنكم ظاهِرًا وباطِنًا، ونِسْبَةُ الشَّرِّ إلى (p-١٨٠) مَكانِهِمْ أعْظَمَ مِن نِسْبَتِهِ إلَيْهِمْ، وإنَّما قَدَّمَ الإخْبارَ بِالإسْرارِ مَعَ اقْتِرانِهِ بِالإضْمارِ قَبْلَ الذِّكْرِ، لِئَلّا يَظُنَّ بادِئَ بَدْءٍ أنَّهم سَمِعُوا ما وصَفَهم بِهِ مِنَ الشَّرِّ ﴿واللَّهُ﴾ [And God] أيِ الَّذِي لَهُ الإحاطَةُ الكامِلَةُ ﴿أعْلَمُ بِما تَصِفُونَ﴾ [is most knowing of what you describe] مِنكُمْ، وأنَّهُ لَيْسَ كَما قُلْتُمْ؛ والوَصْفُ (waṣf, description): كَلِمَةٌ مُشْتَقَّةٌ مِن أصْلِ [مِنَ] الأُصُولِ لِتَجْرِيَ عَلى مَذْكُورٍ فَتَفَرَّقَ بَيْنَهُ وبَيْنَ غَيْرِهِ بِطَرِيقِ النَّقِيضِ (naqīḍ, opposite) كالفَرْقِ بَيْنَ العالِمِ والجاهِلِ ونَحْوِهِما،

Thus it is as if it was said: that statement, despite its vileness, does not avail them or their father anything. So did they limit themselves to it? It is said: No, rather ﴿They said﴾ seeking what would avail them: ﴿O you, the Chief (al-'Azeez)﴾, so they addressed him with what befits the great, so that he would be moved to pity for them. ﴿Indeed he has﴾, i.e., this one who found the cup in his baggage, ﴿an aged father﴾, i.e., in his years and station, ﴿and he is deeply attached to him, unable to bear separation from him and unable to be patient without him.﴾ ﴿So take one of us in his place﴾, and be good to his father by sending him back to him. ﴿Indeed we see you﴾, i.e., we know you with a knowledge that is like sight, or according to what we have seen of you, ﴿to be among the doers of good﴾, i.e., those who excel in the quality of goodness. So apply in our matter your customary goodness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 79 (part 1 of 2):

So it is as if it were said: "What was their reply?" It is said: ﴿He said: "God forbid that we should take anyone but him with whom we found our property."﴾ That is, "We seek refuge in Him, the One to whom nothing is comparable as a refuge." ﴿That we should take﴾ means: for the sake of this matter. ﴿Anyone but﴾ means the person ﴿with whom we found our property﴾. He did not say "who stole our property," because, just as he did not act as a thief regarding the bowl, nothing had previously occurred from him that would justify applying that description to him. He gave the reason in his words: ﴿For then we would indeed be wrongdoers﴾, that is, if we took someone in his place, we would be extreme in wrongdoing according to your own religion, (p-181) so why do you seek what is wrongdoing in your own view?

He mentioned, after what had preceded of this story, from the Tawrah (Torah):

He said: There was famine (al-qaham) — and in one copy, hunger (al-ju'), — and dread spread over the whole face of the earth. Yusuf opened the granaries and began selling to the Egyptians, and the hunger grew severe in the land of Egypt, and all the people of the earth came to buy grain from Yusuf.

When Ya'qub, upon him be blessings and peace, heard that there was provision of grain in Egypt, Ya'qub, upon him be peace, said to his sons: "Do not fear for yourselves, for it has reached me that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy grain for us, that we may live and not die." So the sons of Ya'qub, upon him be blessings and peace, [the ten] went down to buy grain from Egypt. But Binyamin, Yusuf's brother, Ya'qub did not send with his brothers, because he said: "Perhaps some misfortune may befall him." So the sons of Isra'il came to buy grain with those who were going, because the hunger had grown severe in the land of Canaan. Yusuf was the ruler over the land, and he was distributing to all the people of the land. Yusuf's brothers came to him, upon him be (p-182) blessings and peace, and they bowed down before him, prostrating to the ground. Yusuf saw his brothers, recognized them, and pretended to be a stranger to them, and spoke to them harshly and roughly, and said to them: "Where are you from?" They said: "We have come from the land of Canaan to buy grain." Yusuf, upon him be blessings and peace, recalled the dream that they had related to him, and said to them: "You are spies, and you have come only to inspect and observe the land." They said: "No, my lord! Your servants have come only to buy grain. We are all sons of one man, and we are honest, and your servants are not spies." Yusuf said to them: "It is not as you say; rather you have come only to spy upon our land." They said to him: "We are twelve brothers, your servants, sons of one man in the land of Canaan; the youngest is with our father today, and the other is lost." Yusuf said to them: "I only said to you that you are spies. For this reason you are being tested: by Pharaoh's right, I will not let you go out from here until your youngest brother comes to (p-183) here. Then we will examine your statements, whether you have spoken the truth and justice; otherwise, by Pharaoh's right, you are indeed spies." He threw them into prison for three days. On the third day Yusuf, upon him be blessings and peace, called them and said: "Do what I command you, and you will live, for I fear God regarding you. If you are honest, let one of you be held in your prison, and go, you, with the grain for the hunger in your houses. But bring me your youngest brother, so that I may confirm your words, and you will not die." They did as he commanded. Each man said to his companion: "Truly, we have deserved this imprisonment because of our brother, since we saw the distress of his soul when he pleaded with us and we did not pity him or have compassion for him. Therefore this calamity and evil has befallen us." Ruwbil answered and said to them: "Did I not tell you: do not sin against the boy? But you did not accept. And now, behold, we are being held accountable for his blood." They did not know that Yusuf understood their speech, for he had placed an interpreter between himself and them. He withdrew from them and wept, then returned to speak with them, then he took Shim'un from among them and bound him before them.

Yusuf commanded that their sacks be filled with grain, and commanded that the silver of each man be returned into his sack, and that they be given provisions for the journey. This was done for them as Yusuf, upon him be peace, had commanded. They loaded their grain onto their donkeys and set off. But one of them opened his sack (p-184) to give fodder to his donkey at their resting place, and he saw his silver placed at the top of his load. He said to his brothers: "My silver has been returned to me; here it is at the top of my load." Their hearts trembled, their souls were terrified, and each one of them was astonished. They said: "Woe is me! What is this that God has done to us?" They came to their father Ya'qub in the land of Canaan and informed him of everything that had befallen them, and they said: "The man, the lord of the land, spoke to us harshly and roughly. He reckoned us as spies who had come to scout the land. We said: 'We are honest and upright; we are not spies. We are twelve brothers, sons of one father; one of us is lost, and the other is with our father today in the land of Canaan.' The man, the lord and ruler of the land, said to us: 'By this I will know that you are righteous and upright. Leave one of your brothers with me, and take grain for the hunger in your houses. Go, and bring me your youngest brother with you, and then I will know that you are not spies, but that you are honest and upright, and I will order your brother to be delivered to you, and you may trade in the land.'" While they were emptying their sacks, behold, each man's bundle of silver was at the top of his sack. They saw their silver tied up, and they and their father were terrified. Their father said to them: "You have bereaved me of my children; you have deprived me of both of them. Yusuf is gone, and Shim'un is held, (p-185) and now you would take Binyamin too; all calamities have come upon me together." Ruwbil said to his father: "May I lose my own sons if I do not bring him back to you! Entrust him to me, and I will return him to you." He said: "My son will not go down with you, for his brother Yusuf has died, and he alone is left of his mother's children. Some harm may befall him on the road you travel, and you will bring my gray head down to the grave in misery and wretchedness."

The hunger grew severe upon the land. When they had eaten what they had brought from Egypt and used it up, their father Ya'qub, upon him be peace, said to them: "Go down and buy for us some wheat." Yahudha said to him: "The man warned us and gave us a charge, saying: 'You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you.' If you send our brother with us, we will go down and buy grain; but if you do not send him, we will not go." Their father said to them: "Why did you treat me badly by telling the man that you have a brother?" They said: "The man asked about us and about our family, saying: 'Is your father still alive? Do you have another brother?' We informed him according to these questions. How could we have known that he would say: 'Bring your brother down with you?'" Yahudha said to Isra'il his father: "Send the boy with me, and we will set out and live and not die, we and you and our household as well. I will be surety for him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, then I will bear the blame before my father for all days."

Their father Isra'il said: "If it is so, then do what I command you: take from the best produce of this land some of the pistachio, honey, mastic, carob, terebinth and almond in your sacks, and take double the silver that was in your sacks, perhaps that was an oversight on their part. Take your brother and go to the man, and return to me all of you. May the God of promises grant you favor and mercy from the man, so that he sends your other brother with you and Binyamin as well." The men took this gift and double the silver, and set off with Binyamin and came to Yusuf and stood before him. When Yusuf saw Binyamin with them, he said to his steward: "Bring these men into the house, slaughter an animal and prepare a meal, for these men will dine with me at noon." The servant did as Yusuf, upon him be peace, had commanded, and brought the men into Yusuf's house, upon him be peace. They said: "They are bringing us in only because of the silver we found in our sacks before. They intend to fall upon us and deceive us, make us slaves and seize our donkeys." They approached the man, the steward, (in another copy: the treasurer), Yusuf, upon him be peace, and spoke to him at the door of the house, and said: "We beg you, our lord, that we came down here first and bought wheat, but when (p-187) we arrived and entered the house, behold, each one of us found his silver in his sack. We have returned our silver with its weight and brought other silver with us to buy grain, and we do not know who put our silver in our sacks." He said to them: "Peace be upon you. Do not fear, nor be anxious. Your God, the God of promises, the God of your father, has placed this treasure in your sacks for you. Your silver came into my hands." Then he brought Shim'un out to them. The servant brought the men into Yusuf's house, upon him be peace, and brought them water, and they washed their hands and feet, and he gave fodder to their donkeys. The men had prepared their gift before Yusuf, upon him be peace, entered, at midday, because he had informed them that their lunch would be there. Yusuf entered his house, and they brought in their gift and placed it before him in his house, and they bowed down to him, prostrating to the ground. He asked them about their well-being and said: "Is your father well, the old man of whom you told me, is he still alive?" They said: "Our father your servant is well." Then they knelt and prostrated. He raised his eyes and saw Binyamin, his full brother, and said to them: "Is this your brother of whom you told me?" They said: "Yes." He said: "May God show you mercy, my sons." Yusuf, upon him be (p-188) peace, hastened because he was moved and tender toward him and wanted to weep. He went into his chamber and wept there, then washed his face and came out, restraining himself. He commanded that they be served the meal. They set food before him alone, and they served them alone, because the people of Egypt could not eat with the Hebrews, for that was defilement to the Egyptians. He commanded that the eldest be seated according to his age and the youngest according to his age. The men were amazed and remained bewildered and astonished. He gave each one of them a portion from before him, and Binyamin received five times as much as any of them. They drank.

He commanded his steward and said to him: "Fill the containers of these people with grain as much as they can carry, put each man's silver at the mouth of his container, and take the drinking-bowl of silver [tas] and put it in the container of the youngest, along with the silver of his grain-measure." The servant did as Yusuf, peace be upon him, had commanded.

When the next day came, the people were sent off so that they might depart, with them and their donkeys. They went out of the village, and before they had left it, Yusuf said to his steward: "Get up, go after the people, overtake them, and say to them: Why have you repaid good with evil? You have taken the bowl from which my lord drinks and by which he divines (ya'taf, practising divination by the cup), and what you have done is wicked." He overtook them and said these words to them.

They said to him: (p-189) "Do not say such things, O our master! God forbid that your servants should do such deeds! We returned to you the silver we found in our containers from the land of Canaan. How then would we steal gold or silver from the house of your master? Whoever among your servants is found with it, let him die, and we will be slaves to our master!" He said: "It shall be as you say. Whoever is found with it shall become my slave, and you shall be free of blame." Each of them hurried to lower his container, and they searched, beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest. They found the bowl in the container of Binyamin. They tore their garments and rent them. Each man loaded his container onto his donkey, and they returned to the village.

Yahudha and his brothers entered upon Yusuf, who was still in his house, and they fell down on the ground before him. Yusuf said to them: "What is this deed that you have done? Do you not know that a man like me divines (ya'taf) by a cup, or, in another copy, tests (yamtahin) by a cup? Why do you transgress against him and take him?"

Yahudha said: "What shall we say to our master? What shall we speak, and how shall we plead? God has brought this sin upon your servants. Behold, we are slaves to our master, we and the one in whose possession the cup was found." He said: "God forbid that I should do this! Rather, the man in whose possession the cup was found shall be my slave, and as for you, go up in peace to your father."

Yahudha drew near to him and said: "I beg you, O my lord, to permit your servant to speak before you, O my lord! Do not let your anger flare against your servants, for you are like Pharaoh. My lord asked his servants: 'Do you have a father or a brother?' We said to our lord: 'We have an aged father and a young son born in his old age, and his brother has died, and he alone remains of his mother, and his father loves him. You ordered your servants, saying: Bring him down to me, that I may see him and look upon him.' We said to our lord: 'The boy cannot leave his father, for if he leaves his father, his father will die.' I said to your servants: 'Your younger brother did not come down with you, so do not presume to see my face again.' When we went up to our servant, our father, we told him the words of our lord. Our servant, our father, said to us: 'Go back and buy some grain for us.' We said to our father: 'We cannot go down unless we take our younger brother with us, for we cannot look on the face of the man if our brother is not with us.' Our servant, our father, said to us: 'You know that my wife bore me two sons. One went out from me, and you said: He has been killed, a killing. I have not seen him to this day. Will you take this one also from me? Then harm will befall him, and you will bring my gray hairs down in sorrow to the grave of evil. Now, if we go to our servant, our father, and the boy is not with us, while his soul is dear to him, then when he sees that the boy is not with us, he will die. Your servant, the gray head of our father, will go down in misery and grief, for your servant guaranteed the boy to our father. I said: If I do not bring him back to you, I shall bear the blame for all my days. Now, let your servant remain in place of the boy as a slave to my lord, and let the boy go up with his brothers, for I cannot bear to go up to my father without the boy with me, lest I see the evil that will befall my father.'"

Then, when they had despaired of him concerning the release of Benjamin, Allah the Exalted related the opinion that this produced in them, saying: ﴿So when﴾, with the fa' indicating the closeness of the time of those consultations, ﴿they despaired of him﴾, meaning their hope that he would let go of their brother turned into a severe despair, because they saw his kindness, gentleness and mercy, and they saw how firmly he held to taking the one with him and refused to exchange him. ﴿They withdrew apart﴾, meaning they separated themselves from others, while ﴿conferring secretly (najiyyan)﴾, meaning they were people holding a private consultation, with some of them speaking privately with others. Najwa (private consultation) is from munajah, which is raising the meaning from one to another in concealment, from al-najw, which is elevation [from the ground], as said by al-Rummani. Or they became purely a secret consultation, because of their intense absorption in it, as if they were the very form of secret conferring. So it is as if it were said: What did they say? It was said: ﴿The eldest of them said﴾ in age, and he was Ruwabil: ﴿Did you not know﴾, establishing for them what they already knew, given the closeness of the time, so that their resolve would intensify in exerting effort to be freed from their father's anger, ﴿that your father﴾, meaning the elderly old man whom you had bereaved of his dearest son.

Since the situation called for reminding them and for recognizing the true state of affairs in anticipation of what would follow in the speech, he said: ﴿Has taken from you﴾, meaning before he gave you this other son, ﴿a solemn covenant﴾. Since Allah the Exalted is the One who prescribed it, as already passed, it was as if it were from Him, so he said: ﴿from Allah﴾, meaning the oath of the Greatest King: "You will surely bring him back to me unless you are encompassed." ﴿And before this﴾, meaning before this, ﴿you failed in your duty﴾, meaning you fell short by abandoning what was due from you in your father's view, or in what you claimed to your father, a great shortfall. The addition of "mā" indicates his intent in that matter of the loss of ﴿Joseph﴾, so that your father would not believe you at all, but would join this to that, and thereby know your treachery with certainty. The original meaning of tafrit (failing in duty) is precedence, from his saying (ﷺ): "I will precede you (faratukum) to the Basin."

Since the place was one of grief, lamentation and anguish, he emphasized it with the negating "mā", which is the opposite of the affirmed, as has passed more than once. That is, your action concerning Joseph was nothing but a failure beyond doubt. ﴿So I will not leave﴾, meaning I will not depart from this ﴿land﴾ because of this matter. Connecting the verb without a preposition is evidence that he had become strongly attached to it. ﴿Until my father gives me leave﴾ to go from it, ﴿or Allah judges for me﴾, meaning He to whom belongs all perfection, and in whom we trust, regarding the freeing of my brother, or regarding departing from it by some means among the ways that He knows and is able to bring about. ﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, meaning both outwardly and inwardly, for when He wills a matter He accomplishes it through the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the all-encompassing reach of His power, and by making it in the best and most perfect existence.

So it is as though it were said: "This is what he (Yusuf) decided to do concerning himself. Then what did he decide for his brothers?" It was said: he ordered them to return so that they would inform their father, since it was possible that he would wish to come to Egypt to see his son, or that he would have an opinion in the matter that would bring relief. So he said: ﴿Return to your father﴾, that is, without me, "and say" to him, that is, speaking to him gently in your address, ﴿O our father﴾. And emphasize your statement, for he will deny it to you. So say: ﴿Indeed, your son﴾, that is, the full brother of Yusuf, peace be upon him, who is the most perfect of us in sonship to you, ﴿has stolen﴾.

Since they were in the utmost confidence that none of them would commit such an act, they pointed to it with their words: ﴿And we did not testify﴾, that is, in this matter, ﴿except to what we knew﴾, apparently, from our seeing the drinking cup coming out of his bag. Testimony (shahada) is a report based on the perception of a statement or an act, and testimony may also be given to what sound decisive evidence leads to. ﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾, that is, of the matter that was hidden from us, ﴿watchers﴾. Perhaps a stratagem was devised in that matter, the knowledge of which was hidden from us, as he (Yusuf) did in returning our merchandise. (p-194)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 82:

﴿Wa-s'al al-qaryata﴾ meaning: ask its people and its walls, if it could speak, ﴿the town in which we were﴾, which is Egypt, about what we told you; they will inform you of our truthfulness, for the matter has become well known among them. "And ask" ﴿the caravan﴾, meaning its companions, who are a people of Canaan, neighbours of Ya'qub, upon him be peace, ﴿with which we came﴾. The sual (question) is the request for information by means of its particle, such as the hamza (interrogative alif), hal and similar particles. The qarya (town) is the land that gathers together within distinct boundaries, and its origin is from "qaraytu al-ma'" (I gathered the water), meaning I collected it. Its explanation will come at the end of the surah. The 'ir (caravan) is a company of donkeys, from al-'ir, with a fatha, which is the donkey; this is the original meaning, as has preceded, and then it became widespread until it was used for other than donkeys.

Since that was deserving of denial, given what is established of the generosity of their brother, they emphasised it by their saying: ﴿and indeed we are truthful﴾, meaning, by Allah. It is as if it were said: So they returned to their father and told him what their eldest (kabir) had said to them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 83:

It is as if it were said: "What did he say to them?" It is said: ﴿He said, "Rather...",﴾ meaning: the matter is not as they claim. The attribution of your son to theft has not been valid, either outwardly or inwardly; that is, [he did] not take anything from its owner in secrecy. Rather, ﴿your souls have embellished for you a matter,﴾ meaning: they beautified it with an adornment containing error. That is, I related to you a matter from which this consequence followed. The "matter" (al-amr) is the thing that it is in the nature of the soul to command (al-nafs tu'mar) with. Both meanings are correct. As for the negation, it is clear, because Benjamin did not steal the drinking cup (al-suwa') and did not intend to do so. For this reason, neither Joseph, peace be upon him, nor his herald attributed it to him alone. As for the affirmation, it is more evident, because had it not been for their deed against Joseph, peace be upon him, their souls would not have embellished for them this matter concerning him, and this matter would not have befallen Benjamin, peace be upon him. ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ from me, because my opinion of God is beautiful. In His saying ﴿Perhaps God﴾ (ʿasā Allāh), that is, the One encompassing everything in power and knowledge, ﴿will bring them to me all together﴾, that is, Joseph, his full brother Benjamin, and Reuben. The discerning reader is shown by this that he perceived that these actions arose from Joseph, peace be upon him, and that the outcome would be safety and reunion. Then he gave the reason for this in His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Knowing﴾, that is, He alone, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, that is, the thoroughly knowledgeable of what is hidden from us in these matters, so He knows the means that lead to the goals; ﴿the All-Wise﴾, that is, the thorough in firmly arranging affairs and in ordering causes such that no one can undo what He has firmly established of them. The arrangement of the two attributes in the highest degree of firmness, as you see, is because the situation calls for knowledge of what has been hidden of the causes more than it calls for knowledge of their wisdom. He said this statement.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 84:

﴿And he turned away from them﴾, that is, he turned his face away from them, because of the grief that had intensified upon him and reached him with its hardship, and the burning sorrow (ḥaraq) that had been stirred within him by the accumulation of one grief upon another, out of his aversion to what they had brought and his turning toward the One to whom the matter belongs. ﴿And he said﴾, complaining to God alone and not to anyone else, so it is an allusion that is more emphatic than explicit declaration, and a supplication: ﴿Oh, my grief over Joseph!﴾, that is, O my greatest sorrow. The alif in "asafā" is a substitute for the ya' of possessive pronoun, to indicate that the grief has reached a point that has no limit. The paronomasia (jinās) between "al-asaf" (grief) and "Yūsuf" (Joseph) is something not deliberately intended, and therefore it is natural (maṭbū'), reaching the utmost in artistic excellence (nihāyat al-ibdā'); and its like in the Qur'an is abundant. ﴿Over Joseph﴾: this is your time that has filled me with you, so keep me company as I keep you company. He specified him because he was the foundation (qā'ida) of his brothers, upon which what follows was built and from which it branched out. ﴿And his eyes turned white﴾, that is, their blackness changed to a state of whiteness due to excessive weeping, so the sight became blind. ﴿From the grief﴾, which is the cause of constant weeping, which is the cause of the whiteness; so he mentioned the first cause. It is said: the grief of peace be upon him reached the grief of seventy bereaved mothers, and his opinion of God never became bad.

Then he gave the reason for that with his saying: ﴿So he is﴾, that is, because of the grief, ﴿restraining (kaẓīm)﴾, that is, intensely suppressing, being full of distress, restraining himself from doing what such things would require of foolish conduct, by what God had given him of knowledge and wisdom. That is the hardest thing for the soul and the strongest thing for grief. So it is fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl, and it is more emphatic than it, from "kaẓm al-siqā'" (the stopping of a waterskin when one tightly fastens it while full).

The root k-ẓ-m revolves around preventing from manifestation, which entails distress—because it is the nature of what is prevented, being full of it—and entails fullness, because what is restrained has no power of appearance. "Kaẓama ghayẓahu" means he remained silent after being full of it; "kaẓamtu al-siqā'" means you filled it and sealed it; "kaẓama al-ba'īr jarrataḥu" means he returned and held back his cud. Al-kaẓm: the outlet of breath, because by it one prevents oneself from running after one's desire. Al-kaẓāma: a rope tied around a camel's snout to restrain it from what it wants. Also, it is attached to the string of the Arab bow and then turned at the upper end of the notch, to prevent it from loosening. Also, a channel in the depths of the earth through which water flows, because it prevents the water from taking its course downward so that it rises at the spring's location and appears on the surface of the earth. Also, a breach through which water flows from one well to another, because it is only made when one of the two wells is weak; without it the strong one would overflow, so it diverts its water away from its proper course. The kaẓāmat al-mīzān is the pin around which the tongue of the balance turns, because it binds it and prevents it from coming apart. It is said: "mā ziltu kāẓiman yawmī kullahu," meaning I kept abstaining from eating all day while being full of hunger. It may also be applied to any source of water; from it comes Kāẓima, a village on the seashore, because the sea has restrained it from spreading out, and likewise it has restrained the sea from flowing away.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 85:

When they saw that what they had hoped would follow Joseph's departure, namely the improvement of their standing with their father by the concentration of his attention upon them, had escaped them, and this great calamity had befallen their father, the listener became eager to hear what they said to him. So the narration resumes its report of them with His words: "They said" (qālū), that is, out of rage at that. ﴿By God﴾, that is, the Greatest King, [this being] an oath in which there is an expression of wonder. ﴿You will not cease to remember Joseph﴾, that is, you will continue to, being eager to remember him, strong in it, with the eagerness of a vigorous, enduring young man for his desire. ("Until") that is, to the point that ﴿you become one close to death﴾, that is, on the verge of destruction, overlooking it, preparing for it, through wasting of the body and corruption of the mind, as its explanation has passed in Surat al-Anfal at His words ﴿Urge the believers to fighting﴾ [al-Anfal: 65]. ﴿Or you become among those who perish﴾, that is, becoming a settled state, like a natural disposition.

**(p-199)** When the soul longed for what had been lost to him, after seeing the blunder of his sons, he relieved his distress with his saying: ﴿He said, "I only﴾, meaning: Yes, I will not cease to be thus, for it is among the attributes of human perfection, since it indicates tenderness and loyalty. It is blameworthy only when it takes the form of complaining to creatures, and I do not complain to any creature. Rather, ﴿I complain of my anguish﴾. Al-bath (anguish) is the most severe grief. It is so named because, due to its severity, its burden cannot be borne, so it is confided and spread. ﴿and my grief﴾ in general, even if its cause is slight and creatures are able to remove it, ﴿to God﴾, meaning the One who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, seeking exposure to the breezes of His generosity, and not to anyone other than Him. And this, which you heard from me and over which you became agitated, is a little of much.

Since it was possible that they were truthful in saying that they found only Joseph's shirt stained with blood, and that their claim that a wolf had devoured him was based on that, and since Jacob, peace be upon him, was inclined to think that Joseph was alive, and it was expected of God that He would reunite him with him, he said: ﴿And I know from God﴾, meaning from the Supreme King, of the kindness toward us, the people of this house, and of relieving those in distress and gladdening the grieving, ﴿what you do not know.﴾

**(p-200)** The root *fa-ta-ʼa* (فتأ) is attested as a yāʼī (third radical yāʼ), a wāwī (third radical wāw), and hamzated, and in its non-hamzated forms, in every arrangement: *fataʼa, faʼata, tafaʼa, afata*, and *fataʼ, fawata* and *tawafa* [and *tafawu*]. All of these revolve around youth, and they entail strength, intensity of resolve, and soundness of submission. It is said: *mā fataʼa yafʻalu kadhā* (with the ʻayn vowelled in three ways), meaning: *mā zāla kamā afta*, i.e., he continued to do that like a vigorous young man of firm resolve. And *wa-mā fati'a an yafʻala* means: *mā baraḥa*, i.e., he hastened to do it with ease of submission and intensity of resolve. Its real sense is: *mā fati'a ʻan fiʻl kadhā*, i.e., he did not pass beyond it to something else, nor did he forget it, but restricted his youthful vigour, resolve and striving to it.
