From Ibn Mālik, in *Jamʻ al-lughāt al-mushakkala*, attributed to al-Farrāʼ, and he authenticated it in *al-Qāmūs*: *fataʼa*, like *manaʻa*, meant "he broke and extinguished," and it is clear in [the sense of] strength. *Fatiʼa ʻanhu*, like *samiʻa*, meant "he forgot it and desisted from it," i.e., he refrained from it, or it is specific to negation, i.e., there precedes it a particle of negation; its meaning is that his strength surpassed it, so it did not mix with it.

From its yāʼī form: *al-fitāʼ*, like *samāʼ*, is youth, and it is as if it is the origin of the root. *Al-fatiyy*, with a short vowel, is the generous and noble one, i.e., the liberal, high-minded person. *Al-fatā* is the lord, the brave. (It is also said that *al-fatā*) is the slave, even if he is miserly or elderly, because one generally does not buy except young men. *Al-fatā* is also the student, and the follower likewise. *Al-fatā*, like *ghaniy*, is also the young man. *Al-futūwa* is generosity, and one may say *tufta* and *tafātā*. Their *futuwwa*: he surpassed them in it. *Aftāhu fī al-amr* means: he clarified it for him. *Al-futyā*, with a damma, and *al-fatwā*, and with a fatha, is what a jurist has given as a legal opinion, and it returns to generosity and good character. *Al-fatayān* are the night and the day, and for this reason they are called "the two new ones." *Fatiyat al-bint tafthiyatan* means: the girl refrained from playing with the boys, so it is from the removal of youth, i.e., its action. From its inverted hamzated form: *iftaʼata ʻalayya al-bāṭil* means he fabricated falsehood against me, and *bi-raʼyihi* means he acted arbitrarily with his opinion. Both indicate boldness and recklessness, and it is most appropriate for a young man whom time has not yet tempered. *Ufti'a* (in the passive form) means he died suddenly, as if that were the most severe death. From the wāwī form: *fāta al-shayʼ fawtan wa-fawātan*: it went away and passed by, so it was not overtaken. *Fātahu* and *iftātahu*: it went away from him and outstripped him. This indicates the strength of the one who outstrips. Between them is *fawt*, i.e., a gap, as if each of them precedes the other. *Tafāwata al-shayʼān* and *tafawwatā*: the distance between them increased, and this entails difference and disorder, and it entails defect: ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no discrepancy﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], i.e., no defect; the observer says: "If it were thus, it would have been better." *Mawt al-fawāt* is sudden death. It is the escaping of his spear and his hand, i.e., where he sees it but cannot reach it. *Al-fawt* is the gap between two fingers. *Iftāta ʻalayhi bi-raʼyihi* means he preceded him with it. *Fātahu bihi wa-ʻalayhi* means he overpowered him. [And *lā yaftāt ʻalayhi*] means he does not act without his command, i.e., no one is stronger than him so as to outstrip him. *Iftāta al-kalām* means he invented speech, as previously mentioned under the hamzated form. *Iftāta ʻalayhi* means he judged against him, because of his strength. *Al-fuwayt*, like *zubayr*, is the one who is independent in his opinion, for both masculine and feminine, and that is because of the intensity of his resolve. *Tufuwwita ʻalayhi fī mālihi* means: it escaped him with it. From its inverted hamzated form: *tafiʼa*, like *faraḥa*, means he became hot and angry, and that is because of its intensity. *Tafiʼat al-shayʼ* is its time and period, and that is its best condition. *Dakhala ʻalā tafiʼatihi*, i.e., its trace, meaning he did not precede it by much, and that is more severe for him.

From the wāwī form: *al-tufa*, like *qufa*, is the embrace of the earth while it is hunting, and there is a difference of opinion about it, which will be explained, God willing, in His saying: ﴿a full recompense﴾ [al-Isrāʼ: 63] in the chapter of Subḥān. From its inverted wāwī form: *tāfa baṣaruhu yatūfu*, meaning it wandered, as if it were for the removal of intensity, or the meaning is that he fell into a *tawqa*, i.e., a difficulty. *Wa-mā fīhi tūfatun* (with a damma) and *lā tāfatun* means there is no defect, excess or need. *Ṭalaba ʻalayya tawfatan* (with a fatha) means a slip and a sin. All of this indicates its intensity, because a slip and a sin do not befall anything except from their intensity and its weakness. From its inverted hamzated form: *al-aftu* (with a fatha) is the she-camel that has among endurance and staying power what others do not have, and the swift one who overtakes camels in travel, and the noble among camels, and it may be pronounced with a kasra; and the calamity and the marvel. All of this is clearly about strength. *Al-ifit* (with a kasra) is the first, because it is the origin of every counted thing. *Ufituhu ʻan "kadhā": ṣarafahu*, meaning: I turned him away from such-and-such.

When he (peace be upon him) informed them that his knowledge was above their knowledge, he followed it, as a resumptive statement (*istithnaf*), with what indicates it, saying: ﴿O my sons, go﴾. Then he made this going the cause for, and linked to it, his saying: ﴿and search (*fatahassasu*)﴾, meaning with all your effort, ﴿for Joseph and his brother﴾, meaning seek news of the two of them with your senses, so that perhaps you will attain them. This confirms what preceded concerning the likelihood of his suspicion that the one who did that (*fa'il dhalika*) was Joseph, peace be upon them.

Since they did not have the knowledge that he had, he said: ﴿And do not despair (*ta'yasu*)﴾, meaning do not lose hope, ﴿of the comfort (*rawh*) of God﴾, meaning of Him to whom belongs all perfection. *Rawh* (comfort, relief), according to al-Rummani, occurs with a pleasant breeze, and it seems this is its origin. Thus what is meant is His mercy, His relief, His facilitation, and His kindness in gathering the scattered and facilitating what is desired. Then he gave the reason for this prohibition by his saying: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the comfort of God﴾, meaning none loses hope, ﴿of the comfort of God﴾, meaning He who possesses all the attributes of majesty and honor, ﴿except the people﴾, meaning those who have the strength of striving, ﴿who are disbelievers﴾, meaning those who are deeply immersed in disbelief.

So they agreed to what he wished.

Thus they set out for Egypt for that purpose and for the sake of obtaining provisions, since the famine had grown severe upon them, and they made for the Aziz. His saying, ﴿So when they entered upon him﴾, with the particle "fa" (then), indicates that they hastened to return on this occasion. "They said," addressing him with the particle that alerts the listener that what follows it has a great impact: ﴿O Aziz﴾.

Since they had courteously flattered him by exalting him, they softened their speech with their saying: ﴿Adversity has touched us﴾, that is, O company of people you see, ﴿and our family﴾, that is, those whom we left behind in our land, ﴿adversity﴾, that is, it has afflicted us with a contact we feel, ﴿and we have come with meager merchandise﴾, that is, trifling goods, not desired in any respect. Then they based upon this acknowledgment, because it is closer to the mercy of people of generosity, their saying: ﴿So give us full measure﴾, that is, out of compassion for us because of our weakness, ﴿and be charitable to us﴾, that is, grant us favor (tafdil) ﴿upon us﴾, an addition beyond full measure, as you have accustomed us, with a bounty whose reward you hope for.

When they saw that his actions indicated his adherence to the religion of God, they gave the reason for that with their saying: ﴿Indeed, God﴾, that is, He to whom belongs all perfection, ﴿rewards the charitable﴾, that is, absolutely, even if you make it apparent (by what the apparent form conveys), and even if it is toward a wealthy, strong person, so how much more when it is toward people in need and weakness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 89:

When he saw that the matter had reached its end and there remained nothing he feared, he made himself known to them, and God, exalted is He, resumed the report of that with His saying, narrating: ﴿He said, "Do you know what you did with Joseph﴾ — addressing them as settled, after they had become bold toward him and had grown familiar with him. And it is apparent that this was without an interpreter ("ma", i.e., what the ugliness was that) ﴿you did with Joseph﴾, i.e., your brother whom you put between him and his father ﴿and his brother﴾ in your making him a lone one, humiliated among you, then in your saying to him when they found the drinking cup in his baggage: "Calamity never ceases to come upon us from you, O sons of Rachel!" And he informed them that his opinion of them now was good, to calm them, so he said: ﴿when﴾, i.e., at the time when ﴿you were ignorant﴾, i.e., doers of their deed — as an allusion to his recognition of them and a reminder of the sin, so that they would repent, and as a gentle dealing with them in that situation, in which the distressed one breathes freely, the one with a wounded chest exhales, the enraged one with a grudge finds relief, and the one with an unavenged blood-debt attains his revenge, by specifying their ignorance — by the requirement of "when" — to that time, to make them understand that they are now otherwise than that.

Thus it is as if it were said: he had already brought them close to uncovering his affair, for a king like him would not ask this question of people who did not grow up among them, did not follow their circumstances, and are not of their kind. Especially since it is reported that when he said this he smiled, and in his smile there was a beauty that anyone who saw him even once could not fail to recognize. So did they recognize him? It is said that they assumed it with strong conjecture, and for this reason ﴿they said﴾, asking, ﴿"Are you indeed"﴾ and they emphasized with their words, ﴿"Are you indeed Joseph?"﴾

Since what was expected from a man of such greatness in his position was that he would repay them for their evil conduct toward him, he began to explain his generosity, and said: ﴿"I am Joseph"﴾. He added to them the words ﴿"and this is my brother"﴾, meaning Benjamin, my full brother, since he had mentioned him to them in his words ﴿"and his brother"﴾ [Yusuf: 89], and so that this would increase their knowledge of him and strengthen it regarding his affair, by confirming him while he stayed with him during the period of their going and returning, and so that upon it he would build his words ﴿"Indeed Allah has been gracious to us"﴾, that is, the One to whom belong majesty and honor, ﴿"upon us"﴾, by gathering us together in the best of states. Then the particle "thumma" (then, here explanatory) with his words ﴿"Indeed, whoever fears [Allah and] is patient"﴾, and it is jussive because it is the conditional verb. Qunbul, according to a different transmission from him, retained his ya' in both states, treating it like a sound verb, indicating that the attribute of taqwa (God-consciousness) possesses complete soundness, abundant capacity, and constant attachment to it in every state. ﴿And is patient﴾, meaning Allah will fully repay him for his good conduct. ﴿Then indeed Allah﴾, that is, the One who encompasses all attributes of perfection, ﴿does not waste﴾, that is, not even the least waste, ﴿the reward﴾ of him. This was the original wording, but He expressed it in a way that shows that taqwa and patience are part of ihsan (excellence), saying ﴿the reward of the doers of good﴾. Taqwa is the averting of trial by following the path of guidance; patience is restraining the self by swallowing the bitterness of being denied what it desires.

Perhaps he concealed his affair from them up to this point because, had he sent to his father informing him before the king, he would not have been safe from the plotting of his brothers; and had he made himself known to them after this, or at the very first time he saw them, he would not have been safe from their hearts being torn apart upon the sudden uncovering of the matter while he was in that state of honor. They had treated him as a killer treats his victim, without any sin he had committed against them. So they had no doubt that if he gained power over them, he would destroy them because of the evil deed that had preceded from them against him. And if they were spared, they would not feel safe with him, however much he honored them. For great matters, if they are not done gradually, their danger becomes grave and their harm spreads. If he had sent them to bring their father, it was feared that they would deceive their father with the king of Egypt's help and would contrive to make him leave his land, so they would go to a place where he would not know him. And if he sent trustworthy men with them from his side, it was not safe that there would be some evil among them. And if he imprisoned them and sent someone to bring their father to him, this would not be well received by their father, and he would feel distress at the imprisonment of his sons, and talk among the people, both the people of Egypt and others, about this would grow. So he did with them what preceded, so that his goodness, justice, religion, and kindness would be manifest to them, and his restraint from them and his pardon for their deed would come gradually, and so that they would know this from him in word and deed through his brother, who had been raised with them, and with whom they were familiar and intimate. Thus their fright would calm and their slip would be made light. Among what indicates this is that when the attributes they had been described with, as mentioned, were removed from his brother Benjamin, he made himself known to him when he came to him, and forbade him to inform them of the true reality of the matter. He began to prolong the matter so that the causes he intended would be firmly established. When he thought the matter had reached its end, he gave them a sign, and they recognized him, and the excellence of his intellect, the wonder of his beauty and form, and the splendor of his words and deeds had made them forget him. So it was a place of fear and shame, and a place of despair that became hope. Thus the aim was achieved in accordance with sound rectitude, and Allah is the Granter of success. This is an admonition to those to whom it was said at the beginning of the surah:

﴿"So that you may understand"﴾ [Yusuf: 2], by following the example of the guided guides in deliberation, patience, and entrusting matters to the All-Wise, and that they should not hasten Him in any matter, and that they should know that His divine sunnah (way) has proceeded such that difficult matters are not carried out except through prolongation, so that causes are arranged step by step in a manner of firmness. In this there are benefits, among them the testing of those who obey and those who disobey, as the indication of it will come at the end of the surah in His words: ﴿"until when the messengers despaired"﴾ [Yusuf: 110], and so on. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 91:

Since what was mentioned had occurred, it was as if it were said: "There came to them what they had not expected; so what did they say?" It is said: ﴿They said﴾ [amazed to the utmost degree of amazement. For this reason they swore by that which indicates it: ﴿By God﴾, that is, the Greatest King] ﴿Indeed God has preferred you﴾, that is, He to whom all command belongs, ﴿over us﴾, that is, He made for you a mark (athar) that covers our marks by its loftiness. The meaning is: He favoured you over us, that is, in knowledge, intellect, wisdom, beauty, kingship, piety (p-210) and other than that. ﴿And indeed﴾ they lightened it from the heavy form, as an emphasis through brevity, to indicate concern for conveying the apology as quickly as possible, ﴿we were﴾, that is, a state which is our natural disposition, ﴿sinners﴾, that is, deeply immersed in error, which is deliberately committing sin.

Then it is as if it were said: What did he say to them, given his power and authority and what had preceded of their wrongdoing? So it is said: ﴿He said﴾, the words of the noble, following their brothers among the prophets and messengers, may blessings and peace be upon them, ﴿"No reproach"﴾, meaning no blame, no rebuke, and no ruin, ﴿"against you today"﴾, even though this time is the place where blame and reproach are expected. If that is removed in it, then what is to be thought of what comes after it!

The root ﻥ-ث-ر (th-r-b) revolves around *al-barth* (with the *b* first), which is the easiest and best of land. There is also *Thabrah* (with the *th* first): a land of white stones, because it entails settling down and ease. From it comes *thābara ʿalā al-amr* (he persisted in the matter): he continued at it. *Al-muthabbar* (on the pattern of *manzil*) is the place where a child falls out, that is, the place of its birth, and the joint and the articulation. Then laziness and softness come, and then corruption comes. From it comes *al-thubūr* (perdition, destruction). [*Al-batar*] (with the *b* first) is a known boil or abscess. And *al-māʾ al-batr* is water of which only a small amount remains on the ground. *Al-rabth* (also with the *b* first) is the detention of a person, and it also returns to residence and continuance. *Al-tathrīb* is the reproaching of a person for a sin, which is the removal from a person of the veil of pardon. It derives from *al-thurb*, which is the fat that covers the stomach and the intestines and shields them. It is one of the necessary features of easy, fertile land, because of what fertility entails. So *al-tathrīb* is its removal, and that is because of the drought that results from it, which is destruction. Thus the predominant sense of the root is destruction.

When he had exempted them from *al-tathrīb*, they were in a position where they would expect to ask about complete pardon that removes punishment from God. So He followed it with the answer to that by praying for them, with His saying: ﴿"May God forgive you"﴾, that is, He who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿"you"﴾, meaning what you have committed of excess and what may occur from you after this. Perhaps he expressed this prayer in the present tense (*al-muḍāriʿ*) as guidance for them to sincere repentance, to encourage them to it, and to give them hope through the attribute that is the cause of forgiveness. So He said: ﴿"and He is"﴾, that is, He alone, ﴿"the most merciful of the merciful"﴾, that is, to all the servants, and especially to the one who repents. So He is worthy of pouring forth blessings after protection from retribution.

It is narrated that they sent to him: "Indeed you invite us to your food and your honour morning and evening, and we are ashamed of what we committed against you." He said: "The people of Egypt look at me, even though I rule over them, with the eye of servitude. They say: 'Glory be to Him who raised a slave who was sold for twenty dirhams to such a height!' Now I have been honoured with a crown and exalted in the eyes [of the people], since people have come to know that you are my brothers, and that I am of the offspring of Ibrahim, peace be upon him."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 93:

When he had gladdened their eyes after they had been gathered together, by removing what they feared in this world and the next, there remained what concerned their father of that matter. It is as though a question arose about it, and it was answered by his saying: ﴿Go with this shirt of mine﴾. And since this saying of his might have brought to their minds the shirt they had stripped from him, he guarded against that by saying: ﴿Throw it over my father's face; he will regain his sight﴾, that is, immediately upon your arrival ﴿upon my father's face, he will regain his sight﴾, that is, he will return to what he was, ﴿seeing﴾, or he will come to the state of being one who sees. For when he has his sight restored to him and knows my place, he will not be patient in refraining from seeking me, because of the abundance of love he has and the greatness of his longing. And the shirt being one of Joseph's usual garments is more striking and more indicative of honour; and the shirt is the garment closest to the body, so displaying honour through it is more indicative of the perfection of its owner's religion and his firmness in matters of faith. In dreams it is interpreted as religion. This adds to the fullness of joy for Ya'qub, peace be upon him. ﴿And bring me your whole family﴾, that is, bring my father with you, and you, ﴿with your households﴾, that is, accompanied by them, ﴿all together﴾, with none of them left behind. So they returned with the shirt for this purpose. It is said: Yahudha was the one who carried his shirt when they had smeared it with blood, and he said: "No one but I shall carry this, so that I may make him rejoice as I made him sorrowful." So he carried it, barefoot and bareheaded, from Egypt to Canaan, and between them is a distance of eighty farsakhs.

When the caravan set out (فَصَلَتِ العِيرُ) from al-'Arish, the last town of Egypt on the way to the land of Syria, "their father" (قالَ أبُوهُمْ), addressing the son of his son and those around him from his family, emphasizing that he knew they would deny his words, said: "Indeed I perceive the scent of Joseph" (﴿إنِّي لأجِدُ رِيحَ يُوسُفَ﴾), meaning: I say, "Indeed I perceive the scent of Joseph." He prevented them from confronting him with denial by his saying: "Were it not that you think me senile" (﴿لَوْلا أنْ تُفَنِّدُونِ﴾), meaning: had it not been for that, I would have said it without hesitation or hedging, because thinking me senile does not prevent the sensing of the scent. It is like when you say to your companion: "Were it not that you would attribute levity to me, I would have said such-and-such," meaning: I am saying it while knowing that you do not agree with me about it.

"Fasala" (فَصَلَ) here is intransitive; one says: fasala min al-baladi, yafsilu fusulan (he departed from the town). Al-fasl (الفَصْل) is the cutting between two things by a barrier. Al-wijdan (الوِجْدان) is the manifestation through a mode of perception that makes the non-existence of the thing impossible. Al-rih (الرِّيح) is an accident perceived by the sense of smell, that is, by smelling. Al-tafnid (التَّفْنِيد) is the weakening of an opinion, derived from al-fannad (الفَنَد), which is fear and the loss of reason due to old age. It is said: shaykhun mufannid (an aged man who has lost his judgment). One does not say 'ajuzun mufannida (an old woman who has lost her judgment), because she was not, in her youth, a person of opinion whose judgment old age could weaken.

Then he resumed relating their reply, saying: ﴿They said﴾, that is, the listeners to him, who had formed this opinion of them, swearing by that which indicated their astonishment. And it is ﴿By God!﴾, that is, the Greatest King. They emphasized the oath because they knew that he would deny their words, and so would everyone who knows his perfection. ﴿Indeed, you are in your old error﴾, that is, to the extent that it has become a container for you (p-214) ﴿old﴾, that is, your error in thinking that Joseph is alive. Al-Rummani said: al-ḍalāl (going astray) is departing from the direction of what is right.

Thus Allah confirmed his words and fulfilled his hope, and they hastened to him with a bearer of good news, who came quickly after the separation. For this reason the particle "fa" (then) is used in ﴿فَلَمّا﴾ (when), and "anna" (indeed) is added to emphasize that his coming was in that very state; adding it is a regular, consistent usage. ﴿جاءَ البَشِيرُ﴾ (the bearer of good news came), and he was Yahudha (Judah), bearing this news, with the shirt with him. ﴿ألْقاهُ﴾ (he threw it): that is, the shirt, at the moment it reached Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him, without any interval between the first arrival and that. This is what the addition of "anna" conveys, to emphasize what "lamma" (when) indicates of the occurrence of the second event immediately after the first, here the throwing, following upon the arrival, and its being consequent upon it. ﴿عَلى وجْهِهِ﴾ (upon his face): that is, Ya'qub, peace be upon him. ﴿فارْتَدَّ﴾ (and he regained): at once ﴿بَصِيرًا﴾ (sight).

Al-irtidad (regaining) is the reversion of a thing to a state it was previously in. So his mind turned to his former condition, along with his bereavement. Allah, exalted is He, informed of this by His saying, in a new clause: "Qala" (he said), that is, Ya'qub, peace be upon him: ﴿ألَمْ أقُلْ لَكُمْ﴾ (Did I not tell you) that I find his scent. Then he gave a reason for this assertion with His saying, emphasized because their words were those of one who denies: ﴿إنِّي أعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ (Indeed I know from Allah), that is, the One singularly characterized with the attributes of perfection, ﴿ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (what you do not know), because of what Allah, exalted is He, has bestowed upon me of various kinds of gifts. This is general, covering the news of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and other matters, and it is of the kind of speaking of the blessing of Allah.

(p-215) When this had happened, the soul longed to know what would take place between him and his sons over it, so he (Yaʿqub) dispelled this distress from it by saying: ﴿They said, "O our father,"﴾ calling out with the particle that indicates great concern with what follows, because of the great weight it carries: ﴿"Ask forgiveness"﴾, i.e., request from God that He forgive ﴿"us our sins."﴾ Each pronoun among these pronouns refers back to its owner in the utmost clarity, so he did not state explicitly who its owner is.

When they asked him to seek forgiveness for their sins, they gave as the reason the acknowledgment of sin, because acknowledgment is a condition of repentance, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, when the servant acknowledges his sin and then repents, God turns to him in forgiveness." So they said, emphasizing it to confirm sincerity in repentance: ﴿"Indeed, we were sinners,"﴾ i.e., deliberately intending wrongdoing by what we committed in the matter of Joseph, upon him be prayers and peace;

Then he related his answer by saying, as a fresh statement: "He said" — that is, their father, peace be upon him, emphasizing his words: "I shall ask forgiveness for you" — that is, I shall seek that He forgive "you, my Lord" — [that is] the One who has never ceased to show kindness to me and to rear me in the best manner of rearing. He is therefore worthy to forgive my sons, so that He does not separate me from them in the abode of permanence. Lordship (al-rububiyyah) is a dominion which is the most complete of dominions in an absolute sense, and it is the dominion of God, exalted is He, for the bringing into being of souls by originating them and disposing them with the most complete disposal — through existence and annihilation, and turning them from one state to another, in all matters, without any fatigue. Then he gave the reason for that by saying: "Indeed He, He" — that is, He alone — "is the Forgiving, the Merciful." All of that is to calm their hearts and to confirm their hope, so that their expectation grows, and so that He, exalted is He, is in their assumption one who will certainly answer and fulfil his request promptly. Perhaps he expressed it with "sawfa" (soon/later) because of placing these two clauses before the request, for the aims which you have mentioned. It has been said: because he postponed the supplication until the night prayer. It has been said: until the night of Friday. It has also been said: it is derived from this that seeking needs from the young is easier than seeking them from the elderly.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 99:

When what he had mentioned came to pass, and he had sent with them mounts, wealth, and equipment with which to prepare themselves, they set about preparing as Yusuf, peace be upon him, had ordered them. [Then] they came to Egypt, and they were seventy-two persons, males and females. It seems they hastened in this, and therefore He said: ﴿So when﴾ (with the fa', "so") ﴿they entered upon Yusuf﴾ at the place where he met them, among the notables of the people of Egypt, and he pitched his tents there ﴿he took his parents to himself﴾ in honour of them, by that which distinguishes them. It is said: it was the embrace. The apparent meaning is that she was his mother in reality, and this is what al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq said, as transmitted by al-Rummani and Abu Hayyan. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that she was his maternal aunt. The father was given precedence in this dual form because of his masculinity, just as the singular term that is originally singular was given precedence over the one that is in the genitive construction in the two ages. ﴿And he said﴾ honouring all of them: ﴿Enter Egypt﴾ (p-217), that is, the well-known city. He used the conditional for security, not for entry, so he said: ﴿if Allah wills﴾, that is, the Supreme King to whom all command belongs, ﴿secure﴾ from everything that may befall you, even from what you neglected concerning my right and my brother's right.

And when he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration. He said: "O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before; my Lord has made it true. He has been truly good to me, when He brought me out of the prison and brought you from the desert (al-badw), after Satan had sown discord between me and my brothers. Indeed my Lord is Subtle (latif) in what He wills; indeed He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."

Commentary

When he mentioned the security, which is the foundation of well-being through which the pleasure of life is enjoyed, he followed it with the elevation through which the perfection of bliss is attained, so He said: ﴿And he raised his parents﴾, that is, after they had settled in Egypt upon entering it, sitting ﴿upon the throne﴾, that is, the high couch. Al-Rummani said: its origin is raising.

﴿And they fell down﴾, that is, they lowered themselves ﴿before him in prostration﴾, the two parents and the brothers, in fulfilment of his vision, from one who is dominant over every affair. Prostration, whose origin is submission and humbling oneself, was permissible in those eras. ﴿And he said﴾, that is, Yusuf, upon him be peace, ﴿O my father﴾, delighting him by addressing him with fatherhood. ﴿This﴾, that is, what has occurred of prostration, ﴿is the interpretation of my dream﴾ which I saw. He indicated the brevity of the time in which he saw it by the preposition, so He said: ﴿from before﴾. Then he resumed his speech: ﴿My Lord has made it true﴾, that is, the One who nurtured me by that which brought me to it, ﴿truly﴾, that is, by the correspondence of reality with its interpretation, and the interpretation of what you told me, you also confirm [likewise] the choosing of me, my teaching, and the completion of His blessing upon me. Ta'wil is the explanation of what the meaning of speech ultimately leads to. It is related from Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, that the gap between its interpretation and its vision was forty years.

﴿And He has been good﴾, that is, He has bestowed His goodness ﴿to me﴾, confirming what He gave me good news of, namely the completion of the blessing. [The construction of ﴿ahsana﴾ with bi is more indicative of nearness to the benefactor than with ila; and he expressed it with his saying:] ﴿when He brought me out of the prison﴾, turning away from the word "the well" out of caution about alienating his brothers, although the word can bear it in a hidden sense. ﴿And brought you﴾. It was said that they were people of tents and owners of livestock, moving between waters and pastures, therefore he said: ﴿from the desert﴾, from the outskirts of the desert of Palestine. That is among the greatest blessings, as occurs in the hadith: "Whoever Allah wills good for, He moves him from the desert to the settled place." Al-badw is a flat expanse of land in which a person can be seen from afar, and its origin is from manifestness. His brothers were also made comfortable by his saying, affirming the preposition, because their coming was in some periods of distance: ﴿after Satan had sown discord﴾; he expressed it in the past tense so that it is understood that it had passed. ﴿Satan﴾, that is, he corrupted the distant one who was burned by his whisperings, which are like a prick, ﴿between me and my brothers﴾, where he distributed the discord between him and them and did not favour either party over the other in it, and he did not affirm the preposition, indicating the generality of the corruption for the sons. All of this is an indication of the realisation of what Ya'qub, upon him be peace, gave good news of: the completion of the blessing and the perfection of knowledge and wisdom. Then he gave the reason for goodness to them all in his saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to me in ways that are hidden, ﴿is Subtle﴾, that is, He knows the fine details and hidden aspects of benefits, then takes, in conveying them [to] the one who benefits, the path of gentleness rather than harshness; so when gentleness is combined in the act and subtlety in the perception, that is the Subtle, as al-Razi said in al-Lawami'. He, glorified is He, is the doer of subtlety in His management and His mercy, ﴿for whatever He wills﴾; no matter is difficult for Him. Then he gave the reason for this cause in his saying: ﴿Indeed He is﴾, that is, He alone, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, that is, the one profound in knowledge of the subtle and the great, ﴿the All-Wise﴾, that is, the one perfect in mastery of what He does, in accordance with what Ya'qub, upon him be peace, concluded his good news with at the beginning of the surah. That is, He is singular in being characterised by this; none approaches Him in knowledge so as to challenge the nullifying of what He establishes by causes, nor in wisdom so as to expect a flaw in any of them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 101 (part 1 of 2):

When he mentioned these two attributes, he recalled what had befallen him through them of causes, so the station of contemplative witnessing (*shuhud*) overcame him, and his soul grew increasingly averse to this world. So he said, addressing (Allah): (p. 220) ﴿My Lord, You have indeed given me~~~~ some of the kingdom~~~~﴾. He opened with "indeed" (*qad*) because the situation called for the listener to anticipate an explanation of the outcome of the vision. ﴿Some of the kingdom﴾, that is, a part of it, after my great remoteness from it, and its essence is complete power. ﴿And You have taught me﴾, and he limited his claim out of humility by using the prepositional phrase, so he said: ﴿of the interpretation of events﴾, in accordance with what my father had given me good news of and what you informed me of, of empowerment and instruction, before your words. "And Allah is dominant over His affair" (12:21). Then he called Him by an attribute that comprises knowledge and wisdom, so he said: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. Then he informed Him of what He already knows better than he does, namely that he does not rely on anyone else in anything, so he said: ﴿You are my Guardian﴾, that is, the nearest to me, inwardly and outwardly, ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾, that is, I have no guardian other than You. The guardian acts for his master in what is most right and most good, so His goodness to me in the Hereafter is greater than the goodness You showed me in this world.

Since his taking Allah as guardian is not complete except through Allah's taking him as His, he followed it with what conveys that, so he said: ﴿Cause me to die~~~~﴾, that is, take my soul fully complete in all my affairs, both outwardly and in meaning, while I am ﴿a Muslim~~~~﴾. And since the true Muslim is one who is deeply rooted in sincerity, he confirmed this with his words: ﴿and join me with the righteous﴾. So Allah caused him to die as he asked. They said: The people of Egypt disputed concerning him, each of them hoping to be buried in his own quarter, seeking his blessing. Then they agreed to make for him a sarcophagus of marble and bury him in the middle of the Nile, (p. 221) so that the water would spread over all the land, so that all of it would obtain his blessing and be made fertile equally, and so that they would all be equal in the water.

He mentioned what remains of the story from the Tawrah (the Torah):

It says, after what has passed: Joseph could no longer restrain himself, meaning, could no longer restrain himself regarding his brothers' gentleness toward him. So he ordered that everyone who was with him be removed, and no one remained with him when Joseph revealed himself to his brothers. He raised his voice and wept until the Egyptians heard, and it was reported in the house of Pharaoh. Joseph said to his brothers: "I am your brother Joseph. Is my father still alive?" But his brothers could not answer him, because they were terrified of him. So Joseph said to his brothers: "Come close to me," [and they came close], and he said to them: "I am Joseph whom you sold to those who came to Egypt. And now, do not grieve, and let it not trouble you, nor let your selling me here weigh heavily on you, for Allah sent me before you to prepare food for you, since the famine has been two years, and five more years will come in which there will be no planting or harvest. So the Lord sent me before you to be for you a remnant in the land and to save you and deliver you, so that you may live and rejoice upon the earth. Now it was not you who sent me here, but Allah, who sent me and made me a father to Pharaoh and lord over all his household, and a ruler over the whole land of Egypt. So hurry and go up to my father and say to him: 'Thus says your son Joseph: Allah has made me lord over all the people of Egypt. Come down to me and do not delay. Settle in the land of Goshen' (in one copy: Khashan), 'and be near me, you and your children, your household, your grandchildren, your flocks, your herds, and all that you have, and I will provide for you there, for five years of famine remain, lest you and your household and all that you own perish.' And behold, your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin, that it is I who speak to you myself. Tell my father of all my honor and my dignity in the land of Egypt, and of all that you have seen. Hurry and bring my father down here." He embraced his brother Benjamin and wept, and he kissed all his brothers and wept. After that his brothers spoke with him. This reached Pharaoh, and it was told to him that Joseph's brothers had come to him. Pharaoh and his servants (in one copy: and all his commanders) were pleased. Pharaoh said to Joseph: "Tell your brothers: let them do this. Load your animals with provisions, and go to the land of Canaan, and bring back your father and the households of your families [and come to me], and I will give you the best of the land of Egypt and its abundance. Eat the richness of the land. And you are the one in authority; command your brothers to do this. Take from the land of Egypt wagons for your wives and your retinues, and carry your father, and come. Do not worry about your belongings, for all the good things of Egypt and its land and its abundance are yours."

The children of Israel did as Pharaoh commanded. Joseph gave them wagons according to Pharaoh's order, provided them with all the provisions for the road, and clothed each one of them in a robe. As for Benjamin, he gave him three hundred dirhams (in one copy: a weight of silver), and clothed him in five garments, and sent to his father the same, and ten donkeys loaded with wheat and food and provisions for his father's journey. He sent them off, and they departed. He went ahead of them and [said to them]: "Let there be no quarrel among you on the road." So they set out from Egypt and came to the land of Canaan, to Jacob their father. They told him and said: "Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt." Jacob saw the wagon that Joseph had sent to carry him, and his soul was reassured, and he said: "This is indeed great to me, since my son Joseph is still alive. I will go now (p. 224) and see him before I die."

So Israel set out with all that he had, and came to Beersheba, and offered a sacrifice to the God of his father Isaac. Allah spoke to Israel in a vision and said to him: "Jacob! Jacob!" He said: "Here I am!" He said: "I am Iyyil, the God of your father. Do not fear to go down to Egypt, for I will make you there into a great nation" (in one copy: "for I will make from you a great community"). "I will go down with you, and I will bring you up, and Joseph will place his hand over your eyes." Then Jacob arose from Beersheba, and the children of Israel carried their father Jacob, with their households and their wives, on the wagon which Pharaoh had sent to carry him. They drove their animals and their livestock which they had acquired in the land of Canaan, and they came to Egypt, Jacob and all his offspring, his sons with him, and his sons' sons [and his daughters] and his daughters' daughters, and he brought all his offspring into Egypt.

Then he named them one by one, and then said: "All the sons of Jacob who entered Egypt were seventy persons." Then Jacob sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph, peace be upon him, to guide him to al-Sadir (in one copy: Khashan). Joseph harnessed his chariots and went up to meet his father Israel at Khashan (in one copy: al-Sadir). He met him, embraced him, and wept when he embraced him. Then Israel said to Joseph:

(p. 225) "Let me die now, having seen you, my son, for you are still alive." Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's household: "I will go up and inform Pharaoh, and I will say: My brothers and my father's household who were in the land of Canaan [have] come to me, and the people are shepherds of flocks, for they are owners of livestock, and they have brought their sheep and their cattle and everything they own. So when he calls you, say to him: 'We, your servants, have been owners of livestock from our youth until now, we and our fathers before us too, so that you may settle in the land of Khashan' (in one copy: al-Sadir), 'for shepherds of flocks are despised by the Egyptians.'" Joseph came and informed Pharaoh, and said to him: "My father and my brothers have come to me with their flocks, their herds, and all that they own, from the land of Canaan, and they are now in the land of al-Sadir." He took five men from among his brothers and brought them before Pharaoh, and they stood before him. Pharaoh said to Joseph's brothers: "What is your occupation?" They said: "Your servants are shepherds of flocks, we and our fathers before us, from our youth." They said to Pharaoh: "We have come to settle in this land, for the grass, the herbage, and the pasture for your servants' flocks has failed, because the hunger has grown severe in the land of Canaan. So command your servants to settle in the land of al-Sadir." Pharaoh said to Joseph: "Your father and your brothers have come, and this land of Egypt is before you. So settle your father and your brothers in the best and most fertile land, that they may dwell in the land of al-Sadir. And if you know that among them are men of strength, power, and capability, [and vigor], then put them in charge of all my property." Then Joseph, peace be upon him, brought his father Jacob, peace be upon them, before Pharaoh, and he stood him before him. Pharaoh said to Jacob, peace be upon him: "How many years is your life?" Jacob, peace be upon him, said to Pharaoh: "The span of my life is one hundred and thirty years, and the days of my life have been few, and I have not reached the years of my fathers' lives in their days." Jacob blessed Pharaoh and prayed for him, and went out from before him. Joseph, peace be upon him, settled his father Jacob, peace be upon him, and his brothers, and gave them an inheritance in the land of Egypt, in the most fertile and best land, in the land of Ra'msis (in one copy: the land of 'Ayn Shams), as Pharaoh had commanded. Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all his household with food according to the number of their dependents. There was no provision in all the land, because the hunger had grown very severe, so all the land of Egypt and [the land of] Canaan was exhausted. All the silver of [the land of] Egypt and [the land of] Canaan came to Joseph, peace be upon him, (p. 227) as payment for the grain they had been buying. Joseph deposited the silver in Pharaoh's treasury. The silver ran out from the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan. All the Egyptians came to Joseph, peace be upon him, and said to him: "Give us grain for our need, so that we may live and not die, for our silver is finished." Joseph said to them: "Bring me your livestock, since your silver is gone, and I will provide you with food in exchange for your livestock." They brought him their livestock, and Joseph gave them food in exchange for their horses, their flocks of sheep, their herds of cattle, and their donkeys, and he provided for them that year with all their livestock. Then they came to him the next year and said to him: "We will not hide our affair from our lord: our silver and our livestock and our animals are finished and have passed to our lord. Nothing remains before our lord except ourselves and our land. So why should we perish before you? Buy us and our lands in exchange for feeding us bread, so that we become slaves to Pharaoh and our land becomes his possession. Give us seed so that we may live and not die, and the land will not be left empty and ruined for lack of its inhabitants." So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, and the land became Pharaoh's. He moved the people from town to town, and from the far ends of the land toward Egypt, to its regions, except for the land of the commanders (in one copy: their leaders), for he did not buy it, because the commanders were paid a regular allowance and provision by Pharaoh, and they used to eat their wheat that was assigned to them by Pharaoh. For this reason they did not sell their land. Joseph said to the people: "Behold, I have bought you and your land today for Pharaoh. Here, I give you seed to sow in the land. When the harvest comes, give Pharaoh a fifth of it, and four-fifths will be yours, for planting the field, for the food of your households, and for feeding your retinues." They said to him: "You have given us life. Let us find favor and mercy with our lord, and we will be servants to Pharaoh." So Joseph established this practice on the land of Egypt until this day of men. Thus the fifth belongs to Pharaoh, except the land of their leaders (in another narration: the commanders), for it did not belong to Pharaoh.

[p. 229] So Israel settled in the land of Egypt and in the land of al-Sadir. They grew in number, became mighty and prosperous there, and their nobles flourished. Jacob lived in the land of Egypt for seventeen years. The total days of Jacob's life were one hundred and forty-seven years. The days of Israel's death drew near, peace be upon him. Joseph called his son, peace be upon him, and said to him: "If I have found favour and kindness from you, then place your hand under my back until I make you swear by God and I adjure you by Him, and grant me the blessing and the justice: do not bury me in Egypt. Rather, let me lie with my fathers. Carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burial place." Joseph said: "I will do that, as you say and command." He said to him: "Swear to me." So he swore to him. Then Israel leaned on his staff and prostrated in gratitude.

After these reports, Joseph, peace be upon him, received word that his father had fallen ill. He set out with his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. When he arrived, Jacob was told: "Your son Joseph has come to you." Israel gathered his strength and sat up on his couch. Israel said to Joseph: "The God of the promises appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan. He blessed me and said to me: 'Behold, I will bless you and make you numerous, and I will make you a father to many peoples, and I will give your seed after you this land as an inheritance forever.' And I, [p. 230] when I was coming from Paddan-aram, your mother Rachel died in the land of Canaan on the road, when there remained between me and entering Ephrath a distance of a mile, and in another version, a farsakh. I buried her there on the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem." Israel looked at the two sons of Joseph and said to him: "Who are these?" He said: "They are my two sons whom God gave me here." He said: "Bring them near to me." He kissed them and embraced them and said: "I did not expect to see your face, and now God has shown me your offspring as well." Israel said to Joseph, upon both of them be prayer and peace: "Behold, I am about to die, and God, by His help and aid, will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers. Moreover, I have given you preference over your brothers with one portion of the land which the Amorites took by my sword and my bow."

Then Jacob summoned his sons and said: "Gather around me, that I may tell you what will happen to you in the last days." He mentioned that, and then said: "This is what Jacob their father told them. He informed them of this and blessed each one of them according to his station." Then he charged them and said to them: "I am going to my people. Bury me beside my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, in the cave that is in the double field beside Mamre in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought: a field from Ephron the Hittite as a possession for a burial place. There Abraham was buried with Sarah his wife, and there Isaac was buried with Rebekah his wife, and there Leah was buried, in the field purchased and in the cave which is in it, from the sons of Heth." When Jacob finished his charge to his sons, he stretched out his feet on his couch and died, and he was carried to his people.

[p. 231] Joseph fell upon him [and kissed him] and wept over him. He commanded his servants, the physicians, to embalm him. The physicians embalmed Israel, and forty days were completed for him, for this is how the days of embalmers are completed. The Egyptians mourned for him seventy days. Joseph said to the household of Pharaoh: "If I have found favour and kindness from you, then tell Pharaoh that my father made me swear and adjured me, saying to me: 'Behold, I am about to die, so bury me in the grave which you purchased in the land of Canaan.' He will permit me, and I will go up and bury [my father] and then return." Pharaoh said to him: "Go up and bury your father as he adjured you." So Joseph went up to bury his father. There went up with him all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his household, all the elders of Egypt, and all the household of Joseph. There also went up with him his brothers and the family of his father. As for their retainers, their herds and their flocks, they left them in the land of Goshen, and in another version, al-Sadir. Chariots and horsemen also went up, so he was in a great and formidable host. They came to the threshing floors of Atad, and in another version, the threshing floor of the thornbush, which are beyond the Jordan. There they mourned and wailed a great and bitter lamentation. The inhabitants of the land of Canaan saw the mourning and wailing at the threshing floor of the thornbush, and they said: "This is a great mourning for the Egyptians." For this reason that place was called "the mourning of Egypt," which is beyond the Jordan. The children of Israel did as he commanded them. They carried him, went with him to the land of Canaan, and buried him in the double cave in the field which Abraham bought as a possession for a burial place from Ephron the Hittite, which is opposite Mamre.

[p. 233] Then Joseph returned to Egypt, he and his brothers and all who had gone up with him to bury his father. After he buried his father, Joseph's brothers saw that their father had died, and they feared. They said: "Perhaps Joseph will harm us and take revenge on us for all the evil we committed against him." They approached Joseph and said to him: "Your father commanded before his death and said: 'Say to Joseph: We beg you to pardon the ignorance of your brothers and their sins in committing evil against you. Now we beg you to forgive the sin of the servants of your father's God.'" Joseph wept when they said that. His brothers came near, fell down before him in prostration, and said to him: "Behold, we are your servants." He said to them: "Do not fear me, for I fear God. As for you, you intended evil against me, but God turned it into good for me, as He has done this day, so that a great people might be preserved through me. Now, do not fear; I will provide for you and your households." Thus he comforted them and filled their hearts with goodness.

Then Joseph remained in Egypt, he and his family. Joseph lived one hundred and ten years, and Joseph saw the children of his grandchildren. Joseph said to his brothers: "Behold, I am about to die, and God will surely remember you and bring you out of this land to the land which He swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." Joseph made the children of Israel swear [p. 234] and said: "God will surely remember you, so carry my bones up with you." Joseph died at the age of one hundred and ten years. They embalmed him and placed him in a coffin in the land of Egypt. What follows of their enslavement and what comes after it will be mentioned in [Surat al-Qasas], God willing, exalted is He.

What has been mentioned of the story in the Tawrah (the Torah) confirms what is in the Qur'an and bears witness to its inimitability. However, it does not mention the explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately﴾ [Yusuf: 80], namely that after the cup was taken from his brother's baggage, he left them without identifying himself to them. They went back to their father and told him of this. Then they returned a second time to seek provisions and to search for Joseph and his brother. Joseph, peace be upon him, made himself known to them and revealed the matter on this third visit. It seems they removed from the Tawrah what concerned this, through deception and confusion. This does not harm anyone other than them, for what has come into their book does not accord with the laws of reason for one who reflects. It benefited them only in confirming their treachery and ignorance. And God is the Guide "to the right course."

[p. 235]

When what had occurred in their affair was complete, in this most judicious manner and straightest path from its beginning to its end, he said, indicating that it is a sufficient proof in establishing the claim of prophethood. He addressed one who does not grasp this truth as he grasps it, consoling him, strengthening his heart, expanding his breast, and alerting him that this is something one should ask about: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the tidings of high rank that We have related in a narration that would defeat eloquent men among its bearers and transmitters, let alone others, ﴿is among the tidings of the unseen﴾, i.e., its reports that have great importance, ﴿which We reveal to you﴾. He expressed it in the present tense to depict the noble state of revelation and to indicate that he continues with him, unveiling for him what he wills. ﴿And﴾ the situation is that ﴿you were not with them﴾, i.e., with the brothers of Joseph, upon him be peace, during this extremely strange news, ﴿when﴾, i.e., at the time when ﴿they resolved upon their affair﴾ with one opinion concerning casting Joseph, upon him be peace, [into the well] after having sworn otherwise, ﴿while they were scheming﴾, i.e., plotting harm in secret, from makr, which is killing. This is so that you would know it through observation, and so that your learning of it from a human being is negated just as your presence with them at that time is negated. It is certain to every person of intellect that there is no knowledge except through teaching. Thus it is established that you have no teacher except Allah, just as your brothers among the prophets, peace be upon them, learned. What a proof this is, exalted above comparison! This is the method of kalam (scholastic theology), namely presenting an argument that, once its premises are granted, necessarily entails the conclusion. It is a great mockery from those who denied the Prophet ﷺ. (p. 236)

When Quraysh and the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the story of Yusuf (peace be upon him) — as Abu Hayyan transmitted it from Ibn al-Anbari — the revelation came explaining it in this comprehensive manner and clarifying it in this complete way. The Prophet (ﷺ) hoped that this would be the cause of their becoming Muslim, but they opposed his expectation. Allah consoled him with His saying: ﴿And most of mankind⦆ — that is, We reveal it to you in this manner which would necessitate their faith, while the situation is that ﴿most of mankind﴾ — that is, all of them — even with that, because of the agitation they have, ﴿will not believe even if you strive for it﴾ — that is, for their faith — ﴿sincerely believing﴾ — that is, sincere in their faith, describing Allah with what befits Him of transcendence above any flaw of deficiency — so do not think that they will believe because of the sending down of the signs they propose, or because of the abandoning of the warning that angers them. 

Al-Kathir (the many): al-Rummani said: it is the number that exceeds the measure of others. Al-Akthar (the most): the portion that exceeds the other portion of the whole, and its opposite is al-Aqall (the fewest). Al-Nas (the people): the group of humankind, and it derives from nasa yanus, meaning when one moves right and left of its own accord, not by another's pulling.

(p-237) When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned their disbelief, He mentioned what is astonishing alongside it, so He said: ﴿And you do not ask them﴾, meaning: they remain upon that, while the cause of their belief is present. For you, despite calling them to the most upright path and bringing them clear proofs for it, ﴿do not ask them﴾, meaning this Book which We have revealed to you, ﴿for any wage﴾, and he intensified the negation, so He said: ﴿any wage﴾, so that your asking would not be a reason for them to accuse you, or to say: "Why was not a treasure sent down to him, so that he would be independent of us in asking?"

When He negated their giving him a wage, He negated from this Reminder every worldly aim, so He said: ﴿It is not but a reminder﴾, meaning this Book is nothing but an admonition and an honor, ﴿for the worlds﴾. Al-Rummani said: The dhikr (reminder) is the presence of the meaning in the soul, and the 'alam (world) is the large group of living beings who are capable of knowing, since it is derived from 'ilm (knowledge), and it carries the sense of multiplicity. It may also be said: 'alam al-falak (the world of the heavens) and what it contains, following the living beings whom we benefit from and which were made for their sake.

The Mighty Qur'an, being the greatest of signs in what it reports of past events and future occurrences as they are, and in containing judgments and rulings, expressed in eloquent styles that cannot be matched, and in much else that cannot be contained in a single system, as he indicated at the beginning of the surah, might be said: "This perhaps only those firmly rooted (al-rasikhun) in the divine sciences [ilahiyyat] know." [p. 238] Therefore he followed this with an indication that He, may He be exalted, has other signs which, for their clarity, require no more than sound reason, and which cannot be enumerated. Despite this, they did not benefit from them. So He said: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, a great and mighty indication pointing to His oneness, ﴿in the heavens﴾, that is, like the two luminaries, the rest of the stars, the clouds, and other things, ﴿and the earth﴾, from mountains, trees, creatures, and other things that cannot be counted, as will be explained in detail in [Surat al-Ra'd]. ﴿They pass by them﴾, observing them with the senses, plainly and not hidden, ﴿yet they turn away from them﴾, that is, specifically, not from their benefits and desires in them, ﴿disregarding﴾, that is, disregarding what they indicate of happiness through oneness and what follows from it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 106:

Since it might be said: "How can they be described as turning away, when they believe that God is the doer of those signs?" he made clear that their associating partners (shirk) nullifies that. So he said: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God﴾, i.e., the people, ﴿except that they are associators﴾, i.e., they associate with Him whoever cannot do anything, let alone bring a sign. The One in whom they should believe is the One for whom there is nothing but a summons to belief in Him, because He alone is characterized by the attributes of perfection. They used to acknowledge that God is their Creator and Provider, yet they worshipped other than Him. Likewise the hypocrites (munafiqun) display faith and conceal disbelief (kufran). Likewise the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitabayn) believe in their Book and follow their scholars in disbelief in other than it. So it is known that their submission to this faith is not guided by any proof; it is pure imitation (taqlid) of one whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive to him, so he sees it as good, because of what God's knowledge had already determined about him, that he has no capacity (for goodness), so He corrupted him by what resembled it of shirk.

The verse is also capable of referring to the hidden shirk to which the Prophet (ﷺ) pointed with his saying: "Shirk is more hidden among my community than the creeping of an ant." This is the shirk of the means (asbab) through which God has decreed that what reaches the servant arrives by means of them; so how can one who passes beyond the means to their Causer be considered!

Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': Imam Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi said: "It is only doubt (shakk) and shirk. Doubt is constriction of the breast at calamities, and from it comes 'a doubtful garment' (thawb mashkuk). Shirk is the heart's attachment to a thing. Only the light of certainty expands the breast, and one is freed from shirk only by the light of tawhid. At this point God takes him under His care."

Al-Wasiti said: "Except that they are associators" refers to attending to thoughts and movements.

When Allah the Exalted had informed of their entanglement in the snares of their shirk, and that they turn a blind eye to the proofs in this world, and since the general, indefinite command and prohibition, exhortation and admonition addressed to all of them, while they were immersed in their heedlessness, were most of the time definitively decisive about their not believing, and since some people were like the donkey that does not submit except through punishment, Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Do they then feel secure﴾, a rebuke with the meaning of reproach and threat, ﴿that there may come upon them an overwhelming (ghashiyah) [calamity]﴾, that is, something that covers them, settles upon them and encompasses them, ﴿from the punishment of Allah﴾, that is, He to whom belongs all command in this world, as has come in Our mention of their stories from the nations.

Since the intelligent person ought to be wary of every possibility, even if it is not close, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Or the Hour comes upon them﴾, and He pointed to the most severe form of this upon hearts by His saying: ﴿suddenly (baghtah)﴾, that is, while they are in the utmost heedlessness of it, not expecting it at all. Al-Rummani said: Yazid ibn Muqsim al-Thaqafi said:

"But they departed, and I did not know of it suddenly, and the most dreadful thing is when the sudden (al-bagt) comes upon you."

Since this meaning is terrifying, Allah emphasized it by His saying: ﴿while they do not perceive (la yash'urun)﴾, that is, not even a kind of perception, even if it were as slight as a hair, to inform of the intensity of their ignorance, in that their state is that of one who is in the utmost security from what, at the least of its conditions, is possible. For perception (shu'ur) is the apprehension of a thing through something subtle, like the fineness of a hair. I said it is an emphasis because it carries the meaning of suddenness (al-baghtah). Abu Bakr al-Zubaydi said in Mukhtasar al-'Ayn: al-baghtah is sudden onset (al-mufaja'ah). Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qazzaz said in his Diwan: "I surprised the man with a surprise (mufajaʼah)," meaning when you come upon him heedlessly, catching him unawares. Then he said: "And I surprised him with a surprise," meaning when you meet him and he does not perceive you. In Tartib al-Muhkam: fajiahu al-amr [wa-fajaahu] and faja'ahu mufaja'ah: it came upon him without his perceiving it, and this entails haste, which is the core of this root. It also entails al-taghab, with the first letter (ta') vowelled as a fatha... [note: the text reads "بِتَقْدِيمِ المُثَنّاةِ مُحَرِّكًا" — rendered as:] with the dotted letter (ta') placed first and vowelled, and it is ruin (al-halak), because it is the closest thing to a person, since it is the original state at the time of the incident (al-hadath), while safety in it is al-'ajab. Al-taghab also means filth and grime, and taghiba (with kasra on the ghayn) means a defect arose in it, and it is said of drought: taghbah (with fatha). Al-taghb (with sukun) means ugliness and suspicion. All of these reach a person more quickly than their opposites, except for those whom Allah protects, and this is only because this abode is built upon it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 108:

When God, glorified is He, described to the Prophet (ﷺ) the majority of people and what He described of their bad way of blind imitation (taqlid), whose source is turning away from the proofs that necessitate knowledge, He commanded that the way of the sincere ones be mentioned. So He said: ﴿Say﴾, that is, O highest of creation, purest of them, and greatest of them in counsel and sincerity: ﴿This﴾, that is, this call to God according to what the Book of God and His Sunna (ﷺ) call to, ﴿is my way﴾, the path that is easy to reach, clear in its matter, exalted in its station, and very broad and evident. It is as if it were said: What is it? So He said: ﴿I call﴾ everyone whose call is valid, ﴿to God﴾, who possesses all perfection, while I am ﴿upon insight﴾, that is, upon clear evidence from my own consideration of decisive proofs and manifest demonstrations, and abandoning imitation, which indicates dullness and stubbornness. This is because insight is the knowledge by which truth is distinguished from falsehood, in religion and in worldly affairs, to the extent that one seems to see the meaning with the eye.

Since the position is of the utmost nobility, the hidden pronoun was emphasized to specify and to draw attention to the fitness for leadership (imamah) to appear. So He said: ﴿I and whoever﴾, that is, and whoever likewise calls, ﴿follows me﴾, not like one who is in blindness, straying from the aim, bewildered in the error of imitation, who remains heedless, a target for calamities. The following (ittiba') is the seeker of the second to catch up with the first, to agree with him in his place or in his matter that he calls to. Among what enters under "Say," as a conjunction with "I call," is His saying, noting that the condition of every call to Him, glorified is He, is that it be accompanied by declaring Him free of every trace of deficiency: ﴿And glory be to God﴾ (p-243), that is, and I glorify Him who is singled out with the attributes of perfection, with glorification (subhan), that is, I estimate Him as He truly deserves, so I affirm for Him what befits His majesty of attributes of perfection, and I declare Him free of what is exalted above Him, with a declaration by which those who know will recognize that it befits His majesty and is pleasing to Him. In singling out God with this after what He affirmed for Himself and for His followers there is an allusion to attributing deficiency to them out of humility, and an apology for what weakness befalls them, and a request for pardon for it. ﴿And I am not﴾, and He turned away from "mushrikan" (a associator) to something more emphatic, so He said: ﴿of the polytheists﴾, that is, among those who associate anything with Him in any way, because by the insight He has given me I know that He is described with the descriptions of perfection, declared free of the marks of deficiency, exalted above them, and that this is the first obligation, because He is the One who is高 exalted above likeness (mujanasah), the Subduer to whom everything is subject to His will. "Subhan" has been explained by what preceded, because the root s-b-h, in every arrangement, revolves around measure, strength, and expansiveness. Sometimes it is restricted to sufficiency, and from it comes ḥasab: the measure of a thing. Sometimes it is restricted to sufficiency, which implies restriction, and from it comes aḥsabanī al-shay', meaning it sufficed me; iḥtisab al-ajr, meaning being content with it; al-ḥisab, meaning knowing the measure; and al-ḥasab in the sense of supposing also returns to that. Al-aḥsab is one whose skin turned white from a disease and whose hair decayed (p-244), in the sense that this disease sufficed him in corruption against every other disease, as if nothing remained that could accommodate another disease with it. Al-tahsib is shrouding with what suffices the dead, and it is a sufficiency for him that he needs nothing after it. From it comes al-ḥabs, which is prevention from exceeding sufficiency. Sufficiency may be exceeded, so it swims and its range expands and is not confined. From it comes al-ḥasab, with a vowel on the ḥa', which is nobility. From it comes al-saḥb, and by it the cloud (saḥab) was named because of its spreading out in the air. From it comes al-sabḥ in water, and a horse extending its forelegs in running. Al-subḥah is voluntary prayer, because it has no limit confining it, and because it exceeds the obligatory. Al-sabḥ is free time, because with it one has the capacity for expansion. Al-tasbih is declaring God free of deficiency, because it is distancing from deficiency. Al-Rummani said: its origin is disassociation from a thing. Ibn Makhtum said, in combining al-'Ubab and al-Muḥkam: "Subhan Allah" means declaring God free from partners and offspring, and clearing Him of evil. This is its meaning in the language, and the report from the Prophet (ﷺ) came with this. Sibawayh said: Abu al-Khattab claimed that "Subhan Allah" is like your saying "barā'at Allāh min al-sū'" (God's freedom from evil), as if he were saying: "clear the freedom of God from evil." He claimed that a similar thing is the saying of al-A'sha (p-245):

I say, when his boasting came to me: "Glory be to Him who humbled him, the boaster!"

That is, a disassociation from him. By this he inferred that subhan is a definite noun, for if it were indefinite it would be declined. He said: It has come in poetry with nunation as an indefinite, Umayyah said:

"Glory be to Him, then glory returns to Him, and before us the Judi and the flood glorified."

Ibn Jinni said: subhan is a proper name for the meaning of disassociation and declaration of freedom, in the position of 'Uthman and Himran; in subhan are gathered definiteness and the alif and nun, and both are causes preventing declension. End of quote. Al-Zajjaj said: it came from the Prophet (ﷺ) that his saying "Subhan Allah" is clearing God of evil, and the people of language say so as well, without knowing what is in it from the narration from the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: but they agree on its interpretation. The man "sabbaha" (glorified): he said "Subhan Allah." In the revelation: ﴿Each has known its prayer and its glorification﴾ [al-Nur: 41]. Sabbaha is a dialect form of sabaha. Tha'lab reported: sabbaha (tasbih and subhan). Ibn Sidah said: in my view, subhanan is not a verbal noun of sabbaha; it is only the verbal noun of sabbaha (p-246). Al-Nadr said: "Subhan Allah" means hastening toward Him and lightness in obeying Him. Sabuhah (with a fatha on the sin) is the sacred land. Sabbah is the smooth ground near the mine of the Banu Sulaym. Sabahat of God's face are His lights. Al-subhah is supplication, and also voluntary prayer. End of quote. All of this returns to distancing from evil. Al-subhan is the self, and everyone clears himself and raises himself above evil.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 12, verse 109:

When the refutation of what they (the disbelievers) had captiously raised by their saying, "Why has not a treasure been sent down to him?", became clear, He followed it with what makes clear their captiousness in their saying, ﴿Or an angel should accompany him﴾ [Hud: 12], by mentioning the messengers and the people of the straight path, who call to God with insight. So He said: ﴿And We did not send﴾, that is, by what We have of greatness.

Since sending messengers, because of its nobility, cannot be achieved in every age according to what wisdom has decreed, just as not everyone is fit for prophethood, and since the context was to deny support by an angel in His saying ﴿or an angel should accompany him﴾ [Hud: 12], as in the surah of al-Nahl, and not to deny the prophethood of humans, He introduced the preposition as an alert to this, and said: ﴿from before you﴾, that is, to those who are charged (with religious duties), ﴿except men﴾ (p. 247), that is, like you, a man, not angels nor females, as Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said. The word "rajul" (man) is derived from "al-mashy 'ala al-rijl" (walking on foot). ﴿To whom We revealed﴾, that is, through the mediation of the angels, just as revelation is sent to you, ﴿from the people of the towns﴾, just as you are from the people of the towns. That is, the places built of clay and stone and the like, because they are prepared for residence, gathering, and the coming of people of virtues, and that is more fitting for abundance of intellect, soundness of judgment, sharpness of mind, and the generation of knowledge than the desert. Mecca is the "Mother of the Towns" in this respect, because it is a gathering place for all creatures, due to what they were commanded concerning the pilgrimage to the House, and all the Arabs used to come to it. Al-Rummani said: al-Hasan said: God never sent a prophet from the people of the desert, nor from the jinn, nor from women. End of quote.

That is because cities are the places of wisdom, and deserts are the abodes for the manifestation of the word. Since Mecca, or the towns, is a city, and yet it is in the land of the desert, it combined both matters and attained both traits, because the one to whom it was sent combines all that was dispersed among the other messengers, and is the seal of all the prophets, may God's blessings be upon him and upon all of them.

The root "qura" (q-r-y), with its forms with yā' and with wāw, hamzated and unhamzated, in its fifteen permutations, revolves around gathering and requires holding fast, and perhaps the opposite of dispersal is derived from it. So "al-qaryah" (with fatḥah, and kasrah is also possible) is the metropolis that gathers (people). "Aqra" means he remained in the town. "Al-qari" is its inhabitant. "Al-qārriyyah" is the gathering capital. There is a green bird, either because it stays (in one place) or because its color gathers the sight. "Al-qaryatayn" (the two towns), a dual form, and the most common pronunciation of it is with yā': Mecca and al-Ta'if. "Qaryat al-namal" is the gathering of its soil. "Qaraytu al-ma' fi al-hawd" means I gathered the water in the pool. "Al-miqra'" is something like a pool, and any place in which water gathers. "Al-qari" is gathered water. "Al-mudda taqarra fi al-jurh" means the pus gathers in the wound. "Al-qawari" are witnesses, because they gather matters, and "al-qawari" are righteous people, as if it were a softened form of the hamzated word. "Qaraytu al-dayf qira" (with kasrah and short vowel, or with fatḥah and long vowel) means I hosted the guest, like "iqtaraytuhu". "Al-miqra'" is the bowl in which the guest is hosted. "Al-maqari" are cooking pots. "Qara al-ba'ir" and everything that ruminates: he gathers the cud in its jaw. "Qarat al-naqah": its two jaws swelled from toothache, as if it cannot, with that, gather the cud, so this is from the privative. "Qara al-bilad": he followed them, going out from land to land, like "iqtarāhā" and "istaqrāhā", because he gathers them together. "Qariya al-ma'": its channel from the hillsides, or its place from the hill to the meadow, because it is the place of its gathering. "Qura al-khayl": a valley, as if they gathered in it. "Al-qaryah", like "ghaniyyah", is a staff, because the herdsman gathers with it what he herds, and with it he gathers whatever is wanted to be gathered. "A'wād fīhā fard": a piece in which the top of the tent pole is placed, because with it the tent is raised and gathers whom one wants. "'Ūd al-shirā'" is the one on its breadth at its top, because it gathers the sail, folded and spread. "Qaraytu al-saḥīfah" is a dialect form of "qara'tuhā": when I recited it, I gathered its knowledge and its words. "Al-qārriyyah": the lower end of the spear, because it gathers its point, or its upper part, because it gathers its height, or the edge of the spear, because it gathers the aim of its owner; likewise the edge of the sword. "Al-qārriyyah", with shaddah, is a green bird; when they see it they rejoice at rain, as if it were the messenger of rain or the forerunner of the clouds; its plural is "qawārī". It was perhaps named so because it is the cause of gathering the concern for rain. "Al-qīr" and "al-qār" are a black substance with which ships, camels, pots, and jugs are smeared, or they are both pitch (zift). On every interpretation, it fills the cracks and pores, so it was the binder between the parts of the ship and other things. "Hādhā aqyar min hādhā": "this is more bitter", a comparison with the taste of pitch, and "al-murr" (bitterness) also gathers the mouth toward it by contraction. "Al-qayyūr", like "tannūr", is one of obscure lineage; it was also likened to that because pitch, when most people's need for it in many times became little, became little mentioned, and this is the meaning of obscurity. "Al-qayyār", like "shaddād", is the owner of pitch. There is a well of the Banu 'Ijl near Wasit, and perhaps it was named for gathering them. "Qayyār" is the name of a horse, as if because of its excellence it gathers for its owner what he wants. "Al-qārrah" is the bear, likewise. "Al-qārrah" is also a tribe of the Arabs; they were named so because Ibn al-Shaddākh wanted to disperse them among Kinanah, so their poet said:

"We called a qārrah; do not startle us, so that we startle like the startling of the ostrich."

The abridgment of al-'Ayn mentioned it here, and others mentioned it under the letter wāw. "Iqtāra al-ḥadīth iqtiyāran" means he searched into it, because that is a cause of gathering it.
