"Al-qayr", like "hayyin", is the best archers' arrows, because with them one gathers what one wants. "Raqaytu al-rajul" with fatḥah, "ruqyah", means I invoked protection over him and blew into his charm, because the one who recites gathers his saliva and blows. "Raqaytu fī al-shay' raqyan", when I climbed upon it, as if you gathered between its steps. "Al-murqāh", with fatḥah or kasrah, is a step, because height is among the traces of gathering. "Raqqā 'alayhi kalāman tarqiyyah" means he raised it, because he gathered it upon it. "Muraqqiyan al-anf" means its two sides, because they are the two gatherers of it. "Al-rā'iq min al-mā'" is the pure water, because when it becomes pure its parts stick firmly together, the turbidity that used to be mixed among them having disappeared. "Rāq al-mā' yurīq" means it poured out, either because it gathered at the place where it poured, or it is from the privative, like "arāqahu", meaning "ṣabbahu" (poured it). "Rāqa al-sarāb yurīqu" and "turīqu yatarayyaq", when it spread out flat over the ground, that is, it moved about, either from the privative, or as a comparison with what is gathered. "Al-rayq" is the movement of water over the surface of the ground in a thin layer, because it does not move except when it is gathered. "Al-rayq" is also the first and best of every thing, from "al-rā'iq" in the sense of "al-khāliṣ" (pure), and because the first gathers others to it, and the best gathers what is wanted. "Al-rayq" also means falsehood, like "al-ruyūq" with "tannūr", a comparison with the mirage. "Rīq al-fam" (saliva) is well known, because it gathers. "Al-rayq" also means strength, because it gathers what is wanted. "Al-rayq al-rā'iq" means the pure, and everything eaten or drunk on an empty stomach, and the one who has nothing in his hand, as if he were freed from attachments, so that his concern is gathered. "Man huwa 'alā al-rīq", like "rīqī", like "kayyis", and he "yurīq bi-nafsihi", that is, he gives it up at death, from "rāqa al-mā'", poured out. "Al-murīq", like "mu'ẓam", is one whom something never ceases to please; perhaps he is one whom it pleases, "yarūquhu", when it pleases him, so he gathers his concern toward it. "Al-yāriq" is a kind of bracelet, because it gathers the wrist. "Al-yaraqān", with sukūn, means uprightness and a path, and a blight on crops, and a known disease. It will be mentioned under "araqq" at the beginning of surah al-Hijr, God willing, Most High.

Since reflection upon the states of those who passed away is, for salvation from what befell them, the most important of the important matters, He interposed an exhortation to it between the goal and what it relates to, so He said: ﴿Have they not traveled﴾, that is, let these deniers cause travel ﴿in the land﴾, that is, in this kind that is true of little and much. Since the intended travel was the travel of reflection, He made the next clause its consequence, saying ﴿and see﴾, that is, immediately following their travel and by means of it, and He alerted that this is a great matter that deserves concern in inquiring about it, by mentioning the interrogative particle, so He said ﴿how was the end﴾, that is, the final outcome of ﴿those who﴾. Since those whose condition is to be taken as a lesson, because of the great matters that befell them, were in some past times, and the addressees of this Qur'an cannot encompass all the people of the earth, though in the condition of each of them there is a lesson, He brought the preposition and said ﴿before them﴾, in contentment with their desires, in imitating their fathers. This is as was mentioned earlier in [the surah of Yunus], that the signs [do not suffice] for one whose heart God has sealed, and the reminder of the states of those who passed away, of the destruction of the sinners and the salvation of the obedient, and the interposition between that of His saying ﴿Say: "Wait, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ [Yunus: 102], which indicates that He, Most High, is angry with whoever turns away from reflecting on His signs. Travel (al-sayr) is movement that extends in a direction, and from it comes "akhdh al-sayr" (the taking of a route) and "akhdh al-suyūr" (the taking of thongs from leather). Looking (al-nazar) is the seeking of comprehension of a meaning by the eye or the heart, and its origin is facing a thing with sight in order to perceive it.

Since it is possible that one whose insight is obliterated might claim that they had some good kind, He said, in the manner of giving free rein: ﴿And surely the abode﴾, that is, the Hour or the condition, ﴿of the Hereafter﴾, that is, which has been alerted to by matters beyond counting, ﴿is better than the abode of this world, for there is no world except with its nearness﴾ ﴿for those who fear God﴾, that is, fear moved them to make obedience and restraint a shield against a life whose least end is death, even if it were supposed, in that case, as an impossibility, that it extended a thousand years, and its whole life was pleasant without pains.

Since accepting this does not require more than reason, He said, as a consequence of it, [rejecting] against them, rebuking them: ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾, that is, so that they would follow the caller to this straightest path.

[p. 254] Since the meaning is clear from this context, its implied sense is: the messengers called the men to God and strove to warn their people so that they might be saved from wretchedness. They threatened them, on God's behalf, with various kinds of punishment if they did not follow them. The matter dragged on for them, and help was delayed, while their people denied these threats, rebuked them, and mocked them. This continued as their situation and the situation of their people went on. Referring to this, He says: ﴿Until, when the messengers despaired﴾, that is, they despaired of help with a great despair, as if they had brought that despair into being or sought it and invited it from within themselves. ﴿And they thought that they had been lied to﴾, that is, they behaved in the manner of despair, a great despair, that suspects a promise has been broken, turning away from warning, good tidings, and answering those who mocked them and said: "What is holding back what you have promised us?" (They reasoned) that this matter is up to God: if He wills, He will fulfil it, and if He wills, He will delay it, and they have no share in His affair. It is also possible that the meaning is that they were slow to see the help and grew impatient at what they suffered from the enemies' harm and the allies' delay, ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him said﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:214], as the one in despair says, ﴿When will God's help come?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:214], although they knew that God, exalted is He, may do whatever He wills. He expressed their state with what is mentioned here.

Al-Zamakhshari in *al-Kashshaf* and al-Razi in *al-Lawami'* transmitted this meaning from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. This is on the reading with the light form (*takhfif*). As for the reading with the doubled form (*tashdid*), the sense is: "and they thought that their followers had lied to them." 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, indeed denied the reading with the light form. Al-Bukhari in the *Tafsir* section and others narrated from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that he asked her about the recitation: "Is it with the doubled form or the light form?" She said: "It is with the doubled form." He said: "I said: 'But they were certain that their people had denied them, so it is not a matter of assumption.'" She said: "Indeed, by my life, they were certain of that!" I said to her: "Then what about 'and they thought that they had been lied to'?" That is, with the light form. She said: "God forbid! The messengers did not assume that about their Lord." I said: "Then what is this verse?" She said: "They are the followers of the messengers who believed in their Lord and affirmed them. The trial lasted long for them and help was delayed from them, until, when the messengers despaired of those among their people who had denied them, and they thought that their followers had lied to them, God's help came to them at that moment."

﴿Our help came to them﴾ to destroy their enemies. ﴿So whomever We willed was delivered﴾ from among them and from among their enemies. ﴿And Our might is not turned back﴾, that is, Our punishment, because of its greatness, ﴿from the people﴾, that is, even if they were at the height of strength, ﴿the criminals﴾, those whom We have decreed will remain in severance, as We said: ﴿Verily, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them﴾ [Hud 11:8], and as We have established the fate of those among the nations whom We mentioned. All of this is an announcement that His custom proceeds in such a way that He prolongs the test and extends the time of trial and admonition, to urge the followers to patience and to restrain the deniers from persisting in mockery.

[p. 256] The root *k-dh-b* ("to lie") revolves around that which has no reality, and most of its derivatives are clear on this. It is also used for things other than humans. They said: the lightning lied, the dream lied, hope lied, desire lied, and assumption lied. The eye lied: its perception deceived it. He lied about the opinion: the matter became clear contrary to what it really was. His soul lied to him: it desired what was not the truth. And *al-kadhub* means the soul for this reason. The she-camel *akdhabat* and *kadhabat*, when the stallion mounted her, and she raised her tail (*fa-tashulu*), then returned barren, because she failed the expectation of her pregnancy. Likewise when she is thought to have milk but has none. It is said of someone who is shouted at while he is still and thinks he is asleep: "He has been lied to (*qad akdhaba*)," meaning that shout is counted as nothing. The *makdhuba* among women is the weak one, because weakness of womanhood and weakness of her own nature combined in her, so she is counted as nothing. The *makdhuba* by inversion is the righteous woman, as if, because righteousness is rare among women, she is made into nothing. The wild animal *kadhaba* when it runs and then stops to look at what is behind it, as if it did not believe what had frightened it. From this comes *kadhaba 'an kadhā*, when one withdraws from something after wanting it, or because he lied about (*kadhaba*) what he expected in the charge of killing his rivals. *Kadhabaka al-hajj* means it made it possible for you (to perform it). *Kadhabaka al-sayd* is similar, and it leads to exhortation, because the meaning is that the pilgrimage, due to its great hardship and long distance, repels the soul from it, so it is almost not found; likewise the hunt, because of its intense flight, swift escape, and difficulty of settling, one almost cannot obtain it, so its hunting is like a lie with no reality. It has now become clear what the reason is for *kadhaba* carrying the sense of urging (*al-ighra'*). It is evident that his saying: "Three journeys *kadhabna* upon you: the pilgrimage, the lesser pilgrimage, and the holy war," means that because of their great difficulty they hardly let one who wants them attain them, yet because of the strength of one's motive, given the many incentives of reward mentioned concerning them, he becomes like one who has already achieved them. This is supported by what Ibn al-Athir said in *al-Nihaya* from al-Akhfash: "*al-hajj* is in the nominative, but its meaning is accusative, because he intends to command him to perform the pilgrimage, just as one says: 'The hunt made it possible for you (*amkanaka al-sayd*),' meaning: shoot it." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi [p. 258] said about the argument in the verse of 'Antara:

*Kadhaba al-'atiq wa-ma' shann barid*
*in kunti sa'ilati ghabuqan fadh-habi*

"The old wine has lied, and cold water from a waterskin—
if you are asking me for a midday drink, then go away."

And if you wish, you may say: since the word has been used much in urging someone toward a thing and prompting him to seek and attain it, it became as if he had said to her: "Take the old wine," meaning: "Keep to it." He does not intend negation, but rather turning her away from anything else. So *al-'atiq* in meaning is an object if its form is nominative, like "*salamun 'alaykum*" and similar expressions intended as supplication, while the form is nominative. Muhammad ibn al-Sarri, may God have mercy on him, transmitted from some scholars of the language regarding "*kadhaba al-'atiq*" that Mudar puts it in the accusative and Yemen puts it in the nominative, and the reason for that has already been mentioned. That is the end of the quotation. Closer to this, and easier to grasp and take, is that a person remains protected in his honour and guarded in his veil as long as he is bound to truthfulness; when he lies, he has made himself available, and his matter has become lowly. So the meaning of "three journeys *kadhabna* upon you" is: they made themselves available to you. The pilgrimage every year, since the obstacle of the disbelievers to it has been removed; the lesser pilgrimage every part of the year, since the corrupters have been removed by killing and otherwise in the sacred months; and the holy war also every part of the year, since it is permitted in the sacred months and other months. The derivation of similar expressions such as "*kadhabatka al-zahà'ir*" and others on this basis is clear, and there is no hesitation in it. And since the liar hastens to excuses and tries to escape, the expression [here] belongs to the category of urging, that is, he seized the opportunity and hastened before this possibility became difficult.

(p-260) When He, glory be to Him, had mentioned these narratives as they were, and urged reflection upon them through His saying ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth?﴾ [Yusuf: 109], and indicated that by this He has carried out His custom even though the span of time be long, He followed it with the affirmation that in their accounts there is the greatest lesson. So He said, urging reflection upon them and insight through them: ﴿Indeed there was﴾ [i.e., a existence that is at the utmost possibility] ﴿in their stories﴾, that is, in the great report that is recited to you, following the reports of the Messengers, whose trials lengthened until they despaired, from Nuh to Yusuf and those after him, upon all of them be the best of blessings, peace, greeting and honour, ﴿a lesson﴾, that is, a great admonition and a noble reminder, ﴿for people of understanding﴾, that is (p-260) for people of pure intellects, free from the impurities of turbidity, by which they pass over to what makes them happy, through the knowledge that whoever is able to do what He has narrated of the matter of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and others, is able to honour Muhammad (ﷺ), exalt his word and grant him victory over whoever opposes him, whoever he may be, as He did with Yusuf and others, along with other lessons that their stories guide to, in wisdom, and the precious lessons to which they return. "Qisas" (narratives) means the report of things that follow one another, from qassa al-athar (to trace the track). "Al-albab" means intellects, because the intellect is the most precious and noblest thing in a human being.

Since the benefit of this lesson lies in affirming with certainty the truth of the Qur'an, because of the realities of their conditions, the hidden aspects of their affairs and the fine details of their reports that it has set forth in these wonderful methods, clear details and miraculous, overpowering approaches, He drew attention to this by presupposing a question, and said: ﴿It is not﴾, that is, this Arabic Qur'an, which includes their stories and other matters, ﴿a narration that is invented﴾, as the obstinate ones said, referred to by His saying: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾. "Iftira" (invention) means asserting a meaning contrary to what it actually is in reporting about it, from faraytu al-adim (I cut the hide). ﴿But rather it is a confirmation of what was﴾ among the Books and others ﴿before it﴾, that is, prior to it, which is sufficient as testimony to its truthfulness and its being true in itself, ﴿and an elaboration of all things﴾, that is, of what is needed in matters of religion, the world and the Hereafter. "Tafsil" (elaboration) means separating a whole by giving each category its due. ﴿And a guidance and a mercy﴾, and a clarification and honour. Since the one who does not benefit from a thing is not connected to anything of it, He said: ﴿for a people who believe﴾, that is, belief occurs from them, and although it is in the sense of "their belief is possible," it is general. Whatever combines these qualities is the clearest of clarifications. Thus this last point corresponds to the beginning of the surah, in that it is the Clear Book, and it corresponds to what follows these narratives, namely the testimony to the truth of the Qur'an, that the Messengers were not angels [nor were there angels with them] to confirm it appearing to people, and that they did not ask any wage for conveying the message, in accordance with the cause that these narratives followed, which is the meaning of His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿Perhaps you would leave out some of what is revealed to you﴾ [Hud: 12], the verse about their saying ﴿Why has a treasure not been sent down to him, or an angel not come with him?﴾ [Hud: 12], and their saying [that] he "invented it," in order of that, with this last one embracing the first that precedes it. So glory be to Him who sent it down as a miraculous, overpowering proof, and as a judge with the truth that never ceases to be manifest. And how could it not be so, for He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. And God, glory be to Him and exalted, knows best.
